prompt: Write a tragic love story about a lord's daughter falling in love with a servant.

outline.name: The House on the Hill
outline.description: Introduce rain-soaked Valedorn, Greyfen Manor, and the declining House Vey. Lady Elianor observes the estate’s debts, hungry tenants, overworked servants, and her father Lord Alric’s desperate attempts to preserve their lineage. Though treated as a privileged daughter, she feels trapped by the obligations attached to her birth. Alric announces that her marriage to the wealthy Lord Caelan Arbridge is the family’s only hope, establishing the central conflict between duty, compassion, and personal freedom.

outline.name: A Favorable Match
outline.description: Elianor meets Lord Caelan formally at Greyfen. He is polished, intelligent, and courteous in a way that reveals his sense of ownership rather than affection. During negotiations, Caelan makes clear that marriage will give him control over Greyfen’s debts, land, and household. Elianor privately challenges her father about the arrangement, but Alric argues that refusing would ruin the estate and deprive every servant and tenant of protection. Elianor accepts the betrothal, concealing her dread beneath perfect composure.

outline.name: The Falconer’s Son
outline.description: Elianor begins escaping the manor’s suffocating routines by walking in the neglected woods. There she encounters Tomas Vale, the head falconer’s son, who reacts warily to her presence while tending an injured goshawk in an abandoned forester’s lodge. Their conversation is tense: Elianor offers medicine from the manor, while Tomas refuses to flatter her and points out the suffering her family’s authority has caused. Despite their differences, she returns the next day with linen and food, beginning an uneasy connection.

outline.name: Willow Splints
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas work together to treat the goshawk’s broken wing. Their practical cooperation allows them to speak more freely. Tomas explains the risks faced by servants and tenants, including his mother’s death after eviction from a Vey cottage. Elianor admits that privilege has left her isolated and unable to choose her own life. Tomas remains suspicious of her motives, but her willingness to listen begins to change his opinion. Their secret meetings become a recurring refuge.

outline.name: The Shape of Rain
outline.description: As the goshawk slowly recovers, Elianor and Tomas grow closer through stolen hours in the woods. They share food, a cloak, memories, and small confessions. Elianor sees Tomas’s pride and tenderness beneath his guarded manner, while Tomas recognizes that her compassion is more than aristocratic sentiment. Their attraction becomes impossible to deny, though both understand the danger. A near-discovery by a passing groom forces them to separate abruptly and reminds them that their refuge is not safe.

outline.name: The First Flight
outline.description: The goshawk attempts its first flight after its recovery, symbolizing the possibility of freedom that neither lover can yet claim. Tomas and Elianor celebrate beneath the trees, and their restraint finally breaks into a kiss. They acknowledge that their love is forbidden and cannot be made respectable by secrecy. Elianor returns to Greyfen changed, struggling to perform her duties while carrying the memory of the kiss. Tomas warns her that discovery could cost him his life, but neither can bring themselves to end the meetings.

outline.name: Ledgers and Debts
outline.description: The financial crisis at Greyfen worsens. Alric reviews debt ledgers with Elianor and reveals that Caelan can call in the family’s obligations unless the marriage proceeds quickly. Elianor discovers that several tenants are being forced into unpaid labor to compensate for the estate’s losses. She attempts to persuade her father to reduce rents, but he insists that weakness will invite seizure by stronger lords. Caelan arrives to supervise the negotiations, observing Elianor and Tomas from a distance and beginning to suspect their relationship.

outline.name: A Courtesy of Chains
outline.description: Caelan begins exerting control without openly breaking etiquette. He recommends changes to Greyfen’s accounts, dismisses a groom, and offers to take responsibility for managing the estate after the wedding. In private, he questions Elianor about her absences and subtly reminds her that her father’s survival depends on obedience. Tomas notices Caelan watching him and becomes more guarded. Caelan threatens Tomas’s father through an accusation of theft, making clear that the entire household can be punished for one servant’s presumed insolence.

outline.name: The Housekeeper’s Message
outline.description: Tomas meets Mara Quill, a former Greyfen housekeeper who now carries messages among tenant and laborer resistance groups. She explains that nobles across Valedorn are using debt, forced labor, and manipulated courts to seize land. Tomas is tempted by the movement’s promise of dignity, though he fears that rebellion will endanger Elianor. Mara argues that private love cannot survive a public system built on ownership. Tomas agrees to carry a message, beginning his involvement while keeping it secret from Elianor.

outline.name: The Cost of Silence
outline.description: Elianor learns that a village family has been expelled from its cottage after failing to meet a labor demand. She confronts Alric and discovers that he approved the eviction to satisfy Caelan’s creditors. Her father insists that every harsh decision is meant to preserve Greyfen and protect its people from a worse fate. Elianor sees how fear has made him complicit. When she meets Tomas, he challenges her to decide whether sympathy without action is simply another form of silence. Their disagreement briefly wounds their intimacy.

outline.name: The Rebel Road
outline.description: Tomas travels with Mara through the marsh villages and witnesses the breadth of noble exploitation. He meets discharged soldiers, tenant leaders, and laborers preparing to resist. The rebels plan to seize or destroy ledgers proving illegal debts and land seizures. Tomas returns to Greyfen torn between the movement’s purpose and his attachment to Elianor. He tells her only that unrest is spreading, and she realizes he is keeping a dangerous part of his life from her. Their trust becomes strained by unequal risks and concealed loyalties.

outline.name: Winter Betrothal
outline.description: Lord Alric publicly announces that Elianor and Caelan will marry before spring. Preparations force Elianor into elaborate fittings, social visits, and rehearsals of obedience. Caelan privately promises that Tomas and his father may retain employment if Elianor behaves, but he implies that after the wedding the household will be reorganized under his authority. Elianor understands that her marriage may preserve Greyfen only by surrendering it. She asks Alric to guarantee the servants’ safety, and he accepts without grasping the personal cost of the request.

outline.name: The Assassin’s Question
outline.description: Mara reveals that Caelan will gather regional lords at Greyfen to finalize the transfer of Vey lands and coordinate reprisals against suspected rebels. The resistance faction demands that Tomas assassinate Caelan during the gathering. Tomas refuses to become a murderer, even though Mara argues that Caelan’s death could prevent the crushing of the rebellion. She warns that Caelan has already ordered raids and that Elianor will not be safe within his household. Tomas leaves uncertain whether restraint is moral courage or cowardice.

outline.name: A Bargain with Winter
outline.description: Elianor decides to accept the marriage in the belief that she can protect Greyfen’s dependents through compromise. She tells Tomas she will marry Caelan and asks him to understand that she is sacrificing herself for the household. Tomas is devastated, hearing only that she has chosen privilege over him. Their argument exposes the limits of both their ideals: Elianor trusts negotiation with men who have never honored it, while Tomas trusts rebellion that may demand blood. They part angrily, though their love remains unmistakable.

outline.name: The Last Hunting Season
outline.description: The manor prepares for the wedding while winter storms isolate Greyfen. Elianor attempts to use her remaining authority to improve rations and delay evictions, but Caelan counters each effort through debt claims and his influence over Alric. Tomas learns from stable hands that Caelan intends to dismiss many Vey servants after the marriage. He and Mara begin planning an escape route through the woods and marsh. Elianor finds Tomas again, and their anger gives way to a fragile reconciliation.

outline.name: Beyond the Marsh
outline.description: Tomas proposes that he and Elianor flee before the wedding, cross the marsh, and reach a rebel safehouse beyond the border. Elianor fears abandoning the servants and tenants, but Tomas argues that remaining will make them both instruments of Caelan’s power. For one night they imagine a difficult life together without titles or estates. They share a final tender night in the forester’s lodge and promise to meet there before dawn. Unknown to them, Caelan has begun pressuring members of the household for information.

outline.name: The Betrayal
outline.description: Elianor secretly leaves Greyfen in plain clothing and reaches the lodge, where Tomas is waiting with provisions and a route through the marsh. Before they can depart, soldiers surround the building. Their escape has been betrayed by a frightened servant coerced by Caelan, though the betrayer’s identity remains uncertain. Tomas tries to lead Elianor away while surrendering himself, but both are captured. The failed flight destroys their hope of remaining hidden and gives Caelan the evidence he needs to control the entire Vey household.

outline.name: A Public Shame
outline.description: Caelan stages a public hearing in Greyfen’s courtyard, presenting Tomas as a trespasser and would-be abductor while exposing Elianor’s relationship to humiliate her. Alric, terrified of losing the estate, cannot defend his daughter openly. Tomas is beaten and sentenced to hang for violating noble property and attempting to flee with a lady. Elianor is confined to her rooms until the wedding. Caelan expects scandal to make her submissive, but his cruelty convinces her that every compromise has only strengthened him.

outline.name: The Locked Room
outline.description: Confined in her rooms, Elianor reflects on the choices that brought her there and hears rumors of reprisals against villages connected to the rebels. She confronts Alric, demanding that he acknowledge what Caelan has done. He admits that he has surrendered authority piece by piece because he feared losing the family name. Elianor rejects his version of duty. Meanwhile, household women and stable hands begin quietly communicating with her, revealing that Tomas’s punishment has united servants who had previously feared acting.

outline.name: The Women of Greyfen
outline.description: The household women devise a plan to free Elianor from confinement, using wedding preparations, laundry passages, and a distracted guard detail. Elianor learns that rebel sympathizers are hidden among the workers arriving for the wedding and that Mara is trying to reach the estate. She must decide whether to escape alone or return to the courtyard where Tomas will die. Refusing another private sacrifice, she chooses open defiance. The servants help disguise her and arm her with proof of Caelan’s abuses from the estate records.

outline.name: The Gallows in the Rain
outline.description: On the morning of the execution, Elianor reaches the courtyard as Tomas is brought to the gallows. Before the gathered servants, tenants, and nobles, she denounces Caelan and reads evidence of illegal seizures, forced labor, and manipulated debts. Her speech transforms private fear into collective outrage. Caelan orders the guards to silence her, but the stable hands barricade the gates and the workers attack the execution party. The revolt begins within Greyfen itself.

outline.name: The Manor Breaks
outline.description: Chaos spreads through Greyfen as servants seize keys, tenants storm the stores, and rebels among the workers disarm guards. Tomas escapes and immediately helps others rather than pursuing Caelan. Elianor leads a group toward the armory and records room, using her knowledge of the manor’s hidden passages. Alric tries to stop the uprising, then witnesses Caelan’s men attacking unarmed household members and finally turns against the lord who has consumed his authority. The estate’s old hierarchy collapses in a single violent day.

outline.name: The Burning Ledgers
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas reach the records room and uncover ledgers documenting generations of debt, forced labor, and fraudulent land claims. They distribute copies to tenant representatives before setting the records ablaze. Caelan retreats toward the chapel with armed followers, intending to preserve the documents and seize Elianor as a hostage. Tomas insists on opening the manor gates so the servants can escape before confronting him. Elianor wants to remain at Tomas’s side, but he makes her promise to carry the evidence and the people to safety.

outline.name: Dawn at Greyfen
outline.description: Tomas confronts Caelan near the chapel. He refuses to kill him, declaring that the new world cannot be founded on the same ownership and vengeance that shaped the old one. Caelan shoots Tomas before being overwhelmed by the rebels. Mortally wounded, Tomas helps Elianor and the servants open the gates and escape the burning manor, collapsing only after the last prisoners are free. Lord Alric dies amid the destruction, unable to restore the order he sacrificed everything to preserve. At dawn, Elianor holds Tomas as he dies in the rain, with the healed goshawk circling overhead.

outline.name: What Remains
outline.description: After the revolt, Elianor inherits a ruined, bankrupt Greyfen while Caelan survives to face the wider rebellion and its uncertain justice. She refuses his claims, opens the manor stores, and protects servants and tenants from immediate retaliation. Over the following years, she sells portions of the estate, abolishes hereditary service on the remaining lands, and works with rebel leaders to create courts where tenants can challenge noble authority. She is condemned as a traitor by many nobles and remembered as a liberator by others. Elianor continues to mourn Tomas, honoring his request by turning grief into practical freedom rather than a monument to their love. Greyfen remains marked by rain and loss, but no longer depends on fear.

chapters.name: The House on the Hill
chapters.content:
## The House on the Hill

Rain had been falling over Valedorn for eleven days when the west wall of Greyfen Manor began to sweat salt.

It ran in pale threads beneath the portraits of dead Veys, past the carved mouths of their stone faces and down into the paneling, where the damp made the wood swell. Outside, the hill had become a dark island above the flooded fields. The road below was a brown ribbon of mud. Beyond it, the village roofs showed like wet bones, and the river had climbed over its banks to drown the lower meadows.

Lady Elianor Vey stood at the long window of the solar, holding a ledger open against the glass. The ink had blurred where the pages had been touched by wet fingers. Even so, the figures were plain enough.

Three hundred and eighty crowns owed to the Arbridge bank. Forty-two to the grain merchants of Dunmere. Wages due to the stable hands, the kitchen girls, the scullery boys, and the men who had spent the autumn dredging the choked millrace. Interest due before the first frost.

The numbers pressed upon her more heavily than the rain.

Below, in the yard, a woman waited beneath a broken cart awning with two children beside her. The elder boy wore no shoes. His feet were gray with mud, and he clutched a sack so thin that Elianor could see the shape of the few potatoes inside. A guard stood before the kitchen door, preventing them from entering.

Elianor turned from the window.

“Where is Cook?”

Her maid, Nessa, was mending a sleeve by the fire. She did not look up. “In the pantry, my lady.”

“And the woman in the yard?”

“From Lower Fen. She says the rent collector took their winter flour.”

“Then why is she waiting in the rain?”

Nessa’s needle paused. “Because there is no flour to give her.”

The answer was spoken gently, which made it worse. Elianor closed the ledger. She had been dressed for luncheon in a green wool gown that cost more than the woman’s cottage, perhaps more than everything in it. The sleeves were lined with silk. Her boots were dry. A fire warmed the room behind her, and silver gleamed upon the table though no one had eaten from it since morning.

Privilege was not a wall, she thought. It was a room with a locked door, furnished beautifully enough that one might forget to ask who stood outside.

She crossed to the bellpull, then stopped. Her father had forbidden the household to issue provisions without his seal. Yesterday he had signed away the last stores of salted beef to satisfy a creditor. The day before, he had ordered the tenants of Upper Fen to work two extra days each week repairing the estate road, though the road washed apart as quickly as they laid it.

Nessa watched her. “My lady?”

“If I send bread, will Cook obey me?”

“No.”

“Will the guard let it pass?”

“No.”

Elianor’s fingers tightened around the ledger. “Then I shall speak to Father.”

“He is with Master Pell.”

“Still?”

Nessa gave a small, humorless smile. “The debts do not sleep, my lady.”

Neither, Elianor thought, did the men who collected them.

She left the solar and walked through the manor’s central passage. Greyfen had been built to impress visitors: a vaulted hall, a stair of black oak, windows tall enough to make a person feel watched by heaven. Yet age and neglect had entered everywhere. Plaster had fallen from the ceiling above the gallery. The runner on the stairs was threadbare down the middle. In the servants’ corridor, a girl carried a basket of damp linens nearly as large as herself, while two kitchen boys hurried past with their faces gray from smoke.

At the foot of the stair, Elianor found her father’s steward, Pell, arguing with a groom.

“You cannot take the mare,” the groom was saying. “She is lame.”

“I can take whatever belongs to Lord Vey,” Pell replied. He was a narrow man with a red, irritated nose and a coat shining at the elbows. “The Arbridge men will be here tomorrow. If they see an empty stable, they will assume the worst.”

“They will see a horse that cannot stand.”

“They will see an estate that cannot pay.”

Pell noticed Elianor and bowed. The groom lowered his eyes.

“My lady. I was just explaining to Hobb that appearances must be maintained.”

“By selling a lame animal?”

“By preventing questions.”

Elianor looked at the mare in the open stall. The creature’s ribs showed beneath its coat. One hind leg trembled. “Have you asked the farrier to examine her?”

“The farrier has not been paid in six weeks.”

The words hung between them. Pell’s expression did not change, but his embarrassment seemed to deepen the damp in the passage.

“Send for him,” Elianor said.

“With what coin?”

She had no answer. Her purse contained three silver pieces and a button she had mistaken for a coin in the dark. She walked on.

The library door stood ajar. Voices came through it—her father’s, strained and low, and Master Pell’s, brisk as a knife being sharpened. Elianor paused outside.

“—cannot postpone it again,” Pell was saying. “The Arbridge note is secured against Greyfen itself.”

“I know what it is secured against.”

“And the mill. And the east pasture. If Lord Caelan calls the debt, he may take all three.”

There was a long silence.

“Not the house,” Alric said.

“Not yet.”

Elianor entered.

Lord Alric Vey sat behind a desk littered with papers, wax seals, and empty cups. He had once been a broad-shouldered man, according to the portraits, with a red beard and the fearless gaze of a soldier. Now his beard was white at the chin, and his shoulders curved as though he expected blows from the ceiling. A map of the estate lay before him, its edges held down by candlesticks. Several sections had been marked in black ink.

Her father looked from her to the ledger in her hands. “You have been examining the accounts.”

“They were left open.”

“Accounts are not a suitable occupation for you.”

“Neither is watching hungry children turned away from the kitchen.”

Pell’s eyes flicked between them. Alric dismissed him with a gesture. The steward gathered the papers he could carry and left without a word.

For a moment there was only rain striking the windows.

“Elianor,” Alric said, “you must learn that a house is not preserved by pity.”

“No. It is preserved by money.”

“And where do you suppose money comes from?”

“From the tenants who have none? From servants who go unpaid? From selling horses that cannot walk?”

His mouth tightened. “You speak as if I do not see these things.”

“Then what do you see?”

He rose too quickly, bracing himself against the desk. “I see Greyfen under my father’s name and my grandfather’s name. I see the burial stones in the chapel, the lands entrusted to us, the people who depend upon this estate. If Greyfen fails, they do not become free. They become the property of whichever lord buys the debt.”

“Perhaps they already are.”

The words escaped before she could soften them.

Alric flinched. Not from anger, but recognition.

He turned toward the window. “Your mother would have called that brave.”

“Would you?”

“I would call it dangerous.”

He stood watching the woman and her children below. The guard had moved aside; someone had finally given them a loaf, though it was small enough to fit in the boy’s hand. Elianor saw the mother bow repeatedly, gratitude and humiliation bent into the same shape.

“I have tried everything,” Alric said. “I sold the silver from the west chapel. I dismissed half the hounds. I borrowed against the mill to pay wages, then borrowed against the east pasture to repair the mill. I have written to cousins who will not answer and to merchants who answer only with terms.”

“And Lord Caelan Arbridge?”

At that name, her father’s face changed. Hope entered it, and behind hope, shame.

“He has offered a solution.”

Elianor felt the room narrow around her. “What solution?”

“He is wealthy. His holdings are untouched by the floods. His ships bring grain from the southern coast. He can settle the Arbridge note and the Dunmere debt.”

“Why would he?”

Alric did not answer immediately. He returned to his chair and lowered himself into it. “Because he wishes to join our houses.”

The rain seemed suddenly louder.

“You mean marriage.”

“I mean a union that would preserve Greyfen.”

“Mine?”

“Your marriage to Lord Caelan.”

She stared at him. Caelan was older by perhaps ten years, a distant lord whose name appeared on every letter that made her father’s hands shake. She had seen him once, years before, at a winter feast: black hair, pale eyes, a courteous smile that never reached them.

“You have already promised me.”

“I have promised nothing. He is coming tomorrow to speak formally.”

“Formally.” Elianor laughed once, without amusement. “As though he were asking to purchase a horse.”

Alric’s exhaustion hardened into irritation. “Do not make this uglier than it is.”

“It is ugly because you are asking me to marry a man so he can own what remains of us.”

“He will protect the estate.”

“He will control it.”

“Control is protection when the alternative is ruin.”

Elianor thought of the woman in the yard, the trembling mare, the servants carrying work from dawn into night. She thought of the rooms she had been raised to inherit, and how every stone seemed to demand a sacrifice from someone beneath it.

“And if I refuse?” she asked.

Alric looked at her then, fully. His eyes were not those of a lord, but of a frightened old man trying to hold a door shut against a flood.

“Then Greyfen is seized,” he said. “The tenants are evicted or bound to a new master. The servants lose their homes. Our name ends here.”

“Our name,” Elianor repeated.

“It is all I have left to give you.”

She wanted to say that she was not a vessel for a name, nor a key to a locked estate. She wanted to say that a life could not be weighed against roof beams and ancestral portraits. But through the glass, the woman from Lower Fen was leading her children away beneath the rain, carrying the little loaf under her shawl.

Elianor placed the ledger on the desk.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “I will meet Lord Caelan.”

Alric closed his eyes, as if she had granted him mercy.

She left the library before he could thank her. In the passage, the servants moved around her with lowered heads, each careful not to ask what had been decided. Greyfen Manor rose above them all, ancient and watchful, its windows glowing against the storm.

For the first time, Elianor understood that a prison did not need bars. Sometimes it had a family name above the door. Sometimes everyone inside it called the lock duty.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Elianor has just agreed to meet Lord Caelan Arbridge about a possible marriage, though she feels trapped and morally troubled by the estate’s suffering. She wants to protect the hungry tenants and overworked servants while preserving their homes, but distrusts marriage as a solution. She knows Greyfen’s major debts, the household’s deprivation, and that refusal may lead to seizure and evictions. She possesses the estate ledger and her small purse; she is physically well but emotionally distressed, angry, and resigned.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: In the library at Greyfen Manor, Alric is trying desperately to preserve House Vey, Greyfen, and the people dependent on the estate. He believes marriage between Elianor and wealthy Caelan Arbridge is the only remaining protection from ruin, though he is ashamed of the coercion involved. He knows the estate’s debts, has exhausted several resources, and fears the Vey name ending. He possesses the estate maps and debt papers; he is physically weakened and emotionally frightened, defensive, and exhausted.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: Not yet at Greyfen; Lord Caelan Arbridge is expected to arrive tomorrow for a formal marriage discussion. He is wealthy and has the power to settle the Arbridge and Dunmere debts in exchange for joining houses, giving him leverage over Greyfen. He is known to Elianor only from a prior winter feast as polished, courteous, and emotionally unreadable.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa is Elianor’s maid and confidante within the limits imposed by servant hierarchy. She knows the kitchen cannot spare provisions and understands the household’s worsening poverty. She is mending clothing and is physically well but quietly worried and practical.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell serves as Lord Alric’s steward, managing creditors and estate appearances while pressuring or dismissing workers when necessary. He knows the Arbridge note is secured against Greyfen, the mill, and east pasture, and that the estate cannot pay its obligations. He possesses the account papers and is physically well, financially anxious, and rigidly pragmatic.
Lord Alric sold the west chapel silver, dismissed half the hounds, and borrowed against the mill and east pasture to keep Greyfen operating and pay debts.
Lord Caelan Arbridge will arrive at Greyfen tomorrow for a formal discussion of his proposed marriage to Elianor.

chapters.name: A Favorable Match
chapters.content:
## A Favorable Match

Lord Caelan Arbridge arrived beneath a sky the color of pewter, with six mounted men, two wagons, and a carriage whose wheels did not sink into the mud as deeply as Greyfen’s. Elianor watched from the gallery window as the horses came up the hill. Their coats shone with rain. Their harness was black leather, oiled and polished, and the Arbridge crest—a silver heron standing in reeds—had been stitched into every saddlecloth.

Greyfen possessed no saddlecloths that matched.

“Do I look frightened?” Elianor asked.

Nessa fastened the last hook at her throat. “You look like a lady who has been told to stand still while a storm chooses which roof to take.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only honest one.”

Elianor glanced at her reflection in the spotted mirror. Her gown was blue, the color of deep water, with a narrow line of pearl at the sleeves. Her hair had been braided and pinned so severely that her face appeared sharper than usual. She looked composed. Her mother’s portrait, hanging behind her, looked composed too, though Elianor knew from family stories that the woman had once thrown a silver bowl at a visiting bishop.

“I should like to borrow her courage,” Elianor said.

“You may borrow the bowl instead.”

A horn sounded below. Doors opened. Voices rose in the entrance hall.

Nessa’s humor faded. “My lady, if you do not wish this—”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Elianor turned from the mirror. Nessa’s hands were still resting near the hooks of the gown, as though she could undo the entire morning with one movement. “If I say no, my father loses the estate. If I say yes, I lose the right to decide what happens to me. I know both things.”

Nessa looked down. “And which loss is worse?”

Elianor had no answer that would not sound cruel in a warm room, wearing a silk-lined dress, while the kitchen counted its loaves.

Lord Caelan entered the drawing room ten minutes later. He was not handsome in the careless way of young men at court. His appearance had been arranged with greater intention. His dark hair was brushed back from a high brow, his coat was charcoal wool cut close to the body, and a ruby pin rested at his throat. Rain had touched neither his gloves nor his boots. He removed the former before greeting Lord Alric, and the gesture seemed both courteous and a reminder that he could afford servants to protect his hands from weather.

“My lord,” Caelan said. “I hope my arrival has not inconvenienced you.”

“Greyfen is honored,” Alric replied.

Caelan’s pale eyes moved over the room. They paused on the water stain above the mantel, the patched curtain, the silver missing from the sideboard. He took in the evidence of decline without appearing to judge it. That restraint was more unsettling than scorn would have been.

Then he bowed to Elianor.

“Lady Elianor. We met at the winter feast in Dunmere, though I doubt you remember.”

“I remember,” she said. “You were explaining to the mayor why his new bridge would fail.”

“It failed three months later.”

“You sounded pleased.”

“I prefer being correct to being pleased.”

His smile was faint, almost private. It might have charmed her if it had not seemed to measure the distance between them.

Alric gestured toward the chairs. “Perhaps we should begin with refreshments.”

“Of course.” Caelan turned to the footman waiting by the door. “Tea, if you have it. Nothing elaborate.”

The footman bowed and hurried away.

Elianor noticed the hesitation before he moved. The man had not been sure whether Greyfen still possessed tea. Caelan had noticed that too.

They spoke first of weather, roads, and the condition of the river. Caelan asked after the tenants with a concern so polished it left no fingerprints. He knew the names of the flooded villages. He knew the yield of the east pasture and how many carts had been lost in the autumn mud. He knew that the mill had stood idle for three weeks.

“You have studied Greyfen,” Elianor said.

“It would be foolish to discuss joining our houses without understanding what I might be joining.”

“Might?”

He inclined his head. “Your father and I have not yet reached an agreement.”

Alric’s fingers tightened on the arm of his chair. “The broad terms are settled.”

“The broad terms are favorable,” Caelan said. “There is a distinction.”

Tea arrived on a tray bearing four cups, three saucers, and a pot that had lost its silver handle. Caelan accepted his cup without comment. Elianor wondered whether he knew the handle had been sold or whether such details were invisible to a man accustomed to abundance.

He set the tea down untouched.

“The Arbridge family can discharge the three hundred and eighty crowns owed under our note,” he said. “We can also satisfy the Dunmere merchants, provided they agree to a reduction in accumulated interest. In exchange, Greyfen’s debts would be consolidated under Arbridge management.”

“Management,” Elianor repeated.

“A temporary measure, naturally.”

“How temporary?”

“Until the accounts are stable.”

“And who decides when they are stable?”

Caelan looked at her. “The person responsible for making them so.”

Alric cleared his throat. “Lord Caelan would oversee the estate’s financial administration after the marriage.”

“After the marriage,” Elianor said. “Not before.”

“I would not interfere in your father’s household while he remains its master.”

The words were courteous. Their meaning was not. While he remains its master.

Caelan continued. “Greyfen would remain in the Vey family. Your father would retain the title and residence. The tenants would remain under Vey protection, subject to reasonable reforms.”

“What reforms?”

“Rents adjusted according to yield. Labor obligations recorded rather than permitted to drift. Staff reduced where the household no longer requires their services.”

Elianor thought of the scullery boys, the groom with the lame mare, Nessa’s hands reddened by mending. “And who determines what the household requires?”

“Again, my lady, the person bearing its expenses.”

She placed her untouched tea beside the saucer. “You make marriage sound like a purchase agreement.”

Caelan’s expression did not change. “Marriage between houses has always been an agreement concerning property, obligations, and succession. Affection may grow within it, if fortune is kind.”

“Is fortune kind to you often?”

“More often than not. I try not to insult her by relying on her.”

Alric gave a strained laugh. Elianor did not.

Caelan reached into his coat and withdrew a folded document sealed with red wax. He did not open it. He laid it on the table between them, where it resembled a blade carefully sheathed.

“These are the proposed articles,” he said. “Your dowry would consist of Greyfen’s income after debts are discharged, along with the jewels held in your mother’s chest. The land itself would pass to our children. Until then, I would have authority to appoint the steward, direct expenditure, and approve all leases.”

“My dowry is the estate.”

“The estate’s income,” he corrected. “Greyfen remains your father’s property until his death, unless he chooses otherwise.”

“And after his death?”

“Then it becomes the property of my house through our marriage and the succession.”

There it was. Not hidden, not softened. The house on the hill, the mill, the pasture, the servants’ cottages, the fields under rain—all of it reduced to a line of transfer.

“Would I have any authority?” she asked.

“Certainly. You would manage the household, charitable disbursements, and the education of our children.”

“Provided you approved the money.”

“I would hardly leave you to make financial decisions while the estate recovered from insolvency.”

He said it as if he had offered her a crown.

The meeting continued for another hour. Caelan knew when to yield and when to allow a silence to do the work of pressure. He agreed that the servants’ wages should be paid first from the next grain sale, then inserted a clause allowing the estate to postpone wages during “exceptional conditions.” He praised Elianor’s intelligence, then addressed every serious question to her father. When she objected, he apologized with such perfect sincerity that objecting again made her seem unreasonable.

At last he rose.

“I will remain at Greyfen until tomorrow,” he said. “There is no need to hurry a decision that will shape both our lives.”

“Yet you have brought the articles,” Elianor said.

“One may prepare without presuming.”

His gaze rested on her hand. She wore no ring.

“In any event,” he added, “I believe the match is favorable.”

“To whom?”

“To everyone who depends upon Greyfen surviving.”

He bowed and left with Alric. The door closed behind them. Elianor stood very still until the sound of their voices faded down the corridor.

Then she went to find her father.

She found him in the library with the proposed articles open before him. He had removed his coat. His shirt clung damply at the collar, and his face had taken on the gray cast of the rain outside.

“You let him speak of my dowry as though he had already inherited it.”

“He was discussing terms.”

“He was assigning himself the keys.”

“Because he will be responsible for the debts.”

“And the land.”

“Which he will save.”

“By dismissing the servants?”

“By reducing expenses.”

Elianor snatched up the articles. “Here. ‘Household staff may be reduced according to the husband’s judgment.’ There is no promise that Nessa remains, or Pell, or Hobb, or any of them.”

“Your servants are not the estate.”

“They are the people who keep it alive.”

Alric struck the desk with his palm. The inkpot jumped. “And what would you have me do? Refuse him, watch the Arbridge men seize Greyfen, and tell every family in Lower Fen that I preserved your freedom while they slept in the road?”

“Do not make their suffering an argument against me.”

“It is not against you. It is the truth.”

“The truth is that you are selling my life because you cannot bear to see your name end.”

The silence afterward was absolute.

Alric lowered his hand. “You think I do not know what I am asking.”

“I think you have convinced yourself that necessity makes it honorable.”

He looked toward the portraits above the shelves. “When your mother died, I promised her I would keep Greyfen. Not for the stones. For the people. Your grandfather’s tenants had known no other protection. If Arbridge takes the estate outright, he can clear the villages, sell the timber, and replace every cottage with grazing land. He has done it elsewhere.”

“Then why trust him with me?”

“Because you may influence him.”

Elianor stared. “You believe I can soften a man who speaks of human beings as expenses?”

“I believe you can do more from within his house than I can do from beneath its ruin.”

She wanted to despise him for that faith. Instead she saw the terror beneath it. He had exhausted silver, hounds, pasture, credit, and pride. Now he was offering the last thing he could still call his own, though it had never truly belonged to him.

“Will you guarantee the servants are not turned out?” she asked.

“I will put it in the articles.”

“Not merely the household. The tenants.”

“I will ask him to preserve their leases.”

“Ask?”

“It is all I can do.”

“No,” she said. “It is all you are willing to do.”

His face crumpled for an instant before duty rebuilt it.

By evening, Elianor had read the articles three times. She marked the clauses concerning wages, leases, and the appointment of the steward. Caelan accepted two alterations and rejected five. He agreed to retain current servants for one year after the marriage, unless dismissed for cause. He agreed that no tenant would be evicted without a hearing before the estate court. The promises were narrow enough to be nearly useless, but they were more than Greyfen possessed without him.

When the final document was placed before her, the rain had begun again.

Caelan stood beside the window, his reflection pale over the black fields. “You need not answer tonight,” he said.

“Yes,” Elianor replied. “I do.”

Alric looked up.

She took the pen. The nib trembled once, then steadied. Her name moved across the page in a clean, practiced hand: Elianor Vey, daughter of Greyfen, surrendering nothing in words that could not be taken from her and everything in the act of signing.

Caelan approached only after the ink had dried.

“You have my gratitude,” he said.

Elianor met his eyes. “You have my agreement. Do not confuse them.”

Something like approval flickered in his expression. “I would not dream of it.”

He offered his hand. She placed hers in it. His fingers closed around hers with controlled warmth, not tenderness. It was the grip of a man confirming possession of a valuable thing.

“To a favorable match,” he said.

Elianor smiled as she had been taught: gently, modestly, without revealing the heart beneath.

“To Greyfen’s preservation,” she answered.

Outside, the hill disappeared into rain. Somewhere below, servants were still carrying wood, tenants were still waiting for flour, and the old house held its breath around the bargain that would save it.

chapters.name: The Falconer’s Son
chapters.content:
## The Falconer’s Son

By the third morning after the betrothal, Elianor had learned the shape of her cage.

It was not made of iron. It had polished banisters, tall windows, and carpets thick enough to swallow the sound of footsteps. It had Nessa’s careful hands fastening pearl buttons at Elianor’s wrists and Master Pell’s clerks waiting beyond the drawing-room door with papers that required her father’s seal. It had a dozen rooms in which she might sit, provided she sat in the right one, and a hundred questions she was expected to answer with a smile.

Greyfen had never seemed so small.

At breakfast, Lord Alric spoke of Caelan’s departure. The Arbridge party had ridden south at dawn, though Caelan had left behind two men to examine the barns and mill. He would return within the fortnight, Alric said. There were arrangements to be made before winter.

“Arrangements,” Elianor repeated.

Her father looked up from his untouched porridge. “You know what I mean.”

“I know what everyone means now.”

Nessa, standing behind her chair, went still. Alric’s face tightened, but the effort of anger passed quickly through him, leaving only fatigue.

“You signed,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You did not sign blindly.”

“No. I signed with my eyes open.” She pushed her spoon through the cooling porridge. “That is the trouble. I saw precisely what I was doing.”

He had no answer. The hall clock marked the silence between them. Outside, rain crawled down the windows in silver threads, blurring the bare elms and the dark slopes beyond the house.

Elianor rose before breakfast was finished.

She told Nessa she was going to walk. Nessa asked whether she should send a groom. Elianor said no. Nessa looked as if she wished to argue, then glanced toward the corridor where Alric’s steward had gone and swallowed the words.

“Take your cloak, at least,” she said.

“I will.”

“And your boots.”

“I am not going barefoot into the marsh.”

“That is not the same as being sensible.”

Elianor kissed her cheek, partly to stop the lecture and partly because Nessa’s concern was the only uncomplicated tenderness left in the house. Then she went upstairs, exchanged her walking shoes for old riding boots, and fastened a plain wool cloak beneath her chin.

The woods began beyond the east pasture, where the ground rose in a ragged line toward the old hunting road. They had once been managed carefully: paths cleared, bracken cut, fallen timber stacked for winter fuel. Since the debts had tightened around Greyfen, no one had spared the labor. Thorns reached across the trail. Nettles crowded the ditches. The rain had turned the earth black and soft beneath the leaves.

Elianor walked until the manor disappeared behind the trees.

There, for the first time in days, no one watched her face.

She found a fallen beech and sat beneath its roots, listening to water fall from branch to branch. The quiet was not complete. Far off, a crow called. Something small moved through the wet leaves. Once, from the direction of the estate, she heard the faint clatter of a cart and imagined the sacks of grain being counted, weighed, and accounted for before any hungry tenant could touch them.

She closed her eyes.

The woods did not ask her to become Lady Arbridge. They did not ask her to be dutiful, grateful, or calm.

A sharp cry broke the stillness.

Elianor opened her eyes. It came again—thin, ragged, and furious. Not a songbird. A hawk.

She followed the sound along a path almost erased by brambles. It led to an abandoned forester’s lodge crouched in a clearing. The roof sagged above one wall, and the door hung crooked from a single hinge. The place had been empty since the last forester died, though a small plume of smoke rose from a hole in the stones where someone had made a fire.

Elianor stepped through the doorway.

“Stop there.”

The voice came from the shadows to her left.

A young man stood beside the cold hearth, holding a short knife. He was perhaps a year or two older than Elianor, though the weather had put harder marks upon him. His brown hair was damp from the rain, and his coat, once green, had faded nearly gray at the shoulders. A leather glove covered his left hand. On that wrist perched a goshawk with its feathers clumped darkly by blood.

The bird shifted and gave another distressed cry.

“I heard it,” Elianor said.

“That is usually how people find things they were not invited to see.”

His eyes moved over her cloak, her boots, and finally her face. Recognition did not soften him. If anything, it made his grip on the knife more certain.

“You are the falconer’s son,” she said.

“Tomas Vale.”

“I know your name.”

“Then you know enough to leave.”

Elianor looked at the goshawk. Its right wing hung crookedly, the feathers near the joint matted with blood. “It is injured.”

“That also is plain.”

“Can you mend it?”

“I can keep it alive.”

“That is not what I asked.”

For the first time, surprise touched his face. It vanished almost at once.

“Can you mend a broken wing, my lady?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps you should not ask questions that have no use.”

The title, spoken without courtesy, struck her more sharply than open insult would have. Elianor looked past him at the crude shelter assembled on the floor: folded straw, a shallow bowl of water, and strips of cloth already stiff with blood.

“What happened?”

“A snare.”

“Set by poachers?”

“Set by men who wanted rabbits.”

He knelt, and the goshawk leaned toward him. His gloved fingers steadied the bird with an assurance that made the knife seem less threatening. He murmured something too low for Elianor to hear.

“Her wing is broken,” he said. “The joint is torn. If I bind it badly, she will never fly. If I leave it, she will die.”

Elianor remembered the small medicine chest kept in the morning room for household use. “I could bring tincture.”

Tomas laughed once, without amusement. “From the manor?”

“It is medicine.”

“It is medicine meant for people who can afford to be ill.”

“Would you rather let the bird suffer because the bottle has a Vey seal on it?”

“I would rather not owe the Veys anything.”

The rain tapped through the broken roof. Elianor felt heat rise beneath her cold skin.

“You speak as though I personally set the snare.”

“No. You merely live in the house whose men take the rabbits, the timber, and the grain. You are not responsible for every hand that obeys your family.” He lifted his eyes to hers. “Only for the hands you choose to command.”

She thought of the articles folded in the drawer of her desk, of Caelan’s smooth voice promising that Greyfen would be preserved, and of her father saying that protection required obedience. She had come into the woods to escape all of them, and here they had followed her in the mouth of a stranger.

“What would you have me command?” she asked.

“Nothing. That is the first honest thing a lady can do.”

His words should have angered her. They did anger her. Yet she saw the blood on the bird, the frayed cloth, the hunger in the young man’s face. His suspicion was not a game played for the pleasure of wounding her. It had been earned.

Elianor drew back toward the door.

“I will bring the tincture,” she said.

“I did not ask you to.”

“No. You made certain of that.”

She turned before he could reply and walked back through the wet bracken, furious at him, at herself, and at the fact that she was already planning how to return unseen.

In the medicine chest she found a small brown bottle of willowbark tincture, a jar of salve, and a roll of clean bandage. The house physician was away attending a tenant’s child, so no one challenged her when she took them. Nessa watched from the dressing room while Elianor wrapped the supplies in a square of linen.

“Where are you going?” Nessa asked.

“To help an injured hawk.”

Nessa’s expression moved from disbelief to worry. “In this weather?”

“It may die if I do not.”

“Is that what you tell yourself?”

Elianor tied the bundle. “It is what I know.”

Nessa studied her. “Be careful, my lady.”

The warning held more meaning than the words. Elianor nodded.

She did not return to the lodge that afternoon. By the time she reached the clearing, dusk had settled between the trees, and Tomas was gone. The goshawk was gone too. She stood beneath the dripping eaves, holding the medicine she had carried through the house like contraband, and felt foolish.

The next morning, she returned.

This time she brought linen from Nessa’s sewing basket, two apples, a heel of bread, and a small piece of cheese wrapped in paper. She had no explanation for the food except that Tomas looked hungry, and no explanation for why that mattered to her.

He was at the lodge, crouched beside the fire. The goshawk lay beneath a blanket, breathing in shallow, uneven pulls. Tomas looked up as she entered.

“You came back.”

“You sound disappointed.”

“I sound surprised.”

“That is less flattering.”

“I was not attempting to flatter you.”

“No. I had noticed.”

His mouth almost curved. Almost.

Elianor set the bundle beside him. “The tincture. Linen. Food.”

“I cannot pay for it.”

“I did not ask you to.”

“Everything has a price at Greyfen.”

She glanced toward the injured bird. “Then consider it payment for letting me see something alive.”

Tomas’s gaze sharpened. “You think the manor is dead?”

“I think it is very good at pretending not to be.”

For a moment neither spoke. The fire shifted, sending a brief warmth through the damp room. Tomas reached for the linen.

“Hold this,” he said.

Elianor knelt opposite him. He guided her hands toward the goshawk’s body, showing her where to support the breast without crushing it. The bird trembled beneath her fingers. Its eye was bright and black, full of terror.

“Slowly,” Tomas murmured. “Do not fight her fear.”

“I am trying.”

“So is she.”

Together they unwound the old bandage. Blood had seeped through at the joint. Elianor held the bird while Tomas cleaned the wound and set the splints. His hands were steady, though his jaw tightened whenever the goshawk cried.

When it was done, he tied the linen in place.

“There,” he said. “Now we wait.”

Elianor withdrew her hands. “Will she fly again?”

“If the wing heals straight.”

“And if it does not?”

“Then she will live on the ground until something kills her.”

He said it plainly. No promise softened the truth. Elianor looked down at the blood marking her fingers.

Outside, rain began again, veiling the trees and the distant manor beyond them.

Tomas took the bread but did not eat it. “You should not come here.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.” She met his eyes. “That is why I came.”

This time the almost-smile reached his mouth, though it was not kindness. Not yet. It was recognition: of danger, perhaps, and of two people who had found the same narrow place in the world and were not ready to leave it.

Elianor stayed until the fire burned low.

When she returned to Greyfen, the bells were calling her to another lesson in becoming someone else’s wife. She washed the hawk’s blood from her hands before entering the house, but the stain remained beneath one fingernail.

She kept it there.

chapters.name: Willow Splints
chapters.content:
## Willow Splints

For three days, the goshawk did not improve.

Elianor measured the days by the bird’s breathing. At dawn, while Nessa arranged her hair and recited the names of visitors expected after noon, Elianor listened for the shallow rasp beneath the blanket in the forester’s lodge. At breakfast, while Lord Alric and Master Pell argued over the price of oats, she imagined the crooked joint and the darkening skin around it. In the chapel, while the priest praised patience as the virtue of those who had no power, she pictured Tomas changing the dressing with his careful, blood-stained hands.

On the fourth morning, the rain stopped.

Mist lay over the east woods, pale as wool, and the wet branches shone whenever the weak sun found them. Elianor carried a fresh roll of linen beneath her cloak, along with a small jar of rendered fat that Nessa had given her without asking questions.

“You have the look of someone carrying a secret,” Nessa had said.

“I have the look of someone carrying bandages.”

“Those are not mutually exclusive.”

Elianor had kissed her cheek and left before her face betrayed too much.

At the lodge, Tomas was kneeling beside the fire, holding the goshawk against his chest. The bird’s head rested beneath his chin. He looked up as Elianor entered, but this time his hand did not move toward the knife.

“She pulled the splint loose,” he said.

The bird gave a weak, irritated click.

“Perhaps she dislikes your workmanship.”

“Perhaps she dislikes being tied together.”

“Then we have something in common.”

The words escaped before she could stop them. Tomas studied her, the faint humor leaving his face. Elianor set down the jar and knelt beside him.

“Let me hold her.”

“You know how?”

“I remember.”

“You remember because I told you.”

“Then tell me again.”

He hesitated only a moment before passing the goshawk into her hands. Its talons closed over the leather of her glove. The bird was lighter than she expected, all sharp bones and furious life. Tomas unwound the loosened linen and examined the wound.

“The swelling is down,” he said.

“Is that good?”

“It is better than swelling up.”

“You are a great comfort.”

“I have never claimed to be.”

He cut two narrow strips from the willow branches he had soaked beside the fire. They were green and flexible, their bark smooth beneath his thumb. Elianor watched him shave the edges with his knife.

“Why willow?” she asked.

“It bends without breaking. If the splint is stiff, every movement hurts her. If it is too soft, the wing heals wrong.”

“Willow sounds wiser than most people I know.”

“Most people do not let themselves be bent.”

“Some of us are bent by others.”

His knife paused. The little lodge seemed to grow quieter around them.

“Who?” he asked.

Elianor nearly told him to mind his own business. Instead, she looked down at the goshawk’s black eye.

“My father,” she said. “Caelan. Every person who says my future is necessary.”

Tomas resumed shaving the willow. “A lady’s future is usually considered necessary by the men who profit from it.”

“You think I profit from mine?”

“I think you will live in a house protected by it.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No. It is merely what people freezing outside the house can see.”

He laid the splints along the wing and nodded for her to hold them. Elianor pressed the willow lightly against the feathers while he wound the linen around it. His fingers brushed hers once, then again. Both times the contact was accidental. Both times she noticed.

“You could have sent me away,” she said.

“I did.”

“And yet you let me hold her.”

“You have useful hands.”

“Only my hands?”

His eyes lifted. For a heartbeat, something unguarded crossed his face—not tenderness, not yet, but the startled awareness of a door opening in a wall he had built long ago.

“Do not make too much of it,” he said.

“I would not dream of making anything of you.”

“That is a lie.”

She smiled despite herself. Tomas looked away first.

When the splint was tied, he placed the goshawk back in its straw-lined basket. The bird settled with a resentful sigh.

“She will live,” he said.

“Will she fly?”

“That depends on whether the wing mends true.”

“And on whether she is willing.”

“Birds do not have the luxury of willingness.”

Elianor thought of the marriage articles locked in her desk. “Neither do some people.”

Tomas fed a twig to the fire. “You speak of choice as if you have never had one.”

“I have had many choices.”

“Which ones?”

“To wear blue or green. To read in the west room or the library. To ride in the morning or afternoon.”

“That is not choice.”

“It is to someone who has none.”

His gaze sharpened. “You think I have none?”

“I think you cannot refuse an order without risking your father’s wages, your lodging, perhaps your life.”

“And you can refuse a marriage without risking the lives of everyone who eats because Greyfen still stands.”

The accusation was not loud. That made it worse.

Elianor drew her cloak tighter. “My father says the same.”

“Then perhaps he is right.”

“He is not.” She looked toward the broken doorway, where the manor could not be seen through the trees. “He says I must marry to save the household. Caelan says it as if the household were an object he is purchasing. You say it as if I am already guilty for being born here. All of you speak about what I owe. No one asks what I want.”

“What do you want?”

The answer rose so quickly that she feared it had been waiting behind her teeth.

“To wake and not know what is expected of me.”

Tomas’s expression did not change, but his attention did. It settled upon her fully.

“To walk into a room without wondering which part of myself will be useful there,” she continued. “To be angry without being called ungrateful. To say no and have the word remain no.”

She had not meant to tell him so much. The lodge had a way of loosening everything the manor tightened.

Tomas looked at the bird. “My mother wanted a door that locked.”

Elianor waited.

“She worked in the kitchens at first. Then my father took the falconry post, and we were given a cottage near the lower meadows. It was small, but the roof held. There was a pear tree beside it.” He rubbed soot from his thumb with the edge of his sleeve. “When the harvest failed, the rent went up.”

“Why?”

“Because the mill had debts. Because the steward said the estate could not carry idlers. Because someone in a warm room wrote a number beside our names.”

Elianor felt the answer like a stone beneath her ribs. “My father—”

“Approved the eviction.”

She stopped breathing for a moment.

Tomas did not look at her. “Perhaps he never saw the paper. Perhaps Master Pell placed it before him among a hundred others. Perhaps he thought the cottage would be given to someone who could pay. Reasons do not keep rain out.”

“What happened to your mother?”

“We went to my uncle’s village. He had no room. We slept in a shed through the first snow.” His voice remained level, which made the story more terrible. “She caught a fever. By the time my father found work, she was too weak to stand. She died before spring.”

Elianor stared at the fire. “I am sorry.”

“I know.”

The words held no forgiveness.

“I cannot undo it,” she said.

“No.”

“I did not know.”

“That is not the same as innocence.”

She flinched. He saw it and seemed to regret seeing it, but he did not take the words back.

“What would you have me do?” she asked.

“Not ask me to make you feel better.”

“I am not.”

“You are a Vey. You have been trained to believe that every wound near you is a problem you can solve with money, medicine, or a promise.”

“And what have I promised?”

“Nothing. That is why I do not trust you.”

His honesty hurt more than his suspicion had before. She reached for the fresh linen and folded it precisely, though it needed no folding.

“Then I will stop promising,” she said. “I will listen.”

Tomas’s eyes came back to hers.

She held his gaze. “Tell me what happened. Tell me what people at Greyfen need. I may not be able to change everything, but I can know what I am part of.”

“Knowing is easy.”

“Not for me.”

“No,” he said quietly. “Perhaps not for you.”

It was the nearest thing to agreement he had offered.

They remained in the lodge until noon. Tomas told her which cottages had lost roofs, which tenants hid sacks of grain from the steward, and how the men sent to collect rent sometimes took hens and tools when coins were lacking. Elianor told him less, but what she told him was true: that Alric’s debts were worse than she had understood, that Caelan’s marriage articles reached into every room at Greyfen, and that she had no confidence her father could preserve the household without surrendering it.

When she returned the next day, Tomas had marked a path through the bracken so she would not tear her cloak. When she came after that, she brought apples, and he had mended the broken latch. They did not call the meetings appointments. They called them nothing.

The goshawk slept more easily. Its wing remained bound in willow, green against the gray feathers. Each day Tomas loosened the linen a little and checked the joint. Each day Elianor held the bird steady. Their hands learned the work before their hearts learned caution.

At the manor, Elianor resumed her lessons and answered Caelan’s letters with perfect courtesy. In the woods, she removed her gloves and let Tomas place them beside the fire. He stopped calling her my lady when they were alone, though he never used her name carelessly.

One evening, as dusk gathered beneath the branches, the goshawk stirred and opened its wings as far as the splint allowed.

Tomas smiled.

Elianor had never seen his face transformed by joy. It made him look younger, almost unbearably unguarded.

“She remembers,” he said.

“What?”

“Being made for the air.”

The bird folded its wing again. Outside, beyond the lodge, rain began to fall—not heavily, but steadily, threading the trees in silver.

Elianor listened to it and understood that the woods had become a place she could return to. Not safe. Never safe. But honest.

Tomas handed her the lantern for the walk home.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “come after sunset. Fewer eyes on the road.”

It was not a request. It was not quite an invitation.

Elianor took the lantern. “Tomorrow, then.”

He watched until she disappeared among the wet trees. Only afterward did he realize he had begun to wait for her before she arrived.

chapters.name: The Shape of Rain
chapters.content:
## The Shape of Rain

After that first promise of tomorrow, Elianor discovered that time could be divided into two unequal portions: the hours she endured, and the hours she awaited.

At Greyfen, the days still wore their formal faces. Nessa pinned her hair, Master Pell carried ledgers beneath his arm, and Lord Alric asked whether Caelan’s secretary had sent word about the alterations to the marriage articles. Elianor answered, bowed, smiled, and moved through the manor as though nothing had changed.

But beneath her glove she kept a splinter of willow Tomas had discarded beside the fire.

It was no larger than her little finger, green-brown and smooth. She had found it in the fold of her cloak after leaving the lodge and had not been able to throw it away. It seemed ridiculous to treasure a piece of wood. Then again, the whole of her secret had begun with a bird, a strip of linen, and a man who had told her that sympathy was not innocence.

She returned to the woods whenever she could.

Sometimes Tomas met her at the edge of the clearing. Sometimes she found him splitting kindling or standing beneath the dripping eaves, his falconer’s glove tucked into his belt. He no longer reached for his knife when she entered. He no longer watched her as if each kindness concealed a bargain.

He still watched her carefully.

The change was small enough that another person might not have noticed it. Tomas noticed everything. A broken twig. A hare’s track in the mud. The direction of smoke carried by the wind. He could tell from the way Elianor walked whether she had spent the day angry or merely tired.

“You are limping,” he said one afternoon.

“I am not.”

“You are favoring your left foot.”

“My shoe pinches.”

“Then take it off.”

She looked at him. “Here?”

“You think the trees are shocked by feet?”

She laughed, and the sound startled them both. Then she sat on the lodge’s threshold and removed the shoe. A red mark crossed her heel. Tomas knelt, opened a small leather pouch, and drew out a strip of soft cloth.

“I can do that,” she said.

“I know.”

He wrapped her heel with the solemn concentration he gave the goshawk’s wing. His fingers were rough, but his touch was gentle. Elianor watched the bent head, the dark hair damp from rain, the scar along his jaw she had not seen before.

“Where did you get that?” she asked.

“Which?”

“The scar.”

“Fence post.”

“Were you fighting a fence?”

“It started it.”

His mouth shifted. Not a smile, exactly, but the beginning of one. She wanted to place her hand against his cheek and smooth the guardedness from it. The thought came so plainly that she had to look away.

Tomas finished the knot and rose. “You will walk more easily now.”

“Will you inspect all my injuries?”

“Only the ones you complain about.”

“I have not complained once.”

“You arrived wearing a face like a condemned saint.”

“That is simply my face.”

“It is a very expressive face.”

She should have been offended. Instead, she took the heel cloth and folded it into her palm as if it were another keepsake.

They began sharing the food she carried. At first Elianor brought too much: white bread, cheese, dried pears, a heel of ham wrapped in paper. Tomas accepted only what he could imagine replacing with his own labor. The next time she arrived, he had set mushrooms and two small river fish beside the fire.

“Do not tell me these are an equal exchange,” she said.

“They are not.”

“Then why offer them?”

“Because I caught them.”

His pride stood between them, straight-backed and unadorned. Elianor understood that accepting his gift mattered more than giving him hers. She took the fish.

“They are excellent,” she said after a bite.

“They are fish.”

“Must excellence be complicated?”

“With you, apparently.”

The rain came often that month. It drummed on the lodge roof and softened the paths until every walk became a negotiation with mud. Once, Elianor arrived soaked through, her cloak heavy with water. Tomas rose without speaking, took the clasp from her throat, and pulled the cloak from her shoulders.

“You will catch cold.”

“I have survived worse weather.”

“Not while sitting in wet silk.”

He hung the cloak near the fire. Then he took his own, a coarse brown thing smelling of smoke and pine, and held it out.

She hesitated. “If someone sees me wearing this—”

“They will assume you robbed a poor man.”

“Which would be more believable than the truth?”

“What truth?”

“That you lent it to me.”

His eyes held hers. “I am lending it to you.”

She put it on. It was too broad at the shoulders and reached nearly to her ankles. The wool scratched her chin, and beneath the smoke was the unmistakable scent of him. Tomas looked away so quickly that she wondered whether he had noticed her noticing.

For a while they listened to the rain.

“My father used to take me riding when I was small,” Elianor said. “Before his hair went gray. He would let me choose the mare, though there were only three suitable ones, and tell me I had the judgment of a seasoned rider.”

“Did you?”

“No. I fell into a ditch within the month.”

“Did he say you had the judgment of a seasoned rider then?”

“He said I had the stubbornness of one.”

“That sounds more accurate.”

She smiled at the fire. “He was kinder before the debts. Or perhaps I was too young to understand the cost of his kindness.”

Tomas sat opposite her, one knee drawn up. “My father never praised me when I was young.”

“Never?”

“He said praise made a falcon lazy.”

“And did it?”

“I am not a falcon.”

“Perhaps you are simply a badly trained one.”

This time he did smile. It altered him more than she expected. There was tenderness in it, not only toward the bird sleeping in its basket but toward the boy he had once been, wild and impatient beneath his father’s stern lessons.

Elianor reached for a dried pear. “What did you want to be?”

“A falconer.”

“That is what you are.”

“No. That is what I was permitted to become.”

The answer quieted her.

He touched the edge of the basket. The goshawk shifted in its sleep, feathers rustling. “As a child, I wanted to build boats. My mother said I could make one from the old shed boards when I was older. Then the cottage was taken. After she died, my father found us this work. I learned the birds. I learned to mend gloves and read tracks. Wanting things became an expensive habit.”

“I am sorry.”

“I know.”

This time there was no accusation in it. That was worse, and better.

She placed the pear between them. “I wanted to paint.”

Tomas looked genuinely surprised. “Paint what?”

“Everything. The orchard in spring. The chapel windows. Nessa asleep over her sewing. You.”

His stillness changed the air.

“Me?”

“Not now,” she said, though she could feel heat rising in her face. “You would complain about the likeness.”

“I would complain about being looked at.”

“You are looked at all the time.”

“Not like that.”

Neither of them moved. Rain threaded down the broken window. Tomas’s hand rested on the bench between them, close enough that she could see the small crescent of dirt beneath his thumbnail.

Elianor thought of reaching for it.

Outside, a horse whinnied.

Tomas was on his feet before she could breathe. He snatched up the lantern and lowered the flame. “Someone is coming.”

“Who?”

“Stay back.”

The sound came again: the wet clop of hooves, slow and approaching from the north path. Tomas crossed to the doorway and looked through the crack beside the warped frame. His shoulders tightened.

“A groom,” he whispered. “Greyfen colors.”

Elianor’s heart struck hard against her ribs. “Perhaps he is looking for—”

“He is looking at the lodge.”

The goshawk stirred in its basket. Tomas turned and caught Elianor by the wrist, pulling her behind the hanging blanket that divided the room. There was barely space between the wall and the stacked firewood. His body shielded hers. She could feel the warmth of him through the borrowed cloak.

The horse stopped outside.

“Elianor?” a man called.

Her blood went cold. The groom’s voice belonged to Hobb, who tended the carriage horses and had served Greyfen since before Elianor’s mother died.

“Lady Elianor, are you in there?”

Tomas’s hand closed over her mouth. Not hard. A warning, a plea. His face was inches from hers, every line of it alert. She could feel his breath against her temple.

Hobb dismounted. Boots struck the mud. The door creaked as he tested it.

“Strange place for a lady,” he muttered. “Master Pell said she took the east road.”

Tomas’s fingers tightened. Elianor stared into his eyes and understood that if the door opened, he would put himself between her and whatever followed. He would not be able to protect himself as well.

The latch lifted.

A gust of wind shoved rain through the gap, scattering ash across the floor. The goshawk gave a sharp, irritated cry.

Hobb swore. “What in—”

The horse suddenly screamed and reared. From the trees came the crack of a branch, followed by the deep bark of something unseen. Hobb cursed again and stumbled back.

“Wolves,” he said, though there had been no howl. “Damn these woods.”

His boots retreated. A moment later the horse plunged down the path, branches snapping after it.

Tomas waited until the sound vanished. Then he removed his hand.

Elianor drew a breath that shook. “He knows I came this way.”

“He knows someone told him you did.”

“Who?”

“Does it matter?”

“Yes.”

“Not tonight.”

He moved away, and the sudden distance hurt more than his touch had comforted her. He barred the door and extinguished the lantern.

“You must leave by the stream,” he said. “Not the path.”

“I cannot walk through that mud in these shoes.”

“Then carry them.”

“Tomas—”

“No more visits for several days.”

The command struck her like a slap. “You do not decide that alone.”

“I decide whether I want to be hanged.”

“I never asked you to risk your life.”

“You came here.”

“And you waited for me.”

He flinched. There it was between them, the thing neither had named: that he had begun waiting, and she had begun needing him to.

The rain thickened beyond the door.

Tomas lowered his voice. “Go now, my lady.”

She hated the title in his mouth. It restored every wall they had spent the month forgetting.

Elianor removed his cloak and held it out. “You will need this.”

“Keep it.”

“If I return it at the manor, someone will ask where I found it.”

“Then keep it until the danger passes.”

She stepped close enough to place the cloak around his shoulders herself. Her fingers brushed his collar. Neither moved away.

“I will come back,” she whispered.

His eyes closed briefly. “That is what I am afraid of.”

She wanted to kiss him. The knowledge of it was bright and terrifying. Instead she pressed the folded willow splint into his hand.

“Then be afraid with me.”

He looked down at the wood, then back at her. For one suspended moment, the rain seemed to hold its breath.

“Stream,” he said.

She nodded.

Elianor slipped into the darkness, leaving by the rear of the lodge. The water rose above her ankles almost at once. Behind her, Tomas remained at the door until the trees concealed her.

By the time she reached Greyfen, she was shivering. Nessa undressed her without questions and found the brown cloak beneath her own. Her eyes rested on it, then lifted to Elianor’s face.

“Bandages?” Nessa asked.

Elianor folded Tomas’s cloak against her chest.

“Something like that,” she said.
