chapters.name: The First Flight
chapters.content:
## The First Flight

For three mornings the rain held off, though the world remained wet enough to remember it. Water shone in the hollows of the east wood, trembling on every fern. The clouds had drawn themselves thin over the treetops, and a pale, uncertain light moved through them like a hand searching beneath a door.

Elianor came by the stream route with her skirts pinned above her ankles and Tomas’s brown cloak folded over one arm. She had not meant to bring it back. She had slept badly beneath its rough wool, waking whenever the wind struck the shutters, and each time she had found herself listening for the remembered warmth of him in its folds. In the end she had carried it from her room before Nessa could ask why it was there.

Tomas was outside the lodge, standing with his face turned toward the trees. The goshawk perched on his gloved fist.

Elianor stopped among the hazels. “You said to pause my visits.”

“I said you should pause them.”

“And you have been waiting for me every morning?”

He glanced back. The guarded hardness in his face had returned, but it no longer concealed itself well. “I have been waiting for the bird.”

The goshawk clicked its beak, offended by the accusation.

Elianor smiled despite herself. “Then I am only an inconvenience.”

“A dangerous one.”

That ended her smile, though not the warmth beneath it. Tomas looked toward the manor, invisible beyond the dripping trees. “Hobb came because someone told him you had taken the east road. If he had reached the lodge a moment sooner—”

“But he did not.”

“Next time he might. Or Pell might send someone less slow. Or Caelan might notice the household spending more linen than usual.”

“You make my maid sound like a conspirator.”

“She is one, if she is helping you.”

“Nessa has better judgment than either of us.”

“Then she should have stopped you.”

The words were sharp, but his eyes were not. Elianor stepped nearer. “I tried to obey you. I remained in my room until breakfast. I sat through a reading of the marriage articles while my father and Pell argued over figures. I embroidered three leaves onto a cloth I shall never use. Then I discovered that obedience did not make me less afraid for you.”

His mouth tightened. “You think I am afraid only for myself?”

“No. I think you are afraid for me as well, and that you resent me for making the fear necessary.”

For a moment the forest held its breath around them. Then Tomas looked down at the goshawk. Its wing had been unbound two days before. The feathers were still uneven, the joint stiff, but the bird had endured his careful examinations without striking or struggling.

“She has strength,” he said. “The wing is sound enough. Today we see whether she believes it.”

They carried her to the old clearing beyond the lodge, where a dead oak had fallen across the grass. The place was ringed by young birches, their leaves whispering in the faint breeze. Tomas set a low branch between two stones and placed the goshawk upon it. She shifted her talons, restless and suspicious.

Elianor stood several paces away with a strip of rabbit meat in her hand. “Will she come to me?”

“She may.”

“That is not confidence.”

“It is truth.”

“An unusual gift in a falconer.”

“Not in a falconer. In a lord’s daughter, perhaps.”

She looked at him. He regretted it at once, and she saw that too. The old wound between them had never fully closed: his mother’s death, the cottage, her father’s signature among the papers. Yet lately they had learned to stand beside the wound without pretending it was not there.

Tomas lifted his arm. “Call her.”

Elianor raised the meat. “Come, then.”

The goshawk watched her. A breeze passed over the clearing. It stirred the bird’s breast feathers and carried the smell of moss, wet bark, and distant smoke from Greyfen’s kitchens.

“Again,” Tomas said.

“Come.”

The bird opened its wings.

Elianor forgot to breathe. For one instant the goshawk seemed held between earth and air, every feather spread, the repaired wing trembling under the effort. Then she launched herself from the branch. Her first stroke was clumsy. Her second caught the wind. She crossed the space between them in a rush of gray and brown, landed hard upon Elianor’s wrist, and nearly knocked the meat from her hand.

Elianor laughed.

The sound startled the bird, which leapt again. This time she flew to the fallen oak, wheeled around its pale trunk, and returned to Tomas. He caught her with a sudden, helpless joy that transformed his whole face.

“She did it,” Elianor whispered.

“She did.”

“She was afraid.”

“So was I.”

He fed the goshawk, and she tore at the meat with fierce concentration. Elianor watched the bird’s hooked beak, the bright eye, the wing that had nearly failed and now carried her through the clearing.

“Will you let her go?” she asked.

“When she can hunt.”

“And then?”

“Then she will choose where to land.”

The answer moved through her more painfully than she expected. She looked toward the open strip of sky above the birches. “Perhaps she will return.”

“Perhaps.”

“But you will not keep her?”

“She is not mine because I saved her.”

The words settled between them. Tomas had said them of a bird, but Elianor felt their shape against her own life. She was not Caelan’s because he would pay her father’s debts. She was not her father’s because he had given her future away. And yet every road open to her seemed to run through another person’s claim.

Tomas put the goshawk back upon the branch. “You should go.”

“I have only just arrived.”

“That is why you should go while the day still has a chance of remaining harmless.”

“I will not celebrate her first flight by running away from you.”

“Elianor.”

She heard the warning in her name, but also the plea. He removed the glove and set it on the fallen oak. His bare hand was scarred across the knuckles, browned by weather and work. She remembered that hand steadying the splint, offering her the last of his bread, catching her elbow when the mud had taken her shoe.

“I am going to marry Caelan,” she said. “I know what that means. I know what you think it means.”

“I think it means you will go back to a house where every door is watched.”

“I do not love him.”

“That will not stop him from being your husband.”

“No.” She swallowed. “But it does not make what is between us less true.”

He turned away. “Truth does not protect people here.”

“Then what does?”

“Distance. Silence. Forgetting.”

“Have you managed any of those?”

His laugh was low and bitter. “I have tried.”

She moved to stand before him. “So have I.”

He looked at her then. All the careful barriers they had built from caution and rank and fear stood for one last moment between them. Elianor could see the exact instant he chose not to speak. She could see him preparing to send her away.

She touched his cheek.

Tomas went still.

The touch was no grand surrender. Her fingers were cold, and his skin was rough beneath them. Yet his eyes closed as if she had placed a blade against his throat and he would rather endure it than move.

“Elianor,” he said again, but this time her name broke.

She kissed him.

For a heartbeat he did not answer. Then his hands came to her waist, not pulling her closer so much as asking permission, and she gave it by leaning into him. His mouth was warm, his breath uneven. The forest vanished: the manor, the articles sealed with wax, Caelan’s polished courtesy, her father’s exhausted face. There was only the pressure of Tomas’s hands and the astonishing tenderness with which he held her, as though she were something wounded that he had been entrusted to keep alive.

When they parted, their foreheads touched.

“This changes nothing,” Tomas whispered.

“It changes everything.”

“It cannot make us respectable.”

“I did not ask it to.”

“It cannot make your father agree. It cannot make Caelan release you. It cannot make the world see me as anything but a servant who reached above himself.”

“I know.”

“If they find out, they may hang me.”

The plainness of it struck harder than any accusation. Elianor’s hands closed in the front of his shirt. “Do not say that.”

“It is why I said you should pause your visits.”

“Then tell me to stop.”

He stared at her. The goshawk rustled on the branch behind them.

“Tell me,” she insisted. “Tell me to leave and never return, and I will try to obey.”

His expression twisted. “I cannot.”

“Neither can I.”

They kissed again, less cautiously this time, with the grief already inside it. When they separated, Tomas rested his hand over hers.

“We cannot pretend secrecy is a future,” he said.

“No.”

“But it is what we have.”

“For now.”

“For now,” he agreed, though neither of them believed the words promised safety.

The goshawk launched once more, rising above the birches. They watched her circle in the pale sky, her damaged wing no longer visibly different from the other. She climbed until she was only a dark mark against the clouds, then descended toward the woods beyond the clearing.

Elianor returned to Greyfen before noon. Nessa fastened her dress while saying nothing about the brightness in her face. At luncheon, Elianor answered her father’s questions, accepted Caelan’s letter, and listened as Master Pell complained about the cost of lamp oil. She lifted a spoon and discovered that her hand was shaking.

Caelan’s letter lay beside her plate. His handwriting was narrow and exact. He hoped she was well. He hoped preparations might begin in earnest. He hoped she understood that a wife’s influence depended upon her willingness to support her husband’s judgment.

Elianor folded the page.

Outside, somewhere beyond the rain-dark roofs, a hawk cried.

She went through the afternoon as though walking in a dream. She visited the linen room, approved a request for extra blankets, and corrected a servant for miscounting candles. Each ordinary duty seemed newly obscene and newly precious. She had kissed Tomas beneath the trees, and the world had not ended. That was the danger. The world could continue while everything in her had changed.

At dusk, she stood at her window. The east woods were a black line beneath the bruised sky. She knew Tomas would be there tomorrow, despite his warnings. She knew she would go, despite her own fear.

Below, Greyfen’s gates closed for the night. The iron bars met with a sound like a verdict.

Elianor pressed her fingers to her lips and remembered the first flight: the bird rising because, for one bright instant, it trusted the air.

Then she turned from the window and returned to the house that claimed her.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor and the abandoned forester’s lodge in the east woods, Elianor remains betrothed to Caelan Arbridge under marriage articles that trade debt relief for his future authority over Greyfen. She has now kissed Tomas and openly acknowledged their forbidden love, while accepting that secrecy offers no true future and discovery could cost him his life. She continues to intend secret visits despite the danger and has returned to performing household duties while emotionally transformed by the kiss. She possesses the signed marriage articles, estate ledger, small purse, walking cloak, willow splint, and knowledge of the lodge and stream route; she is physically well but frightened, divided, and deeply in love with Tomas, while outwardly composed before Alric, Caelan, and the household.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Alric remains physically weakened and emotionally exhausted, believing Elianor’s marriage to Caelan is necessary to preserve Greyfen and its dependents. He does not know the full truth of Elianor’s meetings with Tomas. He approved the eviction of Tomas Vale’s family from a Vey cottage after a failed harvest and rent increase and remains committed to preserving the estate despite the human cost. He possesses the estate maps, debt papers, and negotiated marriage articles; his goal remains survival of the Vey name, household, and property through Caelan’s settlement.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At Greyfen Manor as Elianor’s betrothed, Caelan remains wealthy, polished, intelligent, courteous, emotionally unreadable, and quietly proprietary. He has formally negotiated marriage articles granting him future authority over Greyfen’s finances, leases, steward, expenditure, and household staffing, with limited one-year employment and tenant-hearing protections. He does not possess proof of Elianor and Tomas’s relationship, though the household’s inquiries into her east-road absences continue. He possesses the sealed marriage articles and travel papers; he is physically well and confident in his expected control.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa remains Elianor’s maid and confidante. She knows Elianor’s east-wood visits conceal a personal attachment and recognizes that Elianor has returned from the latest visit emotionally changed, though she does not know every detail. She continues to protect Elianor through silence and practical assistance. She possesses her sewing materials and personal clothing; she is physically well, watchful, and quietly supportive.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell remains Lord Alric’s steward, managing account papers and creditor obligations while anticipating scrutiny or replacement under Caelan’s marriage articles. He does not know the full nature of Elianor’s meetings in the woods, but he contributed to the inquiry that sent groom Hobb along the east road. He supports rigid cost-cutting as necessary to preserve solvency and appearances and possesses access to estate records and account papers; he is physically well, financially anxious, and pragmatically obedient.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: At the abandoned forester’s lodge and surrounding east woods, Tomas Vale tends the goshawk, whose repaired wing has carried it through its first successful flights. He and Elianor have kissed and acknowledged their forbidden mutual love, but he has warned her that discovery could cost him his life and that secrecy cannot become a future. He cannot bring himself to end their meetings and expects her to return despite urging caution. He remains distrustful of noble promises and alert to Greyfen’s inquiries after Hobb’s search. He possesses a falconer’s glove, knife, lantern, improvised bandages, willow splints, sparse provisions, and the coarse brown cloak; he is physically well, guarded, joyful, frightened, and increasingly committed to Elianor.

Elianor and Tomas kissed beneath the birches and acknowledged that their love was forbidden, dangerous, and unable to become respectable through secrecy.

chapters.name: Ledgers and Debts
chapters.content:
## Ledgers and Debts

The rain returned with the ledgers.

It came before dawn, tapping at the high windows of Greyfen and running in silver threads down the glass. By breakfast the east pasture had become a sheet of brown water, the road a trench of mud. Elianor watched two tenant carts labor toward the village and saw that neither carried grain. The men walked beside them with their shoulders bent, as if even the horses had abandoned the idea of arriving anywhere.

At the end of the meal, her father sent for her.

Lord Alric’s accounting room smelled of damp wool, sealing wax, and the bitter herbs he drank for his cough. Master Pell had spread papers over the table in careful islands, weighing them with inkpots and a brass candlestick. The room seemed smaller than Elianor remembered. Or perhaps the numbers had grown large enough to fill it.

Alric stood by the hearth, one hand braced against the mantel. “Shut the door.”

She did so. “Is Caelan here?”

“Not yet.”

“Then why must we whisper?”

Her father looked toward Pell. The steward lowered his eyes to the ledger.

“Because,” Alric said, “there are matters a daughter should learn from her father before she hears them repeated by a creditor.”

Elianor removed her gloves. “You have already told me the estate is strained.”

“I told you the estate was in difficulty. That was before the miller’s note came due, before the west tenants failed to pay their winter rents, and before Arbridge’s factor sent a second demand.”

Pell pushed a book toward her. Its leather cover was cracked at the corners, and damp had warped the pages. “The totals are here, my lady.”

She bent over the columns. Grain owed. Coin borrowed. Interest accrued. The marks were neat, almost delicate. Beneath them ran the names of families she knew: Orrow, Fenner, Vale, Sedgewick, Tarrow. Some names had been crossed through. Others bore a red stroke in the margin.

“What is this?” she asked.

“Labor credit,” Pell said.

“I know what the words mean.” She turned another page. “I ask why the Orrows owe forty days of it when their rent is paid.”

“Their rent is paid in coin. The estate requires work as well.”

“Since when?”

“Since the harvest failed.”

Alric’s cough shook him. When it passed, he said, “The tenants use Vey land. They must contribute to its preservation.”

“Preservation?” Elianor laid a finger against the page. “The Orrow sons have been repairing the south wall for six weeks.”

“The wall is part of the estate.”

“They have received no wages.”

“They receive the right to remain in their cottage.”

The words struck her with the bluntness of a stone. “That is not payment.”

“It is more than many lords grant.”

Pell shifted uneasily. “My lady, the work is entered against arrears. If the men complete the days required, the account is considered settled.”

“Settled against what? The rent they already paid?”

No one answered.

Elianor turned pages faster. Labor demanded for ditching, hauling timber, clearing the flooded road, cutting peat for the manor ovens. In every case the days were described as relief. In every case the relief appeared beside a debt that seemed to change shape whenever she looked at it.

“Who authorized this?”

Alric’s face hardened, though not with anger. “I did.”

“Father.”

“You think I enjoy it?”

“I think you have made necessity into a law because it is easier to endure when written down.”

Pell inhaled sharply. Alric’s fingers tightened on the mantel.

“You speak as if the accounts are a cruelty I invented,” he said. “The creditors will not accept your pity in place of silver. Arbridge has advanced enough to keep our tenants fed through the last winter. He can call in the obligation if the marriage is delayed.”

Elianor looked at the sealed marriage articles lying beneath the ledger. “How soon?”

“His factor gave us until the first week of the new year.”

“That is less than two months.”

“Less than six weeks.”

The room seemed to tilt. “You said spring.”

“I said the wedding was intended for spring. Caelan has altered his intention.”

“And you let him?”

“What would you have me do? Sell the east wood? It is mortgaged. Sell the mill? Already pledged. Dismiss more servants? Then Greyfen cannot function. Refuse the marriage, and Arbridge claims the debts. Another lord will purchase the notes, take the land, and set his own terms. Do you imagine that man will reduce the rents out of kindness?”

“Perhaps we should reduce them now.”

Pell gave a small, disbelieving laugh before he caught himself. “My lady—”

“The tenants cannot pay and work without end. If we lower the rents, they may survive the winter. A living tenant can pay next year. An evicted one pays nothing.”

“A generous theory,” Alric said. “And with what shall we pay the creditors this year?”

“Use the money Caelan has promised.”

“It is not a gift. It is settlement against the estate.”

“Then let him wait.”

Alric stared at her. “You ask a wolf to wait while it holds the throat of the house.”

“No. I ask you not to feed it our people.”

For a moment only the rain spoke. Behind the wall, somewhere in the passage, a servant hurried past. Elianor thought of the Orrow boys at the south wall, their hands split by cold. She thought of Tomas telling her that compassion without changed commands was only another form of vanity. The memory gave her courage and shame together.

“End the unpaid labor,” she said. “Or at least count it as rent. Reduce the winter demands. Open the stores.”

“The stores are pledged.”

“To whom?”

“Arbridge.”

She looked at the articles again. Caelan had not needed to enter the room to be present in it. His signature seemed to darken every line.

Alric gathered the papers with trembling impatience. “You will be courteous when he arrives.”

“I have always been courteous.”

“Be more than courteous. Be agreeable. If he believes you intend to oppose every measure, he may decide the marriage is not worth the trouble.”

“Would that be a disaster?”

“For everyone who sleeps under this roof.”

His voice broke on the last word. Elianor saw then not the lord of Greyfen but a frightened, exhausted man surrounded by obligations he had mistaken for walls. She almost reached for him. Then she saw the red marks beside the tenant names.

“I am sorry,” she said. “But I cannot call this protection.”

She left before he could answer.

In the lower yard, the rain had slackened to mist. A line of men stood beside the stable, waiting for tools. Elianor recognized Orrow’s eldest son, though she had seen him only once at the harvest supper. His hands were wrapped in dirty linen. Near him, a girl no older than fifteen held a shovel too large for her.

“Why are they here?” Elianor asked the first groom she saw.

“Wall work, my lady.”

“Have they been paid?”

The groom glanced toward the steward’s office. “They are credited.”

“That was not my question.”

He lowered his head. “No, my lady.”

One of the men looked at her. There was no accusation in his expression, which was worse than anger. He looked simply tired of expecting anything from Greyfen.

Elianor turned away, unable to bear the sight without either weeping or commanding something she did not possess the power to enforce.

A horn sounded at the gate.

Caelan’s arrival was announced by the orderly movement of other people. Servants crossed the yard. Pell appeared from the passage, smoothing his coat. Alric’s secretary ran for the receiving room. Two black horses entered through the rain, their harness polished, their hooves scarcely slipping in the mud. Behind them came a carriage bearing the Arbridge crest.

Caelan descended without assistance. He wore a dark traveling coat untouched by road spray, and his gloves were pale gray. He looked first at the manor, then at the yard, taking in the roofline, the stables, the men waiting with tools. His gaze rested on the girl with the shovel.

“Greyfen appears industrious,” he said.

Elianor had not heard him approach. “It appears desperate.”

His eyes moved to her face. “Desperation often produces useful industry.”

“You have come to supervise the negotiations.”

“To prevent further misunderstanding.” He offered her his arm. “Your father has been generous with time. His creditors have been less so.”

She did not take his arm. “Have you ordered these men to work without wages?”

“I have ordered nothing. I am not yet master here.”

“Yet.”

A faint smile touched his mouth. “You listen carefully.”

“I am learning to.”

They entered the manor. In the long gallery, Caelan paused before the windows overlooking the east road. Through the rain, a figure moved near the far boundary where the woods began: a man in a coarse brown cloak, carrying a bundle beneath one arm. Tomas, returning from the falconer’s shed with feed for the goshawk.

Elianor felt the blood leave her face.

Caelan followed her gaze. “Your falconer?”

“Tomas Vale. His father keeps the mews.”

“An unusual amount of freedom for a servant.”

“He tends the birds.”

“Birds require supervision too.”

Tomas had stopped in the yard. For one terrible instant his eyes lifted toward the gallery. Elianor could not tell whether he saw her, Caelan, or only the rain. She forced herself to look away.

Caelan watched the figure a moment longer. “He is the son of the woman whose cottage was lost, is he not?”

Elianor’s hand closed around the edge of her sleeve. “You have been reading old accounts.”

“I read everything that bears upon an investment.”

“He is not an investment.”

“No,” Caelan said softly. “I had not thought so.”

He turned from the window and offered his arm once more. This time she took it, because Pell was waiting at the end of the gallery and because refusing would reveal too much. Caelan’s sleeve was smooth beneath her fingers. His posture remained courteous. Only his gaze had changed, becoming attentive in a way that made the air feel narrower.

Behind them, Tomas crossed the yard and disappeared beneath the stable arch.

Caelan led Elianor toward the accounting room.

“Let us discuss,” he said, “how best to preserve what belongs to your family.”

She looked at the closed door ahead and understood that the words included the house, the land, the servants, and perhaps herself.

Outside, the men lifted their tools. The first hammer struck the south wall, and Greyfen answered with a hollow sound.

chapters.name: A Courtesy of Chains
chapters.content:
## A Courtesy of Chains

Caelan’s first alteration to Greyfen was made in the breakfast room, beneath a ceiling painted with Vey hawks that had long ago lost their eyes to damp.

He did not announce it as an alteration. He merely unfolded a packet of papers beside his coffee and asked Master Pell whether the west pasture was still being charged against the mill debt.

Pell, who had been eating toast over the account book, set down his pen. “It is, my lord.”

“Then it should not be.” Caelan turned a page. “The pasture yields less each season than the interest accruing against it. Separate the leases. Put the pasture under direct management and transfer the mill’s shortfall to general estate expenditure.”

Pell glanced at Alric.

Lord Alric sat at the head of the table, a blanket over his knees despite the fire. He looked from the papers to Caelan’s composed face. “The mill cannot bear another charge.”

“Precisely. Which is why it must not appear to bear one.” Caelan dipped his spoon into the coffee. “A creditor does not need to see every weakness at once, my lord. He needs to see a structure that promises correction.”

Elianor heard the soft scrape of Pell’s pen before she heard her father answer.

“Those accounts have been kept together for thirty years.”

“And for thirty years Greyfen has mistaken habit for prudence.” Caelan smiled, not unkindly. “I do not suggest that the old method was foolish. Only that the circumstances have changed.”

He spoke as if offering a cloak against the rain. Yet, as Elianor watched Pell draw a new line through the ledger, she felt the room grow smaller around them. Caelan had not demanded authority. He had simply used it, and no one had stopped him.

Later, in the gallery, he intercepted Elianor on her way to the chapel.

“Your father has given me permission to make recommendations regarding the household,” he said.

“Recommendations?”

“For now.” His eyes moved over the portraits lining the wall: dead Veys in armor, silk, and fur, each painted with the confidence of a man who had never been refused. “The marriage articles already anticipate my responsibility for Greyfen’s finances after the ceremony. It would be foolish to wait until then before correcting what can still be corrected.”

“You mean to manage the estate before you own it.”

“After the wedding, it will be our estate.”

“Our?” The word escaped her more sharply than she intended.

Caelan’s expression remained courteous. “You will have a household to govern. I will have debts to settle, contracts to renegotiate, and creditors to reassure. We need not mistake different duties for unequal respect.”

“And the tenants?”

“Will benefit from competent oversight.”

“They are already laboring without pay.”

“Credited labor,” he corrected. “A distinction you understand perfectly well.”

Elianor felt the marriage articles hidden beneath the folded papers in her hand, though she had left them in her room. Their clauses returned to her with the precision of a lock turning: steward, leases, staffing, expenditure. Caelan had not added anything to the agreement. He was merely bringing its future into the present.

“Your courtesy is very careful,” she said.

“I have been told it is one of my better qualities.”

Before she could answer, a footman approached to say that Hobb, the east-road groom, had been dismissed.

The news moved through the servants’ quarters before noon. Hobb had been called to Caelan’s study and questioned about missing oats, though no count had shown a loss. He was to receive three days’ wages and leave Greyfen by sunset.

Elianor found Caelan in the stable yard, watching two men inspect the tack room. Hobb stood near the gate with his cap crushed between his hands. Rain had darkened his hair and run from the end of his nose.

“You cannot dismiss a servant on an unproved suspicion,” Elianor said.

Caelan turned. “I can, as your father’s future steward.”

“Future.”

“Again, for now.” He gestured toward Hobb. “The man failed to account for feed. Greyfen cannot afford careless habits.”

Hobb’s face tightened. “I told the steward the oats were spoiled. The sacks came wet from the south store.”

“And yet you signed for them.”

“Because Pell told me to.”

The stable hands went still. Elianor saw fear pass among them like a draft beneath a door.

Caelan did not raise his voice. “You are dismissed.”

Hobb looked to Elianor, not expecting rescue, only witnessing. She hated him for that helpless appeal and hated herself more for understanding it.

“Father should hear this.”

“Your father is aware.”

She turned toward the manor, but Caelan caught her wrist—not hard enough to leave a mark, not gently enough to be mistaken for affection.

“Do not make a scene over a groom,” he murmured. “Greyfen’s people are already anxious. They need to see that someone is willing to impose order.”

She pulled free. “Order is not the same as fear.”

“No. But fear is often the only language disorder understands.”

He released her with a slight bow, as though the moment had been nothing more than a disagreement over weather.

That afternoon Elianor went to the accounting room. Pell sat alone among the ledgers, rubbing his temples. The revised accounts lay open before him, their columns divided and rejoined according to Caelan’s instructions.

“Did my father truly authorize this?” she asked.

Pell did not look up. “Your father authorized Caelan to advise.”

“And you obeyed.”

“I obey the hand holding the seal.” He touched the Vey signet stamped at the bottom of the transfer order. “It remains your father’s hand.”

“But not his will.”

Pell’s mouth tightened. “My lady, a steward learns early not to distinguish between those things.”

She saw then what Caelan’s courtesy accomplished. A command could be resisted. A suggestion, especially one made before witnesses and dressed in reason, became a burden passed from hand to hand until no one knew who had first placed it there.

At dusk, Nessa helped Elianor remove her wet cloak.

“Was Hobb truly stealing?” Nessa asked.

“No.”

“Then why—”

“Because he could.”

Nessa folded the cloak over a chair. “Will he do the same to others?”

Elianor thought of Tomas, of the way Caelan’s gaze had rested on him beside the east road. “He has already begun.”

She waited until the lamps were lit, then slipped from the house by the old passage behind the kitchens. She told herself she needed to warn Tomas. In truth, she needed the sight of him to steady the ground beneath her.

The woods received her with wet branches and the smell of leaf mold. At the lodge, Tomas stood beside the open door, a lantern in one hand and the goshawk’s jesses in the other. The bird watched from its perch, bright-eyed and restless.

“You should not have come,” he said.

“You say that every time.”

“Today I mean it.”

His face was guarded. He did not move aside immediately to let her enter.

“Caelan dismissed Hobb,” she said. “He accused him of stealing feed.”

“I heard.”

“From whom?”

“Stable hands talk.” His eyes went beyond her, toward the path. “And Caelan watches.”

The warning settled between them. Elianor stepped inside, and Tomas shut the door.

“He knows about us?”

“He knows I was near the east road when he arrived. That may be enough for a man looking for a reason.”

“Tomas—”

“My father was summoned to the mews this morning.”

The lantern flame trembled as he set it down. “Caelan had one of his clerks there. They asked about hawk feed, leather, the sale of feathers. My father has kept those accounts for twenty years. They know every glove and hood in the mews.”

“Did they accuse him?”

“Not yet.” Tomas gave a humorless smile. “They said there was an irregularity. A missing silver clasp from a hunting hood. They said perhaps it had been sold.”

Elianor felt cold despite the fireless room. “That is absurd.”

“Absurd things can hang a man when the right seal is pressed beneath them.”

He turned away, checking the goshawk’s jesses though they were already secure. “Caelan asked whether my father had ever sent me beyond the east road on estate business. He knew the answer before he asked.”

Elianor reached for him. Tomas flinched—not from her touch, but from the window behind her. He crossed the room and pulled the shutter closed.

“I am not afraid of him,” she said.

“You should be.”

“I am afraid of what he will do to you.”

“That is the same thing.”

The words struck harder than anger. She lowered her hand.

“My father can stop him.”

“Can he?” Tomas faced her. “Caelan dismisses a groom, rewrites the accounts, questions my father, and calls it advice. Your father watches him do it.”

“He believes he has no choice.”

“Then he has given Caelan the choice.”

Outside, a horse moved through the trees. Both of them froze. The sound faded, but Tomas remained near the shutter, one hand on the knife at his belt.

Elianor understood suddenly that the lodge was no longer a refuge. Even the silence had become something that could be searched.

“What do you want me to do?” she whispered.

“Stay away.”

“No.”

“Then lie better. Do not come by the east road. Do not let anyone see you leave. Do not speak to me where another person can hear.”

“You make our love sound like a crime.”

“To Caelan, it is.”

The goshawk rustled its wings. A few pale feathers drifted to the floor.

Elianor stepped close enough to feel the warmth of Tomas’s body, though he kept his arms at his sides. “He cannot own every road.”

“He does not need to. He only needs to make every road dangerous.”

She looked at him, at the fear he tried to bury beneath caution, and knew that Caelan had already reached them. Not with chains, not with soldiers, but with the knowledge that any touch between them could become an accusation against someone else.

At last Tomas took her hand. His fingers were rough and cold.

“If they question you,” he said, “say nothing about this place.”

“I will not betray you.”

“It may not be betrayal they require. It may be one frightened word.”

She held his hand tighter. “Then I will be frightened and silent.”

He looked toward the shutter again. “Silence is what men like him depend on.”

The rain began in earnest, striking the roof in a thousand small demands. Elianor wanted to promise that she would defeat Caelan, expose him, compel her father to act. Instead she pressed Tomas’s hand to her lips, and he closed his eyes.

When she left, he did not kiss her goodbye. He stood in the doorway until the trees hid her, watching the path as if expecting the whole manor to come searching.

By morning, a new notice hung beside the kitchen entrance: all household accounts were to be reviewed under Lord Caelan Arbridge’s direction, and no servant was to leave the grounds without permission.

It was written in a graceful hand.

At the bottom, beneath the seal, was the word courtesy.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor and the abandoned forester’s lodge, Lady Elianor remains betrothed to Caelan under marriage articles that trade debt relief for his future authority over Greyfen. Caelan has now begun exercising that authority before the wedding by directing account changes, dismissing Hobb, and restricting servants. Elianor has warned Tomas of Caelan’s scrutiny and promised silence, while recognizing that her secret meetings endanger Tomas and his father. She possesses the signed marriage articles, estate ledger access, small purse, walking cloak, willow splint, and knowledge of the lodge and stream route; she is physically well, morally distressed, defiant, frightened, and deeply in love with Tomas.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Alric remains physically weakened and emotionally exhausted, trying to preserve the Vey name, estate, servants, and tenants through Caelan’s settlement. He has allowed Caelan to direct account restructuring and dismiss Hobb under the guise of recommendations, surrendering practical authority piece by piece while remaining dependent on Caelan. He possesses estate maps, debt papers, negotiated marriage articles, and formal authority over Greyfen commands; he does not know the full truth of Elianor and Tomas’s relationship. He is desperate, defensive, guilty, and increasingly powerless.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Caelan Arbridge remains wealthy, polished, intelligent, courteous, emotionally unreadable, and quietly proprietary. Before the wedding he has begun directing Greyfen’s accounts, dismissing Hobb over an unproved feed accusation, questioning Tomas’s father about an alleged missing silver clasp, and ordering household account review and restrictions on servants leaving the grounds. He suspects Elianor and Tomas’s relationship and is using threats against the Vale family to enforce obedience. He possesses the sealed marriage articles, travel papers, creditor authority over the advance, and growing practical control of Greyfen; he is physically well, confident, attentive, and increasingly controlling.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa remains Elianor’s maid and confidante. She knows Elianor’s east-wood visits conceal a personal attachment and now understands that Caelan’s control is spreading through dismissals and household restrictions, though she does not know every detail of the relationship. She continues to protect Elianor through silence and practical assistance. She possesses her sewing materials and personal clothing; she is physically well, watchful, and quietly supportive.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell remains Alric’s steward, managing the ledgers, labor credits, creditor obligations, and household accounts while anticipating scrutiny or replacement under Caelan’s authority. He carried out Caelan’s instructions to separate the west pasture and mill liabilities, recognizing that practical obedience is replacing Alric’s independent will. He knows tenants work without wages under the estate’s labor-credit system and possesses access to estate records and account papers. He is physically well but financially anxious, cautious, and obedient to the hand holding the seal.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: At the falconer’s shed, mews, abandoned forester’s lodge, and surrounding Greyfen grounds, Tomas remains employed under his father’s household and tends the recovered goshawk, whose wing has carried it through successful first flights. He and Elianor have kissed and acknowledged their forbidden mutual love. After learning that Caelan is watching him, he has become more guarded and warned Elianor to conceal the lodge and their meetings. Caelan’s clerks have questioned Tomas’s father over an alleged missing silver clasp, making clear that the Vale family may be punished for Tomas’s presumed insolence. Tomas possesses a falconer’s glove, knife, lantern, improvised bandages, willow splints, sparse provisions, and coarse brown cloak; he is physically well, wary, frightened, protective, and increasingly committed to Elianor.

Caelan began directing Greyfen’s accounts under the marriage articles, separating the west pasture and mill liabilities and placing household financial review under his supervision before the wedding.
Caelan dismissed the groom Hobb over an unproved accusation concerning spoiled feed, demonstrating that he could impose staffing decisions through courteous recommendations.

Caelan’s clerks questioned Tomas’s father about an alleged missing silver clasp and implied that the falconer’s household could face theft charges, using the accusation to intimidate Tomas and warn against insolence.
Caelan ordered that household accounts be reviewed under his direction and that servants leave Greyfen only with permission, extending his control over the estate before the marriage.

chapters.name: The Housekeeper’s Message
chapters.content:
## The Housekeeper’s Message

The first snow came as a rumor before it came as weather.

It silvered the north fence, whitened the roofs of the tenant cottages, and vanished by noon beneath a gray rain. By evening the ground had hardened in patches, and the puddles along the stable yard held a skin thin enough to break beneath a boot but strong enough to catch the light.

Tomas noticed none of it until he returned from the mews and found his father standing beside the empty hawk shed.

Old Vale was holding a scrap of paper.

“Another question?” Tomas asked.

His father folded the paper once, carefully, as if it were a wing. “Another visit from the clerk. He says the silver clasp has not been found.”

“Did he search the shed?”

“He searched the house.”

Tomas looked toward the manor. Its windows glowed amber through the dusk, each one a square of warmth that belonged to somebody else. “And what did you tell him?”

“That I have no clasp.”

“Then it is finished.”

His father’s mouth tightened. “You know it is not.”

Tomas did know. A charge did not require truth when the person accused had no money, no friends of rank, and no safe road away from the estate. The clasp might be found beneath a mattress. It might be discovered in a drawer Tomas’s father had never opened. It might simply be entered into a ledger as evidence.

“Go to the old lime kiln,” his father said.

Tomas turned. “Why?”

“Because a woman is waiting there.”

The answer was so unexpected that for a moment Tomas thought he had misheard. His father looked toward the manor before continuing.

“She came before sundown. Asked for me by the name my mother used. Not Vale. The other one.”

Tomas felt the cold enter him more sharply than the wind. “Who?”

“She called herself Mara Quill.”

The name stirred a half-memory. House stories, perhaps. A woman who had kept Greyfen before Master Pell, when Lord Alric’s hair had still been dark and Elianor had been a child. Tomas remembered hearing that she had left after a disagreement over the winter stores. Others said she had been dismissed for stealing. Neither story had ever been spoken loudly.

“What does she want?”

His father gave him the folded paper. “She said you would know.”

There was no writing on it. Only a mark drawn in charcoal: three short strokes beneath a crooked circle.

Tomas thought of Elianor at once. Of the way Caelan’s eyes had followed him across the yard. Of the clerk asking questions about a piece of silver no one had seen. A message meant danger, and danger at Greyfen had begun to move through every doorway.

“I’ll go,” he said.

His father caught his sleeve. “If it concerns the clasp, burn it.”

“If it concerns us, burning it will not make it vanish.”

“No,” his father said. “But it may keep you alive long enough to regret not doing so.”

The lime kiln stood beyond the old orchard, where the estate boundary ran into a belt of alder and thorn. Tomas waited until the stable lamps were lit, then crossed the grounds with a sack over his shoulder and a hood pulled low. Anyone seeing him would assume he was carrying feed to the outlying pens.

The rain had stopped, but the trees dripped steadily. At the kiln, the darkness smelled of wet ash and stone.

A woman stepped from behind the broken wall.

She was perhaps fifty, though hardship made age difficult to judge. Her hair, iron-gray and tightly braided, showed beneath a wool cap. She wore a patched brown coat and men’s boots, and carried a walking stick that might have been a weapon. Her eyes were pale and direct.

“Tomas Vale,” she said.

“Who told you I would come?”

“Your father.”

“He did not know what you wanted.”

“He knew enough to send you.”

She studied him as if measuring timber. “You have your mother’s face.”

“My mother never met you.”

“She did. The year before she left Greyfen. She brought me eggs when I was sick.”

Tomas lowered his gaze. “You were the housekeeper.”

“I was.”

“What happened?”

“Mistress Vey died. Lord Alric took charge of the household. Master Pell took charge of the keys. I told them the winter stores would not last if they kept counting spoiled grain as good grain.” Her expression did not alter. “They said I had become troublesome. I was given three days to leave.”

“And did you steal anything?”

“Only the truth.”

She reached inside her coat and drew out a bundle of folded papers bound with thread. “This is a list of cottages emptied in the last seven years. These are labor credits assigned against families who could not pay rent. Here are names of magistrates who accepted gifts before declaring Vey tenants in arrears.”

Tomas did not take the bundle.

“Why show me?”

“Because the Vey name is not the only name doing this.”

Mara spread the papers across a flat stone. The pages were crowded with figures, places, and brief notes. At first they looked like the ledgers Tomas had seen in the steward’s office: columns made to turn hunger into arithmetic. Then he recognized names from beyond Greyfen. Brackenmere. Hollow Ford. The marsh villages east of Valedorn. Estates owned by lords he had heard praised at feast days and blamed in tavern whispers.

“Everywhere the same,” Mara said. “A failed harvest. A debt advanced at interest. Rent raised when the crop fails. Labor demanded in place of coin. Then the labor is valued too cheaply, and the family remains in arrears. A court confirms it. The land changes hands.”

“Those courts belong to the lords.”

“Yes.”

“Then what are people meant to do?”

“Remember that lords are not the only people who can keep records.”

The words landed more heavily than any declaration of revolt. Tomas thought of the Orrows bent over the west pasture, working against a debt that seemed designed never to end. He thought of the clerk’s accusation against his father, a small silver clasp made into a rope.

“Who are you working for?” he asked.

“Tenant committees. Discharged soldiers. Laborers who have discovered that hunger makes them less afraid of punishment.”

“Rebels.”

“Call us what the people in the manor call us when they want the word to sound like a crime.”

“And what do you call yourselves?”

Mara folded the pages again. “People who intend to remain people.”

The wind moved through the alder branches. Tomas heard, or imagined he heard, the faint cry of the goshawk from the direction of the mews. Its wing was healed now. It flew beyond the clearing and returned when called, though lately it had begun to circle longer before coming down.

Mara saw him glance toward Greyfen. “You are thinking of someone there.”

“I am thinking of my father.”

“No. You are thinking of Lady Elianor.”

His hand closed around the strap of the feed sack.

“I know her name,” Mara said. “I know she walks in the east wood. I know she has been seen with you. I know Caelan Arbridge has noticed.”

“Then you know enough to keep her out of this.”

“Out of what? The world?”

“She has no part in your committees.”

“She has a part in the system that starves them.”

“She is not Caelan.”

“No,” Mara said. “She is the daughter of the man whose seal makes the debt legal. That is not the same as being innocent.”

Tomas stepped toward her. “Do not speak of her as if she were a mark in one of your lists.”

“I speak of her as a person who may be forced to choose.”

“She has chosen nothing against you.”

“Nor has she chosen for you.” Mara’s voice softened, which made it worse. “Listen to me, boy. I am not asking you to stop loving her. I am asking you to understand what love cannot mend. A private promise cannot survive a public system built on ownership. Sooner or later, the hand that owns the house will reach for the people inside it.”

Tomas wanted to deny her. He saw instead Caelan at the account table, touching Greyfen’s papers as though they were already his. He saw Elianor standing rigid while her father defended unpaid labor as necessity. He remembered her hands binding a bird’s wing with willow, careful and trembling, as if tenderness could become a law if practiced long enough.

“What do you want from me?” he asked.

Mara took one page from the bundle. “A message carried to the laborers at Fenwater. They need to know whether Greyfen’s west pasture has been separated from the mill debt. That information will tell them which accounts Caelan means to call first.”

“How would I know?”

“You work near the people who do.”

“If I am caught carrying this, my father is charged with theft. I may be charged with conspiracy.”

“Yes.”

“And you say that plainly.”

“I say plainly what the lords hide behind courtesy.”

She offered him the page. On it were only six lines of figures and a sentence written in a different hand: *The lock is weakest where the new hinge has been fitted.*

Tomas read it twice.

“Why me?”

“Because you can move between the manor and the woods. Because you know which paths are watched. Because you have already learned that obedience does not protect the obedient.”

He thought of Elianor. If he accepted, he would be carrying another secret to the lodge. If he refused, the message would go with someone less careful, or not at all. Neither choice was clean. He had believed love meant keeping danger away from her. Mara suggested that danger was already inside the walls, wearing a courteous face.

“When must it be delivered?”

“Before the next market day.”

“Where?”

“Under the broken saint’s bridge, beyond the reed beds. A woman named Sella will ask whether the hawk has found its weather.”

“And what do I answer?”

“That it has.”

Mara tucked the remaining papers into her coat. “Tell no one. Not your father. Not the lady.”

Tomas looked sharply at her.

“Especially not the lady,” she said. “If Caelan is watching you, he will use her to learn what you know.”

The warning struck him because it was true. Elianor’s compassion was not weakness, but it was visible. Men like Caelan knew how to turn visible things into levers.

Tomas folded the message and slipped it inside his shirt.

Mara watched him do it. “You have agreed.”

“I have agreed to carry a page.”

“That is how every larger act begins.”

She disappeared among the trees before he could answer.

Tomas remained by the kiln until the darkness settled fully. Then he returned toward Greyfen, taking the long route along the stream. The manor rose ahead, its windows bright, its walls dark with rain. Somewhere within it, Elianor was perhaps looking toward the east wood, waiting for the hour when he would come.

He had promised her silence as protection.

Now silence had become another burden he would carry between them.

chapters.name: The Cost of Silence
chapters.content:
## The Cost of Silence

The first sign was the empty chimney.

Elianor saw it from the western gallery while the morning lay grey over the lower fields. Every other cottage sent up a thin, reluctant thread of smoke. The village fires had been fed with damp peat, and the smoke clung low beneath the rain, but it rose. At the far edge of the lane, where three cottages leaned together beneath the hill, one roof gave nothing back to the sky.

She stopped with one hand on the cold stone of the window embrasure.

“Whose house is that?”

Nessa, carrying a folded gown over one arm, followed her gaze. “The Orrows’.”

“Why is there no fire?”

Nessa’s mouth tightened. “They were turned out yesterday.”

Elianor looked at her. “Turned out by whom?”

Nessa glanced toward the corridor, though no one stood there. “The bailiff came with two men from the creditor’s office. The family had not completed the extra labor days.”

“Extra labor days.” Elianor heard the phrase as if it belonged to another language. “They worked the west pasture all week.”

“They were short by four days.”

The folded gown slid a little on Nessa’s arm. Elianor caught it automatically, though her fingers were numb.

“Where are they?”

“Under the cart shed, I heard. The mother has a fever. There are three children.”

Beyond the glass, the empty cottage seemed to withdraw from her. Its shutters hung open. A child’s wooden hoop lay half-buried in the mud beside the threshold.

Elianor turned from the window.

“Take this gown to my room. Tell no one where I have gone.”

Nessa caught her wrist. “My lady.”

It was not a protest. It was a plea to remember the walls around them.

Elianor remembered. She remembered Caelan’s sealed articles in the escritoire, the permission required for servants to leave the grounds, Hobb’s dismissal, and the accusation hanging over Tomas’s father like a noose not yet tied. She remembered that every door in Greyfen had become easier for Caelan to close.

“I am only going to speak with my father,” she said.

Nessa released her. “That is not always safer.”

“No,” Elianor answered. “But it is necessary.”

Lord Alric was in the account room, though the fire there had been allowed to sink to coals. Master Pell sat at the long table with three ledgers open before him. Caelan’s clerk, a narrow young man named Venn, stood at the shelves sorting papers into bundles marked with red thread.

Alric looked up sharply when Elianor entered. He had aged in the weeks since the betrothal. His hair, once iron-grey, was now nearly white at the temples, and the hand resting on the ledger trembled before he folded it beneath the table’s edge.

“Elianor,” he said. “You should be with Nessa.”

“Where is the Orrow family?”

Pell’s pen halted.

Alric’s expression did not change, but his eyes moved toward Venn. The clerk lowered his head and continued sorting.

“The Orrows failed their labor credit,” Alric said.

“They failed by four days.”

“Four days the estate cannot absorb.”

“They have three children and a sick mother.”

“The cottage is required for another family.”

“Which family?”

Alric rose. The movement cost him; he steadied himself against the table. “Do not make this into a moral performance, Elianor.”

Her anger came so quickly that it steadied her. “I am asking why a family was put into the rain.”

“You are asking as though I ordered it for pleasure.”

“Did you order it?”

Silence settled between them. Outside, water tapped against the leaded panes.

Pell looked down at his accounts. Venn’s hand paused over a bundle.

At last Alric said, “Yes.”

The word was small. Its consequence was not.

Elianor stared at him. She had known he was frightened. She had known he had accepted Caelan’s direction because Greyfen’s debts stood at the door like armed men. But knowing was not the same as hearing him claim the act.

“Why?” she asked.

“Because Arbridge’s creditor required the west pasture labor accounts cleared before the next review. Because the Orrows had been warned. Because if the creditor calls the advance, Greyfen is seized—not merely one cottage, but the mill, the pasture, the kitchens, the mews, every room where people still draw wages.”

“They do not draw wages. They work against a debt that never diminishes.”

Alric flinched. “You think I do not know that?”

“Then why do you continue it?”

“Because the alternative is worse.”

He moved around the table, his face pale in the fireless room. “You have seen the roads. You know what happens when an estate is broken apart. The creditor sends men to strip the stores. Tenants are driven from their holdings. Servants are dismissed without payment. The land goes to someone who has no memory of the people living on it. I am trying to preserve the house so it can shield them.”

“A house that shields people by throwing them into the cold?”

“A house that survives may take them back.”

“Will it?”

The question struck harder than she intended. Alric stopped.

For a moment she saw him not as Lord Vey but as the father who had once lifted her onto the library ladder, laughing when she reached for books above her height. He had taught her the names of every tenant family. He had told her that a lord’s first duty was to know the faces of those who depended on him.

Now he could not meet her eyes.

“Caelan demanded the account be settled,” she said.

“Caelan did not demand it in those words.”

“Did he need to?”

Pell shifted uneasily. “My lady, the labor figures were already—”

“Master Pell, I did not ask you.”

The steward closed his mouth. His gaze was tired, not offended.

Alric said, “The articles give him authority to review the debts. He has advanced money when no one else would. If I defy him over every measure, he will call the advance.”

“Then admit that he governs Greyfen already.”

“I govern it.”

“You sign what he places before you.”

His hand struck the table. The ledgers jumped. “I sign what keeps it standing!”

Venn lowered his eyes, but Elianor saw the young clerk’s mouth tighten, as if even he had grown accustomed to the shape of that excuse.

Alric’s anger collapsed as quickly as it had risen. He pressed his fingers to his brow.

“I have buried a son,” he said quietly. “I have sold silver from the chapel. I have dismissed men who served this house before you were born. I have watched grain leave our stores while knowing we could not replace it. Do you imagine I do not understand the cost?”

“I imagine you understand it so well that you can no longer bear to name who pays it.”

He looked at her then.

That was the wound. She saw it pass through him, and hated herself for the satisfaction of having struck it. But beneath the pain was something else: recognition. He knew she was right, or feared she might be.

“You will be Caelan’s wife,” he said. “You must learn that choices are not always clean.”

“I know they are not clean. I am asking why the dirt must always fall on the same hands.”

He turned away.

Elianor left before he could make her pity him more than she pitied the Orrows.

She found the family beneath the cart shed at noon. Rain drummed on the planks overhead and ran in black rivulets along the packed earth. The children sat close together on an overturned trough. Their mother, Mara Orrow, lay wrapped in a horse blanket, her face shining with fever. The father stood when Elianor approached, then seemed to think better of the gesture.

“My lady,” he said.

His voice held no gratitude.

Elianor knelt in the mud beside the blanket. “I am sorry.”

He gave a humorless laugh. “That is a fine cloak for a sick woman.”

The words entered her more deeply than Alric’s anger.

“I will send a physician.”

“You sent a bailiff.”

“I did not.”

“No. You sent your father, and he sent the bailiff.”

There was no answer that did not sound like another arrangement of blame. Elianor removed her cloak and placed it over the children. She promised food, medicine, and a room in the old laundry until the family could find shelter. It was something. It was pitifully little.

The father accepted the promise with the stillness of a man who had learned not to trust promises made above him.

By dusk, Elianor walked to the east woods.

She told herself she went to warn Tomas about the new restrictions, about the danger to his father, about Caelan’s growing reach. She told herself she needed the lodge because it was the only place where her thoughts did not echo against polished walls.

The goshawk was perched on the split branch outside the lodge, feathers lifted against the wet. It turned its bright eye toward her but did not fly.

Tomas emerged from the doorway carrying a bundle of kindling. He saw her face and set the wood down.

“What happened?”

“The Orrows were expelled.”

His expression hardened. “I know.”

“You know?”

“Word travels faster than you think.”

She stepped beneath the trees. “My father ordered it.”

“And now you know what his orders mean.”

The accusation was quiet. That made it worse.

“I confronted him.”

“Did you bring them back?”

“I found them shelter. I am sending a physician.”

“Are they in their cottage?”

“No.”

Tomas looked toward the grey line of the manor through the branches. “Then the cottage is still empty.”

Elianor felt the familiar tenderness between them draw taut, like thread pulled too far. “What would you have me do? Break the door and declare the estate theirs?”

“I would have you do something that costs you more than feeling sorry.”

Her breath caught. “You think I have done nothing.”

“I think you have done what the house allows you to do, and called that resistance.”

“I have argued with my father. I have opened stores when I could. I have given away my own money.”

“Your own money comes from the same land.”

She recoiled as if he had slapped her. “Then I should give away everything and watch Greyfen fall? What happens to the servants when Caelan takes it? What happens to your father?”

“Perhaps Greyfen deserves to fall.”

“No.” She heard the word before she understood it. “No. You do not get to say that as though the stones are the ones who suffer.”

“The stones do not suffer. The people do. And they suffer now, while everyone waits for a more convenient time to oppose the men ordering it.”

He was wet from the rain, his hair dark against his brow. She wanted to touch him. She wanted to shake him.

“You speak as though action is simple,” she said. “As though you are not hiding something from me.”

His face closed.

The silence between them changed.

Elianor remembered, suddenly, how he had looked when she arrived: already troubled, already carrying a burden he had not named. There was mud on his boots that did not belong to the path from the mews. A corner of paper showed beneath his collar before he tucked it away.

“What have you been doing?” she asked.

“Nothing that concerns you.”

“Everything that concerns you concerns me.”

“Does it?” His voice broke on the question, and he turned aside. “You return to the manor. You speak of your father’s intentions. You ask me to be careful. Then you go back to the rooms of the man you will marry, and I am meant to believe that your carefulness is enough.”

“I am trying to protect you.”

“I know.”

The gentleness of it left her defenseless.

He looked at her again. “But sympathy without action is only silence, Elianor. And silence is what men like Caelan rely upon.”

She wanted to deny him. Instead, she saw the empty chimney, Mara Orrow’s fever-bright face, her father’s hand covering the ledger, and Caelan’s red-threaded papers being sorted in the account room.

“What action do you want from me?” she whispered.

“I do not know.”

“Then do not condemn me for not choosing it.”

“I am condemning myself as much as you.”

The words softened nothing. They only revealed how near the fracture ran.

The goshawk lifted from the branch. Its wings beat once, twice, and carried it into the rain-dark canopy. Tomas watched until it vanished.

Elianor pulled her cloakless shoulders together. “You should tell me what you are afraid of.”

“I am afraid that if I tell you, you will try to save me.”

“And if you do not?”

“Then perhaps I will become someone you cannot save.”

She reached for his hand. He let her take it, but his fingers remained tense in hers. For one breath they stood as they had stood so many times beneath the trees, joined by warmth against the weather.

Then Tomas withdrew.

“Go back,” he said. “Before they notice.”

Elianor looked at the lodge, at the bed of straw where they had once laughed over a bird’s first flight, at the man she loved who was already walking toward a life he would not share with her.

She returned her hand to her side.

“Do not mistake my silence for surrender,” she said.

Tomas’s eyes met hers. “Do not mistake your intentions for change.”

She left him there.

Behind her, the manor’s lamps shone through the rain, each window a small square of obedient gold. Ahead, the path disappeared among the trees. Between them lay every promise she had made, and the widening cost of keeping it.
