Tomas had told her to follow the stream until it bent toward the old lodge. He had said nothing more, but she had understood the urgency beneath his calm.

The woods received her.

She walked with her hood low and the cloak gathered at her throat. Branches scratched her sleeves. The stream ran beneath a skin of ice, speaking in small, concealed voices. She crossed where the stones showed through and climbed the alder bank, slipping once to one knee. Mud darkened the hem of her gown.

At last the lodge appeared between the trees.

Smoke rose from its chimney.

Tomas came out before she reached the door. He wore his coarse brown cloak, and a falconer’s glove hung from his belt though he had brought no bird. A pack rested on his shoulder. For an instant they only looked at one another, as if either might still turn back and preserve the life they had known.

“You came,” he said.

“You asked me to.”

“I did not know if you would forgive me for asking.”

“I have not decided.”

His eyes moved over her plain clothes, the mud on her hem, the absence of jewels. Something in his face broke open. “Then decide after we are across the marsh.”

She entered. The fire had been built high, and the lodge smelled of smoke, damp wool, and the dried herbs Mara kept hanging from the rafters. Provisions were arranged on a blanket: oatcakes, smoked fish, a flask, spare stockings, a coil of rope, and a wrapped bundle of papers.

Elianor stared at the papers. “What are those?”

“Copies. Debt tallies, labor credits, names of families pushed out. Mara says Sella can get them beyond the border if we reach Fenwater.”

“So even fleeing is a task for the resistance.”

“So is staying.”

She turned on him. “You make it sound simple.”

“No.” Tomas set down the pack. “I make it sound possible.”

Elianor paced to the narrow window. Snow lay unbroken across the clearing. “If I go, Caelan will punish everyone here. Nessa could be dismissed. Your father could be accused again. The Orrows are still in the laundry. The tenants have no one to speak for them.”

“Do you think you speak for them now?”

She flinched.

Tomas came nearer but did not touch her. “I know what you have tried to do. I know you opened the stores in your mind a hundred times before Caelan closed them in fact. But he uses your name when he denies them. He says the lady of Greyfen has agreed. He uses your marriage to make obedience look like mercy.”

“I can still delay him.”

“For how long?”

“Long enough for the roads to clear. Long enough to put the guarantee in force.”

“Caelan has already made Alric’s authority a decoration. After the wedding, he will have the seal, the accounts, and you.”

“I am not a ledger.”

“To him, you are the signature that makes the ledger lawful.”

The fire snapped. Elianor looked toward the papers, then at the rope and the small knife tucked into Tomas’s belt. “And what am I to be beyond the marsh?”

“Alive.”

“That is not a life.”

“It can become one.”

His voice was quiet, but it carried the stubbornness she had loved before she knew it was love. “Sella knows a safehouse beyond the border. It is a fisher’s place, hidden among reed islands. We would sleep on boards and mend nets. I would work with horses, birds, whatever hands were needed. You could teach children their letters, or keep accounts if anyone trusted you with them.”

“They may not.”

“Then you will learn something else.”

“And you?”

“I will learn not to bow every time a man wears a better coat.”

She laughed once, painfully. “You will starve.”

“Probably.”

“You hate bad bread.”

“I hate being told it is good bread.”

She moved toward him. “I have never washed clothes in winter.”

“I have.”

“I have never slept in a room without a lock.”

“I have.”

“I have never lived without Greyfen.”

Tomas’s expression softened. “Neither have I. That is why we will grieve it together.”

Outside, a crow called from the birches. The sound seemed to come from very far away.

Elianor sat beside the fire. “Tell me the route.”

He knelt and spread Mara’s map across the floorboards. It was drawn on old account paper, the ink faded where rain had touched it. He traced the stream with one finger.

“We leave before dawn tomorrow,” he said. “Not today. Today the roads are watched, and anyone seeing us together would carry the news before we reached the alder bank. We meet here again. From the lodge we go east, cross the shallow water, and follow the bank until the ground rises. There is an abandoned charcoal path beyond the reeds. It leads to the fishers’ track. Sella’s people will meet us at the old willow marker.”

“And if the crossing is flooded?”

“We use the rope.”

“If soldiers are there?”

“We turn south and lose a day.”

“If they follow?”

“We keep walking.”

She studied the map. “You have planned all this.”

“Mara planned the roads. I planned to ask you.”

“Why did you wait?”

“Because asking you to abandon everyone felt like asking you to become someone else.”

“And now?”

“Now I think Caelan is becoming someone else for both of us.”

She folded the map carefully. “I will come tomorrow.”

Tomas closed his eyes. Not in triumph. In relief so profound it looked like pain.

They spent the day in the lodge while the manor remained hidden beyond the trees. They ate sparingly, spoke in fragments, and tried to make a future from ordinary things. Elianor confessed that she had always wanted to see the sea, though she had been afraid to admit wanting anything that could not be inherited. Tomas told her he had once stolen a pear from the kitchens and blamed it on a hound. They argued over whether a cottage should have a red door. He insisted on blue. She said blue doors belonged to people who wished to be noticed.

By evening, the cold had deepened. They barred the door and fed the fire.

There was no promise that could make the lodge safe, no blessing to make their flight just, no name they could give their love that would cause the world to accept it. Yet when Tomas reached for her hand, she gave it to him.

They kissed beside the hearth, slowly at first, then with the hunger of people who had been taught that every tender moment might be their last. He touched her hair, her face, the scar where a bramble had caught her near the stream. She unfastened his cloak and rested her cheek against his chest.

That night they lay together beneath the patched blankets. The fire sank low. Tomas spoke of the hard life beyond Fenwater, and Elianor listened with her head on his shoulder. When fear returned, as it always did, he held her until it passed. When his own fear found him, she held him in turn.

Near midnight she said, “If we had met somewhere else—”

“We did meet here.”

“You know what I mean.”

“I do.” He kissed her brow. “Somewhere without Greyfen.”

“Somewhere without Caelan.”

“Somewhere you were only Elianor.”

“And you were only Tomas.”

He smiled against her hair. “I have always only been Tomas.”

“No,” she whispered. “You have been more than what they allowed you to be.”

Before dawn, he rose to add wood to the fire. Elianor woke at the movement and caught his wrist.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Tomorrow.”

“Do not leave without me.”

“Never.”

They slept again, their hands joined between them.

At Greyfen, Caelan Arbridge had not slept at all. In the steward’s room he questioned Master Pell until the old man’s fingers shook over the ledgers. He asked which servants carried messages, who used the east door, and whether the falconer had taken provisions from the stores. Pell denied knowing anything. Caelan dismissed him only after warning that silence could be entered as complicity.

Then Caelan summoned one of the younger kitchen maids. He spoke gently. He promised her wages after the wedding, if she proved useful, and hinted that useless servants would be sent away with winter still on the roads.

By sunrise, he had learned that Lady Elianor had left the manor before breakfast.

He did not yet know where she had gone. But he knew whom to ask next.

In the forester’s lodge, beyond the sleeping birches, Elianor and Tomas dreamed of a blue door opening onto a life neither of them had earned and both intended to build.

Neither heard the distant stir of men preparing to search the woods.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: At the abandoned forester’s lodge beyond Greyfen’s east woods, Lady Elianor Vey is disguised in plain wool clothing and has agreed to meet Tomas before dawn to flee through the marsh toward Sella’s safehouse beyond the border. She still loves Tomas and fears abandoning Nessa, his father, the Orrows, servants, and tenants to Caelan’s reprisals, but now believes remaining would make her an instrument of Caelan’s authority. She knows the first stages of Mara’s route—stream crossing, alder bank, charcoal path, and fishers’ track—and possesses the small purse, walking cloak borrowed from Nessa, willow splint, signed marriage articles, and knowledge of Greyfen’s passages. She is physically well but cold, exhausted, frightened, and newly resolute.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Caelan Arbridge has begun coercing household members for information about Elianor’s movements and Tomas’s possible access to provisions and routes. He threatened Master Pell with treating silence as complicity and pressured a young kitchen maid with promises of future wages and threats of dismissal. By sunrise he knows Elianor left the manor, though he does not yet know she is at the forester’s lodge or the full escape route. He remains physically well, polished, confident, proprietary, and increasingly ruthless, possessing creditor authority, staffing rolls, marriage papers, and influence over Greyfen’s clerks and bailiff.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa has helped Elianor leave in plain clothing by lending her brother’s wool cloak and agreeing to misdirect questions by saying Elianor went to the chapel. She knows Elianor may not return and is frightened of interrogation, dismissal, and Caelan’s control, but remains loyal and discreet. She possesses sewing materials, personal clothing, and knowledge of the women’s passages and household routines; she is physically well, anxious, and watchful.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor’s steward’s room, Master Pell has been questioned and threatened by Caelan about servants’ messages, the east door, provisions, and the falconer. He denied knowledge and was warned that silence could be treated as complicity. He remains in possession of estate records, account papers, and household seal procedures, but is anxious, physically well, and increasingly endangered by his obedience and knowledge.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: At the abandoned forester’s lodge beyond Greyfen’s east woods, Tomas Vale has prepared provisions, rope, spare stockings, a knife, lantern, bandages, concealed resistance papers, and Mara’s route map for a pre-dawn flight with Elianor. He has proposed reaching Sella’s safehouse beyond the border by crossing the stream, following the alder bank and charcoal path, and taking the fishers’ track toward Fenwater. He loves Elianor, has imagined a poor but self-made life with her, and remains protective and opposed to assassination, unaware that Caelan has begun searching for them. He is physically well but winter-weary, tense, hopeful, and afraid.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: At the abandoned forester’s lodge and within the marsh resistance network, Mara Quill’s mapped route is being used by Tomas and Elianor for their planned flight toward Fenwater and Sella’s safehouse. She remains unaware that Caelan has begun extracting information inside Greyfen, but her practical route planning and resistance papers support the couple’s escape. She possesses resistance records, coded communications, a walking stick usable as a weapon, a concealed blade, and knowledge of estate stores and paths; she is physically weathered and resolute.

Tomas proposed that Elianor flee with him before the wedding through the east woods, stream crossing, alder bank, charcoal path, and fishers’ track to Sella’s safehouse; Elianor agreed to meet him at the forester’s lodge before dawn and resolved the escape requirement.
Elianor and Tomas spent a final tender night together in the forester’s lodge, imagining a difficult life without titles or estates and reaffirming that they would leave together.

Caelan began coercing Greyfen household members for information, threatening Master Pell and offering a young kitchen maid favor and continued wages in exchange for useful knowledge; by sunrise he learned that Elianor had left the manor.

Caelan must use the information extracted from Greyfen household members to send soldiers to the forester’s lodge and intercept Elianor and Tomas before they cross the marsh; the coerced informant’s identity should remain uncertain until later revelations.

Elianor and Tomas must attempt to flee through the east woods and marsh toward Sella’s safehouse beyond the border, forcing them to choose between surrendering themselves and risking the people who helped them.

chapters.name: The Betrayal
chapters.content:
## The Betrayal

Before dawn, Greyfen Manor held its breath.

The rain had stopped, but water fell steadily from the eaves, ticking against the stones below Elianor’s window. In the darkness, the house seemed less like a place built for living than a great animal sleeping under a hand upon its throat. No fire burned in the corridor. No maid crossed the passage. Caelan’s men had made the household quiet.

Elianor dressed by touch.

Nessa’s brother’s wool shirt scratched her wrists, and the borrowed cloak smelled faintly of stable smoke. She bound her hair beneath a plain cap, tucked the small purse into her bodice, and tied the marriage articles beneath the cloak. The folded papers pressed against her ribs like a second, colder heart. She carried no jewelry. Even the silver clasp at her throat, a gift from her mother, remained on the dressing table.

At the door she paused.

Beyond it lay the chapel, where she had told Nessa she meant to pray. Beyond the chapel lay the east passage, the servants’ stair, and the garden door. If she moved carefully, she could reach the woods before the first bell.

She thought of Alric asleep in his room, of his thin voice saying that surrender was sometimes the only form of preservation left to a man. She thought of Nessa’s frightened eyes. She thought of Tomas waiting with a knife, provisions, and a road that led away from every name she had ever borne.

Then she opened the door.

The corridor was empty.

That frightened her more than a guard would have done.

She went down the servants’ stair, one hand on the wall, and passed through the laundry passage. The old stones sweated damp beneath her palm. At the garden door, a bar had been drawn across from the inside, but Nessa had shown her how the latch could be lifted with a thin knife. Elianor worked it loose. The bar shifted with a small wooden groan.

She stood still until the house settled again.

Then she slipped outside.

The cold struck through the wool immediately. Frost silvered the dead grass, and her shoes sank into the mud beneath it. She crossed the garden with her head lowered, avoiding the pale windows. At the wall, she found the loose coping stone, climbed over, and dropped into the ditch beyond.

For half an hour she followed the stream.

The woods received her reluctantly. Branches caught at her cloak; brambles tore the hem. Once, an owl lifted from a fir and vanished without a sound. She stumbled twice, and on the second occasion fell to one knee in the wet leaves. The willow splint she had carried from the lodge pressed against her palm. She had taken it without knowing why. Perhaps because it had once held a broken wing together. Perhaps because she needed proof that something damaged could still be made to fly.

The first grey light was showing when she saw the roof of the forester’s lodge.

Smoke rose from the chimney.

Elianor stopped behind the trees, nearly laughing with relief. A figure stood near the door, tall and motionless, a pack at his feet. Tomas turned at the sound of her breathing.

For one instant they only looked at each other.

Then he crossed the clearing.

“You came.”

“I promised.”

His hands closed around hers. They were cold, rough, and shaking. He lifted them to his mouth, pressing his lips to her knuckles as if he could restore warmth by devotion alone.

“I thought—” he began.

“You were afraid I would not.”

“I was afraid you would.”

She saw the exhaustion in his face. He had not slept. A lantern burned inside the lodge, throwing gold across the threshold. Behind him were two packs, a coil of rope, spare stockings, bandages, a loaf wrapped in cloth, dried meat, and a small flask.

“Is that all?” she asked.

“It is enough to get us past the marsh. After that, Sella has a place near Fenwater.”

“And if she does not?”

“Then we find work. I can trap. I can mend harness. You can—”

“Can I?”

“You can learn.”

The answer was so simple that tears sprang into her eyes. He brushed one away with his thumb.

“We will be very poor,” he said.

“I have been very rich and unhappy.”

“Then perhaps we shall be poor with better judgment.”

She kissed him, not gently. The lodge, the woods, the manor, and the entire cruel architecture of their lives seemed to fall away beneath the urgency of his mouth. When they parted, Tomas rested his forehead against hers.

“The stream first,” he murmured. “We cross where it narrows. Then the alder bank. We take the charcoal path until it breaks toward Fenwater. No talking once we reach the fishers’ track.”

“Could we leave now?”

He glanced toward the trees.

“Yes.”

A bird called beyond the clearing.

Tomas’s expression changed.

It was not a birdcall. Three notes, low and rising, came from the eastern woods. He reached for the knife at his belt.

Elianor heard nothing else. Then, from somewhere behind the lodge, a branch cracked.

Tomas moved between her and the sound.

“Inside,” he whispered.

They had taken only two steps when a voice rang through the trees.

“By authority of Lord Caelan Arbridge, come out and surrender.”

The words were followed by the click of crossbows being drawn.

Elianor’s blood went cold.

Figures emerged between the trunks—men in dark wool and boiled leather, their boots black with marsh mud. More stood along the stream, and more behind the lodge. They had not found the place by chance. They had come prepared to close every road.

Tomas seized the lantern and threw it against the wall.

Flame burst across the dry timber.

“Back door,” he said.

They ran inside. Smoke immediately filled the room. Tomas kicked aside a stool and dragged up the square trapdoor beneath it. A narrow storage pit opened below, but Elianor knew from the map that it led nowhere; the earth had collapsed years ago.

“The roof,” he said.

He pushed her toward the ladder. A crossbow bolt punched through the window and buried itself in the opposite wall.

“Elianor, climb.”

She went up. The rafters were low, and smoke streamed beneath them. Tomas followed with the packs, abandoning the provisions one by one as the fire climbed. Through a gap in the roof, she saw soldiers spreading around the clearing.

“There’s no way out,” she said.

“There is always—”

A second bolt struck the beam beside his head.

He looked at her then, and the lie died between them.

The soldiers shouted for them to come down. One voice called her by name. Another called Tomas a thief and an abductor. The accusation seemed absurd until she understood its purpose. They did not need truth. They needed words that would make the world interpret what had happened on their behalf.

Tomas pulled off his pack.

“If I go out first, they may let you pass.”

“No.”

“I can tell them I forced you here.”

“No.”

“Elianor.”

“If you surrender yourself, they will kill you.”

“If we both run, they may kill others to retrieve us.”

Outside, a soldier shouted that the lodge would be burned with them inside.

Tomas took her face between his hands. His palms smelled of ash.

“Listen to me. Go through the roof and down the western side. There is a hollow behind the ash trees. If you reach the stream, keep going.”

“And leave you?”

“I am trying to keep you alive.”

“You are trying to make my choice for me.”

His eyes closed briefly. “Then choose.”

The fire cracked below them. Smoke made her cough. Through it, she saw the rope looped over his shoulder and the knife at his belt. She saw the hopelessness of the roof, the ring of armed men, and the narrow strip of dawn beyond the trees.

She also saw the life they had imagined: a room with a leaking roof, bread earned by work, his hands repairing a snare while she learned to split kindling. It was not a promise the world had made them. It had been only a door they had tried to open.

“I choose you,” she said.

He kissed her once, fiercely.

Then he pushed her toward the ladder.

She fought him. He caught her around the waist, and for several seconds they struggled in the smoke, whispering each other’s names like accusations. At last the roof beam groaned above them. Tomas shoved her down the ladder and jumped after her.

The door burst inward.

Men rushed through the smoke. Tomas struck the first with the lantern’s iron handle, then drove his shoulder into the second. Elianor reached for the knife, but a soldier caught her wrist and twisted it behind her back. Pain shot up her arm.

“Tomas!”

He was on his knees, three men holding him. Blood ran from his temple. He looked toward her, not at the soldiers, and the terror in his face was not for himself.

“Do not resist,” she told him.

The words tasted like surrender.

He stopped struggling.

They bound his wrists with rope. Another soldier pulled Elianor’s arms behind her and tied them so tightly her fingers numbed. When they dragged them outside, the morning had fully arrived. The lodge roof burned, sending a black column into the pale sky. Tomas watched the flames consume the packs, the map, the food, and the last physical shape of their intended life.

At the edge of the clearing stood a Greyfen groom beneath guard.

Elianor saw only a bent shoulder and a face turned away. It might have been Pell’s under-steward. It might have been one of the kitchen boys. It might have been no one she knew. The man was crying.

A soldier shoved him toward the path.

“Move,” the captain ordered.

The groom stumbled. “I only told them what they wanted. They said my sister would—”

“Silence.”

The rest vanished beneath the crackle of the fire.

Elianor stared after him, trying to fix his face in memory. Caelan had reached into the household and found the place where fear lived. That was the betrayal—not merely that someone had spoken, but that the manor had taught everyone how necessary speaking might become.

They were marched toward Greyfen.

Tomas walked beside her when the path allowed it, their shoulders almost touching despite the soldiers between them. His wrists were bound, and blood darkened his hair. Elianor’s own hands throbbed behind her.

“Are you hurt?” he asked.

“Only frightened.”

“That is not only.”

She turned her head. “Are you?”

“Yes.”

The honesty steadied her more than courage would have done.

Behind them, the lodge collapsed in a burst of sparks. The sound rolled through the trees like a door being barred.

Ahead, Greyfen’s towers rose above the wet branches. Its windows caught the morning light, one by one, until the manor looked awake and watchful.

Caelan would have her now. He would have Tomas, the servants, the household guarantee, the marriage articles, and every frightened mouth beneath his command. Their flight had not freed them. It had given him a story, and with that story he could turn love into evidence, fear into law, and Greyfen itself into a prison with witnesses.

Elianor walked on beside Tomas.

Neither of them looked back again.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Captured outside the burned forester’s lodge and being marched back toward Greyfen with Tomas, Lady Elianor Vey remains bound and disguised in Nessa’s borrowed plain wool clothing. She chose to stay with Tomas rather than escape alone when soldiers surrounded the lodge, and now understands that Caelan can turn their love and failed flight into legal and social weapons. She still possesses the marriage articles beneath her cloak and the willow splint, though her small purse and escape provisions were lost or seized; her wrists are painful and numb from binding, and she is frightened, exhausted, grieving the destroyed refuge, and newly unwilling to submit quietly.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Alric Vey is unaware of the full circumstances of the capture or is about to receive Caelan’s account of it. He remains physically weakened, dependent on Caelan, and unable to protect Elianor or Tomas without risking the estate and Vey name. His guilt and fear are poised to become public submission when Caelan turns the failed escape into a charge against his daughter and her beloved.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Caelan Arbridge has successfully used coerced household information to locate the forester’s lodge and capture Elianor and Tomas before they crossed the marsh. He now possesses custody of both captives, their failed escape as evidence, the burned lodge and recovered provisions as proof of flight, and increased leverage over Alric, the servants, and the marriage. He remains physically well, polished, confident, and ruthless, preparing to define Tomas publicly as a criminal and Elianor as a disgraced woman whose obedience must be forced.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa remains behind after helping Elianor escape in borrowed clothing and misdirecting questions toward the chapel. She does not know whether Caelan has identified her role, but the capture has made her vulnerable to interrogation, dismissal, or accusation. She is physically well, frightened, watchful, and still loyal to Elianor, with knowledge of the women’s passages and the household’s movements.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell remains under Caelan’s scrutiny after being threatened about servants’ messages and silence. The capture confirms that information reached Caelan from within the household, increasing Pell’s fear that his records, seal procedures, and knowledge of the estate can be used against him. He remains physically well but anxious and endangered, still holding account papers and estate records under Caelan’s creditor authority.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Captured and bound after trying to draw the soldiers away from Elianor, Tomas Vale is being marched beside her toward Greyfen. He was struck at the lodge and has blood from a cut at his temple, but remains conscious, protective, and determined to keep Elianor from being made to bear the blame alone. His provisions, rope, route map, resistance papers, and lantern were lost or destroyed when the lodge burned; he retains only his clothing and perhaps the knife removed by the soldiers. He knows Caelan has military custody and fears execution, yet still loves Elianor and refuses to regret choosing her.
Elianor left Greyfen in Nessa’s borrowed plain clothing, crossed the garden and east woods, and reached the forester’s lodge before dawn to join Tomas’s planned escape.
Soldiers sent by Caelan surrounded and entered the forester’s lodge before Elianor and Tomas could begin their marsh route; the lodge was set alight during the capture.
Tomas and Elianor were captured and bound after Tomas attempted to draw the soldiers’ attention and surrender himself so Elianor could escape.
A frightened Greyfen household member was brought to the lodge under guard and appeared to admit that Caelan had coerced information about the escape, but the person’s identity remained uncertain.
Caelan gained physical evidence of Elianor and Tomas’s relationship and intended flight, along with custody of both captives, strengthening his control over the Vey household.
Caelan must stage a public hearing at Greyfen, present Tomas as a trespasser and would-be abductor, expose Elianor’s relationship to humiliate her, and use Alric’s fear to prevent an open defense.
Tomas must be beaten and sentenced to hang for violating noble property and attempting to flee with Elianor, while Elianor is confined to her rooms until the wedding.

chapters.name: A Public Shame
chapters.content:
By noon, the rain had polished the stones of Greyfen’s courtyard to a dark, reflecting shine.

The household had been summoned there as if for a proclamation. Servants stood beneath the covered walkways, shoulder to shoulder with stable hands and kitchen boys. Beyond them, tenants who had come to deliver winter accounts were held at the gate by armed men. The soldiers occupied the steps, the gallery, and the space before the old well. No one spoke above a murmur.

Elianor was brought out between two guards.

She had been given no time to change. Nessa’s plain wool dress hung damp and crooked from her body, its hem black with marsh mud. Her wrists were bruised where the cord had cut them. She kept her chin lifted, though every gaze seemed a hand laid against her skin.

At the center of the courtyard stood Tomas.

They had bound his hands behind him and fastened a rope around his neck—not yet tied to anything, but displayed like a promise. Blood had dried beside the cut at his temple. One eye was swollen. His coat was torn, and one sleeve had been darkened by rain or blood. He was upright only because two soldiers held him by the arms.

When he saw her, the pain in his face changed.

Not lessened. Sharpened.

“Elianor,” he said.

The guards shoved her forward. She nearly stumbled, then recovered herself. “Tomas.”

A stir passed through the servants. The name itself was an admission, Caelan had arranged it so.

Lord Caelan stood beneath the manor’s stone arch in a black coat untouched by the weather. His gloves were pale, his boots clean. Beside him stood Lord Alric, gray and unsteady, one hand gripping the carved head of his cane. Master Pell hovered behind them with a sheaf of papers clutched against his chest.

Caelan surveyed the courtyard as though he owned it already.

“Let the record show,” he announced, “that this hearing is called under the authority granted to Lord Arbridge by the marriage articles and by the debts owed to his house. We are gathered to establish the truth of an attempted abduction, trespass, theft, and conspiracy against the peace of Greyfen.”

Elianor laughed once. It came out raw. “You call this a hearing?”

Caelan turned his head toward her. “I call it an opportunity for truth to replace rumor.”

“You burned the lodge.”

“A fire began during the arrest of a fugitive.”

“You sent soldiers to seize us before any accusation was spoken.”

“Because your companion was preparing to flee across the border with you.”

Tomas strained against the soldiers. “She was leaving of her own will.”

Caelan smiled faintly. “That is precisely what a servant would say after corrupting a lady’s judgment.”

The word servant fell into the courtyard like a stone.

Caelan gestured. One of the soldiers stepped forward and emptied a leather pouch onto a table. Tomas’s folded route map landed first, scorched along one edge. Then a coil of rope, a flint, a lantern hook, and several pages of Mara’s copied accounts, their writing blurred by water. Last came the marriage articles, creased and mud-stained.

Elianor’s breath caught.

Caelan lifted the articles between two fingers. “Here is the proof of her promised union with Lord Arbridge. Here is the legal position from which she was removed. And here”—he indicated the papers—“is evidence that the accused intended to carry her into territory held by rebels.”

“They are records of stolen land,” Tomas said.

“They are stolen from Greyfen.”

“They were stolen from the people who made the land yield.”

Caelan nodded toward him. “You hear the language of sedition. The court should hear it too.”

“There is no court here,” Elianor said. “Only your men.”

For the first time, a flush touched Caelan’s cheek. “There is the authority of Greyfen, Lady Elianor. Your father is lord of this estate.”

All eyes moved to Alric.

He seemed to shrink beneath them. His face was the color of old parchment. “Elianor,” he said, barely loudly enough to be heard, “come inside. We can discuss this privately.”

“Privately?” Her voice carried now. “You let him bind Tomas in the courtyard, and you ask me to protect your comfort by whispering?”

Alric’s mouth worked. He looked toward the soldiers, then toward the manor windows, where other faces watched from behind glass. “You must understand what has been done. Caelan has authority under the articles. If I contest him here, he can call the debt. Greyfen will be seized. Everyone employed here—”

“Will suffer,” she finished. “So you will let him punish one man in front of them all.”

“I am trying to save them.”

“No. You are trying to save the name Vey.”

A silence followed, so complete that Elianor heard rain dripping from the eaves.

Caelan allowed it to linger. He wanted the servants to see her father defeated. He wanted them to see her isolated, disobedient, and exposed. He had chosen the courtyard because shame required witnesses.

A young kitchen maid near the scullery door began to cry. An older woman put an arm around her. Nessa stood farther back, pale and motionless, her hands clenched in her apron. Elianor found her eyes and saw terror there—not guilt, not yet. The sight steadied her.

Caelan unfolded another paper. “The accused entered a noble property without permission, concealed a lady promised to another house, carried tools associated with flight, and resisted lawful arrest. His own statements establish that he intended to deprive Lord Arbridge of his future wife.”

“I am not a possession,” Elianor said.

“No,” Caelan replied. “You are a woman whose reputation is now endangered by the reckless conduct of a man beneath her station.”

He faced the household. “Let every person present understand the consequence of confusing kindness with license. A servant may be treated generously, but generosity does not make him equal to his master. A lady may feel pity, but pity does not dissolve her obligations.”

Tomas looked at Elianor. “Do not listen to him.”

Caelan’s expression hardened. “Kneel.”

The soldiers forced Tomas down. His knees struck the wet stones. Elianor moved toward him, but a guard caught her arm.

“Let him go.”

“Stand back, my lady.”

Tomas lifted his head. “I’m all right.”

“You are bleeding.”

“I’ve bled before.”

The soldier nearest him drove a fist into his ribs. The sound was dull and intimate. Tomas folded, breath leaving him in a broken gasp.

Elianor screamed.

The courtyard erupted in movement. Someone shouted that the beating was enough. A stable hand took one step from the wall before another soldier raised a sword. Pell dropped his papers. Alric gripped his cane with both hands but did not move.

Caelan did not look at the man who had struck Tomas. “The accused has shown continued defiance.”

“Stop,” Elianor said. “I will go through with the marriage.”

Tomas twisted toward her. “No.”

“I will sign whatever you require. I will remain at Greyfen. Only stop this.”

Caelan looked pleased, but not surprised. “You see? Beneath the romantic fiction, reason survives.”

Tomas forced himself upright. “Do not bargain with him.”

“Be silent,” Caelan said.

Another blow struck Tomas across the mouth. Blood ran down his chin. Elianor felt the guard’s fingers tighten around her arm until her bones hurt.

The compromise she had offered—marriage to preserve the estate, obedience to protect the servants, silence to delay the worst—stood before her in the shape of Tomas on his knees.

It had not protected him.

It had not protected the Orrows, or the stores, or the household guarantee Alric had promised and Caelan had ignored. Every concession had been laid beneath Caelan’s boots as another stone in the road toward this courtyard.

Caelan read the sentence in a calm voice.

“Tomas Vale is found guilty of trespass upon noble property, conspiracy with rebels, attempted abduction, and resistance to lawful authority. He will be held in the lower guardroom and hanged at dawn three days hence. The execution shall serve as notice that Greyfen remains under lawful order.”

A woman cried out. Someone behind Elianor whispered a prayer.

“Tomas is not guilty,” she said.

Caelan turned to the guards. “Take Lady Elianor to her rooms. She is confined there until the wedding. No visitors. No correspondence. Her door is to remain locked from the outside.”

“You cannot confine me.”

“I can, and your father will confirm it.”

Alric closed his eyes.

Elianor looked at him. “Father.”

His shoulders sagged. “Do as he says.”

The words were softer than Caelan’s, and therefore more terrible.

The guards pulled her away. Tomas surged forward with a cry, but the soldiers struck him again and dragged him toward the side passage. Their boots left red smears on the shining stones.

“Elianor!”

She fought the guards until her plain wool sleeve tore. “Tomas!”

He turned his head, one eye nearly closed. For an instant the courtyard vanished: there was only the lodge, the broken-winged goshawk, the warmth of his hand over hers.

Then the door swallowed him.

Elianor was forced up the stairs. At the landing she looked back. Caelan remained beneath the arch, watching her with the composed satisfaction of a man who believed the battle finished.

He had expected scandal to make her obedient. He had mistaken the nature of shame.

Shame did not make her smaller. It showed her exactly what she had helped him build.

At the end of the corridor, the guards opened her chamber and pushed her inside. The lock turned behind her. A key scraped once in the mechanism, then disappeared.

Elianor stood in the center of the room, listening to the rain and the distant sounds of men carrying Tomas away.

On the floor lay the torn edge of Nessa’s sleeve. In her pocket, hidden beneath the borrowed wool, her fingers found the willow splint she had carried from the lodge.

She closed her hand around it until the wood pressed painfully into her palm.

Three days.

Caelan had given her three days to become submissive.

He had given her three days to decide what a woman could do when every respectable path led to a gallows.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Locked in her chamber at Greyfen Manor after being publicly exposed and separated from Tomas, Lady Elianor Vey is still wearing Nessa’s torn plain wool dress and retains the willow splint hidden in her pocket. Her wrists and arm are bruised from binding and guards, and she is exhausted, humiliated, furious, and newly resolved to resist Caelan rather than rely on compromise. She knows Tomas has been sentenced to hang at dawn in three days, Alric will not defend them openly, Caelan controls the hearing and guards through creditor authority, and her relationship with Tomas is known to the household. She wants to save Tomas, reach the servants, confront her father, and find a way out of confinement before the execution.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Alric Vey witnessed Caelan’s public hearing and failed to defend Elianor or Tomas, confirming Elianor’s confinement because he feared Caelan calling the debts and seizing Greyfen. He remains physically weakened, guilty, frightened, and dependent on Caelan, while still claiming that submission protects the household and its servants. He knows Tomas is sentenced to hang in three days and that Elianor has been publicly disgraced, and he is increasingly exposed as having surrendered his authority to preserve the Vey name.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Lord Caelan Arbridge has staged the public hearing, publicly exposed Elianor and Tomas’s relationship, beaten and sentenced Tomas, and confined Elianor until the wedding. He controls the guards, the hearing record, and Greyfen’s debts, and possesses the recovered escape map, provisions, resistance papers, and marriage articles as evidence. He remains physically well, polished, confident, and ruthless, believing scandal and the threat to Tomas will force Elianor into obedience and secure his control of the estate.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa witnessed Caelan’s public hearing and saw Elianor confined after Tomas’s sentencing. She remains physically well but pale, frightened, and watchful, with her loyalty to Elianor intact and her role in providing the borrowed clothing still potentially discoverable. She knows the household has seen the lovers exposed, Tomas is due to hang in three days, and Caelan’s guards control the passages. She retains knowledge of the women’s routes and household movements and may help Elianor despite the danger.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell witnessed Caelan’s hearing and dropped the records he had been carrying when Tomas was beaten. He remains physically well but anxious and endangered under Caelan’s creditor authority. He knows Caelan has converted the failed escape into a public legal charge, Tomas is sentenced to hang, Elianor is confined, and Alric has submitted. He still possesses his account knowledge and access to estate papers, though Caelan’s scrutiny makes using them dangerous.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Held under guard in the lower guardroom at Greyfen Manor, Tomas Vale has been publicly beaten and sentenced to hang at dawn in three days. His temple cut and swollen eye are joined by blood at his mouth and bruised ribs; his hands remain bound or under guard. He knows Elianor’s relationship with him has been exposed, that Alric would not defend them, and that Caelan intends his execution as a warning. He still loves Elianor, urges her not to bargain with Caelan, and wants to protect her and resist without surrendering his principles.

Caelan staged a public hearing in Greyfen’s courtyard, displayed the recovered escape map, provisions, resistance papers, and marriage articles, and exposed Elianor and Tomas’s relationship before servants and household witnesses.

Caelan had Tomas beaten in the courtyard and sentenced him to hang at dawn three days later for trespass, conspiracy, attempted abduction, and resistance to authority; Elianor was ordered confined to her locked rooms until the wedding.
Alric refused to defend Elianor and Tomas openly, confirming Caelan’s confinement order because he feared Caelan calling Greyfen’s debts and seizing the estate.
Elianor recognized that her compromises with Caelan had failed to protect Greyfen’s dependents and resolved to resist rather than become submissive after witnessing Tomas’s sentencing.

While confined, Elianor must confront Alric about surrendering Greyfen’s authority to Caelan and learn whether he will acknowledge or resist what has been done; household women and stable hands must begin quietly communicating with her despite the locked room.
The household must develop a way to free or reach Elianor during the wedding preparations before Tomas’s execution, using servants’ knowledge of Greyfen’s passages and movements.

chapters.name: The Locked Room
chapters.content:
## The Locked Room

The room had three windows, but none of them opened far enough to admit a person.

Elianor tested them at dawn, though she already knew what she would find. The left casement had been fastened with an iron bar on the outer side. The middle one looked free until she pressed her fingers against it and felt the new nails biting through the frame. The right window opened upon the inner courtyard, where a guard stood beneath the dripping eave with his cloak drawn over his head.

He looked up when she appeared.

She stepped back.

The room smelled of wet stone, extinguished fire, and the lavender water some unseen servant had left on the washstand. Her borrowed wool dress hung from her body in stiff, torn folds. One sleeve was dark with the stain from the lodge fire. Her wrists had gone yellow and purple where the binding had cut them. When she lifted her arm, pain moved from her elbow to her shoulder, a thin bright wire beneath the skin.

In her pocket, hidden beneath the seam, lay the willow splint Tomas had carved for the goshawk’s wing.

She held it now in her palm. It was no longer smooth. The years and her nervous fingers had raised a faint grain along its length. Tomas had cut it with his knife while she held the bird, his head bent close to hers, his voice quiet as rain through leaves.

The thought of his voice was worse than the memory of the hearing.

At the hearing, he had stood with blood at his mouth and still looked at her as if she were the only person in the courtyard. Not accusing. Not pleading. That had been the cruelty of it. He had looked afraid for her.

She sat on the edge of the bed and pressed the splint into her palm until it hurt.

Three days, the guards had said. Three days until dawn and the rope.

Beyond the walls, Greyfen moved with the strained silence of a house waiting for a storm to break. Doors opened and closed softly. Boots crossed the passage. Somewhere below, a woman dropped a pan and began to weep before anyone could scold her.

By midmorning, the rumors found their way to Elianor.

Nessa brought the first one with the breakfast tray. She entered with her eyes lowered, set down bread, watered milk, and a heel of cheese, then stood too long beside the table.

“What is it?” Elianor asked.

Nessa glanced at the door. “The kitchen boy says men rode east last night.”

“Caelan’s men?”

“He did not know. They took sacks from the stores and asked for the names of every family who had kin in the marsh.” Nessa’s hands trembled as she folded the napkin. “They say three cottages near Fenwater were searched. One was burned.”

Elianor rose. “Who says this?”

“Everyone says it, and no one says it. That is how things are now.”

The guard shifted outside. Nessa flinched, then bent over the tray as though correcting its arrangement.

“Listen to me,” Elianor whispered. “Are you in danger because of the dress?”

“No more than anyone.”

“That is not an answer.”

Nessa looked at her then. Fear had made her face thin, but beneath it was something harder than fear. “They already know someone lent you clothing. They have not decided who. Master Pell has been questioned twice.”

“About the escape?”

“About everything.” She swallowed. “But the women are speaking to one another. Not in the open. In the laundry, mostly.”

“What are they saying?”

Nessa picked up the empty cup, though it was not empty. “That if they hang Tomas, they may as well hang the rest of us one by one.”

The guard knocked once.

Nessa took the cup and went out.

Elianor did not eat. She stood at the locked door until the guard grew tired of looking at her, then returned to the window. In the courtyard, men carried fresh timber toward the north wall. Not gallows timber, she told herself. Repairs. A barrier against the wind. But she knew the shape of the beams.

The door opened after noon.

Alric entered alone.

For a moment she did not recognize him. He had always seemed larger than the rooms he occupied, his presence filling them with the authority of generations. Now his shoulders sagged beneath a plain black coat, and rain had silvered his hair. He looked like a man who had been left outside too long.

The guard closed the door behind him but did not lock it.

“Father,” Elianor said.

He stopped several paces away. “How are you?”

She laughed once. “You saw me dragged from the courtyard.”

“I saw.”

“You saw Tomas beaten.”

His mouth tightened. “I could not prevent it.”

“You could have spoken.”

“And done what?” His voice broke into anger, not at her but at the helplessness she had forced him to name. “Overruled Caelan in front of every servant? Declared that the debts were false? Summoned men I do not have to fight men he can pay?”

“You could have said it was wrong.”

“Wrong does not stop a creditor.”

“No,” she said. “But silence permits him.”

Alric walked to the cold hearth. He stared into the ash, as though the answer to her accusation might be hidden there. “You think I do not know what he has done?”

“I think you know each piece separately. The dismissed servants. The forced labor. The Orrows beneath the cart shed. The raids in the marsh. Tomas in the guardroom. You call each thing necessary until necessity becomes the name of your obedience.”

He closed his eyes.

“The estate was dying,” he said. “I borrowed against the mill to keep wages paid. I sold the chapel silver. I dismissed the hounds. Every choice bought another month. Then Caelan offered terms. Terms that would preserve the land and the name.”

“The name.”

“It is not nothing.”

“It is ink on old deeds.”

“It is protection.”

“For whom?”

He turned toward her. “For you. For every person who depends upon this house. If Greyfen falls, Caelan is not the only man who will come. There are lords who would strip the villages bare. I thought—”

“You thought you could surrender one room at a time and still call the house yours.”

His face changed.

Elianor felt the force of the truth between them. It was not enough to make her cruel. It made cruelty unnecessary.

“I gave him the accounts,” Alric said quietly. “Then the leases. Then the staffing rolls. I signed the order concerning the Orrows. I let him question the servants. Yesterday, when he sentenced Tomas, I did not stand.” He pressed a hand to his brow. “Each time I believed I was preserving the next thing. The estate. The household. The family name. By the time I understood that I had given him authority, there was nothing left in me that could take it back.”

“And so you give him me.”

His hand fell.

“The marriage can still protect you.”

“No.” She stepped closer. “It protects the story you tell yourself. You did not save Greyfen. You taught Caelan that fear is a leash, and now he holds it around every throat in this house.”

“Do not speak to me as though I wanted this.”

“Wanting is not the measure of guilt.”

For several breaths, neither moved. Rain whispered against the windows.

At last Alric said, “What would you have had me do?”

“Refuse.”

“With what army?”

“With your name, if it ever meant what you claim.”

He looked toward the door. “You are my daughter.”

“And Tomas is a man you sentenced by silence.”

The words struck him visibly. He gripped the back of a chair. “I cannot free him.”

“Will you ask Caelan to spare him?”

“I have asked.”

“Not publicly.”

“No.”

“Then you have not asked. You have bargained.”

Alric’s eyes filled, but the tears did not fall. “If I oppose him now, he will call the debt. Greyfen will be seized before the week ends.”

“It is already seized.”

He looked at her as though she had spoken in a foreign tongue.

“The keys are his. The guards are his. The judgments are his. You have kept the name and surrendered the house.” She closed her fingers around the splint. “Do not ask me to honor the ruin you made of duty.”

The guard knocked again, harder this time.

Alric straightened, though the movement seemed to cost him. “They will not let me come again.”

“Will you do anything before then?”

He had no answer.

She watched him leave. The lock turned. His footsteps went away along the corridor, slow and uneven, until the house swallowed them.

That evening, the second message came hidden in a bundle of linens.

Nessa pushed it beneath the blanket while pretending to shake out the sheet. Elianor waited until the guard’s shadow moved beyond the strip of light under the door. Then she unfolded the scrap.

Three words had been written in charcoal.

THE STABLES REMEMBER.

No name. No instruction.

The next morning there was another message, tucked inside a loaf that had been cut open and poorly mended with crust. It contained only a mark: a small circle crossed by two lines, the sign Tomas had once used to indicate the stream crossing on Mara’s map.

Elianor pressed the paper to her lips.

By noon, a stable hand came to the window with a bucket. He was young, no more than sixteen, and kept his face turned toward the courtyard.

“Lady Elianor,” he said without looking up, “the east tack room has a loose hinge.”

She understood nothing of it, yet everything. “Why tell me?”

“Because old Bram says Tomas never left a horse shod lame, even when the horse belonged to a man who cursed him.” The boy’s grip tightened on the bucket. “And because if they kill him, we know what they are willing to do to any of us.”

“Who is speaking?”

“Everyone, now. Quietly.”

He lifted the bucket and walked away before the guard could question him.

The locked room had not grown larger. The bars remained. Tomas was still below, and dawn was still approaching.

But the silence outside had changed.

It was no longer the silence of people waiting to be punished. It was the silence of people listening for one another.

Elianor placed the willow splint on the table. Beside it she set the charcoal messages, smoothing their creases flat. She thought of Alric’s bent shoulders, of Caelan’s polished hand resting upon the law, of Tomas looking at her through blood and rain.

She had believed resistance began with a grand refusal, spoken by someone powerful enough to survive its consequences.

Now she understood that it might begin with a woman carrying linens, a boy naming a loose hinge, a stable door left unlatched for one breath longer than it should be.

She went to the window again.

Below, the guard watched the door. Beyond him, servants crossed the courtyard with their heads bowed. None looked toward her.

Yet one by one, as they passed beneath the rain, they touched two fingers to their palms—the old stable sign for a bird held safely in the hand.

Elianor answered by lifting her own hand against the glass.

Then she began to plan.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Locked in her chamber at Greyfen Manor, Elianor remains bruised at the wrists and arm, exhausted and humiliated but increasingly resolute. She wears Nessa’s torn plain wool dress and keeps Tomas’s willow splint and the servants’ charcoal messages. She has confronted Alric and rejected his claim that surrender preserved duty, learning that he gave Caelan the accounts, leases, staffing rolls, and practical authority over Greyfen. She knows Tomas is due to hang at dawn in two days, Caelan controls the guards and legal process, and reprisals have reached villages near Fenwater. Household women and stable hands are secretly communicating with her, and she now intends to use their network to resist and reach Tomas rather than bargain with Caelan.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Alric is physically weakened, guilty, and emotionally shaken after visiting Elianor in confinement. He admitted that fear of losing the Vey name led him to surrender Greyfen’s accounts, leases, staffing rolls, and authority piece by piece to Caelan, and acknowledged that he failed to defend Tomas publicly. He still fears Caelan calling the debts and seizing the estate, but Elianor’s accusation that Greyfen is already seized has exposed the emptiness of his claimed duty. He has privately asked Caelan to spare Tomas but has not opposed him openly, and Elianor no longer trusts his protection.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa remains physically well but pale, frightened, and loyal to Elianor. She delivered food and concealed messages in linens while warning Elianor that Caelan’s men are searching marsh villages and that Master Pell has been questioned. She knows Elianor’s borrowed dress may be traced to her, understands the women are communicating in the laundry, and is helping sustain the secret network despite the guards’ control of the passages. Her knowledge of household routes and movements remains an important resource for the planned escape.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Tomas remains held under guard in the lower guardroom, bruised and sentenced to hang at dawn in two days. He is separated from Elianor, but his impending execution has become a focus for the household’s growing, concealed solidarity. He still loves Elianor, rejects bargaining with Caelan, and remains committed to resisting without becoming a murderer. His reputation for fairness among the stable hands is helping unite servants against Caelan, though he does not yet know the extent of their communication network.

Alric admitted to Elianor that he surrendered Greyfen’s accounts, leases, staffing authority, and judgment to Caelan piece by piece in fear of losing the family name, and acknowledged that he failed to defend Tomas publicly.
Elianor learned through Nessa and household rumors that Caelan’s men were searching marsh villages for rebel connections and had burned at least one cottage near Fenwater.

Household women and stable hands began secretly communicating with Elianor through laundry bundles, bread, coded marks, and stable signals, united by Tomas’s impending execution and their fear of Caelan’s authority.

chapters.name: The Women of Greyfen
chapters.content:
## The Women of Greyfen

The first message came sewn into the hem of a wedding veil.

Elianor found it when Nessa brought the veil for inspection, folded in a cedar chest among lengths of pearl-colored silk. The room smelled of starch, lavender, and the cold stone that climbed through the floor. Nessa set the veil across the bed and began to smooth it with both hands, her face lowered as though the embroidery required all her attention.

“Three white stitches,” she murmured. “Then two. Then one.”

Elianor bent over the veil. At the inner edge, where the thread had been drawn through the silk, three tiny knots stood in a row, followed by two and one.

“How many guards?”

“Three at the stair. Two at the service door. One walking the gallery when the bells mark the quarter hour.” Nessa’s fingers trembled once, then steadied. “The wedding women arrive tomorrow with flowers and ribbons. The laundry carts come before them. Brida says the guards have been told to search anything leaving the house, but not anything entering it.”

“Because Caelan expects danger to flee.”

“Because men who own a house rarely imagine it can open from within.”

Nessa looked up then. She was pale beneath the freckles scattered over her nose, and there was a bruise-colored shadow beneath each eye. Elianor remembered the borrowed wool dress, the dress that had become evidence against them and perhaps against Nessa herself.

“What will happen to you when he learns?” Elianor asked.

“He already knows enough to be dangerous.” Nessa folded the veil again. “I would rather choose the danger.”

The words entered Elianor more sharply than any accusation. For two days she had thought of resistance as something that must be done by those with weapons, maps, or courage enough to stand before a lord. She had not understood that courage could be a woman carrying soiled sheets past a guard, or a cook putting extra salt in a pot so a signal might be read in the kitchen, or a maid choosing not to save herself by giving up another person.

“Who else?” Elianor asked.

“Ysabet in the laundry. Brida in the kitchens. Old Fenner at the linen press. Two stable hands—Jory and Pell’s nephew, Renn. They do not speak of it together. That is how we keep it from becoming a confession.”

“And Master Pell?”

Nessa’s mouth tightened. “Frightened. Not faithless.”

A knock sounded beyond the door. Both women froze. The key turned, and a guard thrust in his head.

“The veil,” he said. “It is to be ready for Lady Elianor’s fitting.”

“It will be,” Nessa answered, with a servant’s mildness. “Unless your lordship means to wear it himself.”

The guard snorted and shut the door.

Only when his steps faded did Elianor breathe again.

That afternoon the laundry passage became a river of white cloth. Sheets, napkins, table runners, and lengths of altar linen moved through the manor in baskets borne by women who looked too busy to notice one another. Elianor watched from her doorway while Nessa argued loudly with a guard about a missing inventory mark. Behind the guard, Ysabet stumbled against the wall and spilled a basket of damp linen.

The guard swore. Ysabet apologized. Brida appeared from nowhere, shouting that the wedding broth had been ruined because nobody could count a basket properly. Three women began speaking at once.

In the confusion, a folded cloth slid across the threshold and touched Elianor’s slipper.

Inside was a strip of paper, a lump of black charcoal, and a message in a cramped hand.

WORKERS COME WITH THE FLOWERS. TWO ARE OURS. MARA IS ON THE NORTH ROAD. SHE HAS HEARD OF THE EXECUTION.

Beneath this, in a different hand:

RECORDS ROOM. THIRD SHELF. MILL ACCOUNTS. PELL KNOWS.

Elianor stared at the words until they blurred. Mara was coming. Not safely, perhaps not in time, but coming. The knowledge did not comfort her. It made the walls seem thinner and the hours more violent.

Nessa closed the door. “We can take you out tonight.”

“To where?”

“Through the laundry court, down the old stair, and into the workers’ lodging. Renn says a cart will leave at dawn.”

“Alone?”

Nessa hesitated.

There it was—the shape of the bargain everyone had been avoiding. Elianor could be smuggled away while the household women returned to their work. She could reach the marsh, perhaps find Sella, perhaps live long enough to become a story told by those who had remained behind. Tomas would still stand in the courtyard beneath a rope. The women who had risked themselves for her would still wake under Caelan’s authority. Her flight would be another private sacrifice, beautiful only because others paid for it.

“I will not go to the marsh,” Elianor said.

Nessa’s expression tightened with fear. “My lady—”

“I will go to the courtyard.”

“To Tomas?”

“To everyone.”

The word seemed to alter the room. Outside, rain ticked against the leaded panes. Elianor felt the old instinct rise in her—the instinct to be careful, to make her defiance appear reasonable, to preserve some narrow bridge by which her father might still claim innocence and Caelan might still pretend courtesy. She had crossed that bridge already. It had led to the locked room, to Tomas’s blood on the stones, to villages burning beyond Fenwater.

“No more bargains made in private,” she said. “If Caelan means to call it law, let him hear the truth in public.”

Nessa swallowed. “Then we need proof.”

They found Master Pell after midnight in the passage behind the linen press. He came carrying a lamp with its wick turned low. His shoulders had collapsed inward since the hearing, but his eyes remained keen.

“I thought the records were under Caelan’s seal,” Elianor said.

“Some are. Not all.” Pell glanced toward the dark stair. “He took the ledgers he understood—the debt summaries, the marriage articles, the staffing rolls. But the old working books remain. Men like Caelan trust totals. They do not read the hands that made them.”

He led them through a narrow door concealed behind hanging blankets. The passage beyond smelled of dust and mouse nests. Elianor had lived at Greyfen all her life and never known it existed.

At the third shelf, Pell drew out three ledgers. Their leather bindings were cracked, their pages warped by damp. He opened the first to a mill account. Beside a tenant’s name, the labor tally had been entered in one hand and altered in another. A charge for four days had become nine. A rent payment marked received had been crossed out and replaced with arrears.

“Here,” Pell whispered. “And here. The ink differs. The dates do not.”

The second book held eviction orders. The third contained lists of grain seized from Fenwater and neighboring villages, all marked as creditor recovery though no court seal appeared beside them.

Elianor’s hands grew cold.

“Take the pages,” Pell said. “Not the books. Pages can hide. Books announce themselves.”

He gave her a thin knife used for trimming quills. She cut out the entries while he copied names and dates onto scraps. For the Orrows, she took the page bearing the false labor tally. For Fenwater, she took the grain seizure list. At the back of the third ledger she found a memorandum in Caelan’s clerk’s hand: AFTER MARRIAGE, REMOVE EXCESS STAFF; RESISTANCE SYMPATHIZERS TO BE TRANSFERRED OR CHARGED.

Elianor folded the memorandum against her skin.

The disguise was Nessa’s idea. The plain wool dress had been burned at the hem during the capture, but another dress was found in the laundry—a widow’s brown gown, broad at the waist and smelling faintly of lye. Ysabet cut Elianor’s hair beneath a linen cap. Brida rubbed flour into her face and tied a red cloth over her mouth.

“Your hands,” Brida said. “A lady’s hands will betray you.”

She pressed Elianor’s palms into a basin of cold ash and soap until the skin reddened. Nessa placed a basket in her arms, heavy with folded sheets. Beneath the sheets lay the copied records, the knife, and a length of cord knotted three times.

“If the first guard stops you,” Nessa said, “you are carrying linen to the chapel.”

“And if the second stops me?”

“Drop the basket.”

“And the third?”

Nessa met her eyes. “Then we make him choose whether to touch every woman in Greyfen.”

For the first time in days, Elianor almost smiled.

The plan began with a bell. At the quarter hour before dawn, Brida would send a kitchen boy running for the physician, claiming that one of the visiting flower women had collapsed. Ysabet would loose the laundry carts into the lower court. Renn and Jory would jam the stable gate with a broken axle. The two rebel sympathizers among the incoming workers would not reveal themselves until the courtyard filled.

And Elianor would walk out among the women.

Not flee. Walk.

At the door, Nessa caught her sleeve. “If you reach Tomas, do not let him make you go.”

“He will try.”

“He believes saving you is the same as saving the world.”

Elianor looked down at the hidden papers pressing against her ribs. “Then tomorrow I will teach him that the world must be saved with him in it.”

Beyond the walls, somewhere on the north road, Mara was fighting her way toward Greyfen. In the lower guardroom, Tomas waited for dawn. Around them, the women of the manor carried their baskets, stirred their pots, folded their linens, and made ready to turn a wedding into an accusation.

Elianor lifted the basket.

The locked room opened.

She stepped into the passage, and Greyfen held its breath.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Elianor has chosen public defiance rather than escape alone. Disguised as a laundry worker in a widow’s brown gown, linen cap, and red face cloth, she is moving through the service passage before dawn toward the courtyard where Tomas is to die. She carries copied records proving falsified labor tallies, fraudulent arrears, grain seizures, and Caelan’s plan to purge staff and punish sympathizers, along with a quill knife and cord. She knows two rebel sympathizers are among the incoming wedding workers and that Mara is approaching from the north road. She remains bruised, exhausted, and afraid, but is resolved to expose Caelan before servants, tenants, and nobles rather than make another private sacrifice.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Nessa is physically well but pale, frightened, and committed to Elianor’s resistance. She has organized the women’s covert communication and escape plan, knows the laundry routes and guard movements, and helped disguise Elianor and conceal the copied records. She intends to create distractions with Ysabet, Brida, Fenner, and the stable hands during the wedding preparations, despite the danger of Caelan’s retaliation. Her relationship with Elianor has shifted from servant and mistress toward trusted conspirators.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Master Pell remains anxious and under Caelan’s scrutiny but has chosen to aid Elianor. He knows the location and meaning of concealed working ledgers, guided Elianor through the hidden records passage, and helped copy evidence of altered labor tallies, false arrears, grain seizures, and planned punishment of sympathizers. He remains physically well and possesses his account knowledge, though discovery could expose him to accusation or arrest.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: At Greyfen Manor, Tomas remains bruised and imprisoned in the lower guardroom, sentenced to hang at dawn. He does not yet know that Elianor has rejected escape alone or that the women and stable hands are organizing a public intervention. He remains committed to protecting Elianor without murdering Caelan, and his impending execution continues to unite the household against Caelan.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Mara Quill is approaching Greyfen by the north road after receiving word of Tomas’s impending execution. She remains connected to the marsh resistance, carries her practical knowledge of routes and resistance organization, and is trying to reach the estate before the execution. Her exact position and whether she can enter Greyfen remain unknown.

Nessa, Ysabet, Brida, Fenner, and allied stable hands organized a covert route through the laundry passage and lower stair to free Elianor from confinement during the wedding preparations, while arranging distractions at the guards and stable gate.
Elianor rejected escaping alone and chose to enter the public courtyard to oppose Caelan before Tomas’s execution, turning the servants’ private aid into open defiance.

Master Pell led Elianor to concealed estate records showing falsified labor tallies, fraudulent arrears, grain seizures from Fenwater, and Caelan’s plan to remove excess staff and punish resistance sympathizers; Elianor concealed copied pages as evidence.
The household disguised Elianor as a laundry worker in a widow’s brown gown and prepared to move her through the manor carrying the copied records, a knife, and cord before dawn.
Household messages revealed that two rebel sympathizers were arriving among the wedding workers and that Mara was approaching Greyfen by the north road after learning of Tomas’s execution.

chapters.name: The Gallows in the Rain
chapters.content:
## The Gallows in the Rain

Rain had begun before dawn and did not fall so much as inhabit Greyfen.

It slicked the flagstones, darkened the walls, and streamed from the mouths of the carved stone hounds above the courtyard gate. It gathered in the ruts where carts had carried wedding timber, turning the earth the color of old blood. Beyond the eastern roofs, the sky was a single low sheet of iron.

In the service passage, Elianor heard the bells.

One. Two. Three.

The execution bell had a cracked tongue. Each stroke seemed to hesitate before it died, as though even the bell understood what it was being made to announce.

Nessa caught Elianor’s arm. “Not yet.”

“I must go now.”

“The guard at the lower stair has moved.”

“Then we go while he is moving.”

Nessa looked at her borrowed gown, the coarse brown wool hanging from her shoulders, the linen cap hiding her hair, and the red cloth tied over the lower half of her face. Only her eyes belonged to Lady Elianor Vey. They were gray, sleepless, and fixed upon the strip of daylight beneath the passage door.

From the courtyard came the muffled stir of a crowd. Boots. Hooves. The creak of the gallows being tested. Voices kept low by fear.

Nessa’s fingers tightened. “If they catch you before you speak—”

“They will catch me after I speak.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No,” Elianor said. “It is the only difference that matters.”

Nessa’s face folded for an instant. Then she nodded and opened the door.

They passed into the laundry yard with a basket between them. Steam rose from the stones. Women moved around the boiling vats, bent beneath sheets and wedding linens, their hands red from lye and cold. No one looked directly at Elianor. That was the disguise: not the gown, nor the cap, nor the cloth, but the certainty that a servant might pass unseen.

At the far end, Ysabet dropped a stack of folded napkins.

The crash made the nearest guard turn. Brida began shouting that the wedding tablecloths had been ruined. Two kitchen boys ran across the yard with armfuls of wet linen, blocking the archway. Fenner, broad as a door and gray with age, stood beside the laundry gate and leaned heavily upon a broom.

“Go,” he said without looking at her.

Elianor left the basket with Nessa and crossed beneath the arch.

The courtyard opened before her.

It had been dressed for a wedding and prepared for a hanging. White ribbons clung wetly to the posts. Laurel garlands sagged from the balcony. At the center stood the gallows, newly raised from black timber, the rope pale against the rain. A table had been set beneath an awning for the witnessing lords, though no food waited upon it. Caelan had wanted ceremony without comfort, spectacle without mercy.

Tomas was being brought from the lower passage.

His hands were tied before him. His face was swollen where the guards had beaten him, and one eye had narrowed almost shut. He walked slowly, but he did not stumble. His hair was wet against his brow. The gray shirt they had given him clung to his shoulders, and dark stains marked the bandage at his ribs.

Elianor stopped breathing.

For three days she had imagined this moment in fragments: Tomas dead, Tomas afraid, Tomas looking at her with the wound of her failure in his eyes. None of those imaginings had prepared her for his living face.

He saw the laundry worker standing beside the rain barrel.

His gaze moved past her once, then returned.

Elianor touched the cord hidden beneath her gown. A signal, if he understood. A promise, if he did not.

Tomas’s expression changed. Not relief. Terror.

He shook his head.

She stepped into the open.

“Stop.”

Her voice was muffled by the red cloth, but it carried farther than she expected. The guards halted. The crowd shifted. A tenant woman near the wall lifted her head. At the awning, Lord Caelan turned from the magistrate seated beside him.

Elianor untied the cloth and let it fall.

Rain struck her uncovered face.

“Stop,” she said again. “This sentence is false.”

A murmur moved through the courtyard. Someone whispered her name. Someone else made the sign against evil.

Caelan’s composure did not break, but it hardened. “Lady Elianor,” he said. “You have been confined by lawful order.”

“By your order.”

“Return to your rooms.”

“No.”

The word seemed too small for the courtyard, yet it stood there between them.

Alric was beneath the awning, seated in a carved chair as though his failing body required the protection of ceremony. He looked older than he had the night before. His hands trembled on the arms of the chair. At the sight of Elianor, he rose halfway and then sank back.

“Daughter,” he whispered.

She did not look at him. If she looked, she might remember him as the man who had carried her through the east garden when she was a child, or who had taught her the names of the winter stars. Today he was the lord of Greyfen, and Greyfen was watching.

Caelan descended from the awning. His boots made small splashes in the mud.

“You are distressed,” he said. “The conditions of your confinement have affected your judgment.”

“My judgment is written in your ledgers.”

She drew the copied pages from beneath her gown. The cord had kept them dry enough, though the edges were damp and curling. She held them overhead.

“This is the labor account for Fenwater. It says forty-three days of unpaid work were owed by the fishers there. The original tally, before your clerk altered it, records twenty-seven. Sixteen days were invented.”

The tenant woman by the wall made a sound like a swallowed sob.

Elianor turned so all could hear. “Here is the arrears book for the Orrow family. They were expelled for missing four labor-credit days. Their rent was raised after the harvest failed, then the days required to pay it were increased when they could not meet the first demand. Their debt was made impossible by design.”

Caelan glanced toward the guards. “Seize those papers.”

No one moved.

The guards looked at the crowd, at the servants lining the walls, at the stable gate where three men had quietly dragged a bar into place.

Caelan’s voice sharpened. “Seize her.”

Elianor raised the next page.

“This is a grain seizure order, bearing Lord Caelan Arbridge’s seal. It removed winter grain from Fenwater after the first raid. It says the grain was payment for rebellion. No judgment was issued. No hearing was held. The families were left with seed grain taken from their hands.”

A man in a patched fisher’s coat shouted, “My children ate reeds that week!”

Another voice answered from the crowd, “They took ours too!”

The magistrate stood. “This proceeding cannot continue amid disorder.”

“It has never been a proceeding,” Elianor said. “It is an execution dressed in law.”

Tomas had reached the foot of the gallows. The executioner stood behind him, hooded and silent, one hand upon the rope. He looked toward the gate, measuring the distance.

Elianor saw Caelan’s men begin to close around him.

She drew the quill knife from her sleeve. Not to use against Caelan. She slashed the cord binding the pages together, and the wet sheets scattered across the courtyard.

“Read them!” she cried. “If you can read, read what they have done to you.”

The wind took several pages. They skittered over the stones and lodged against boots. A stable boy snatched one up. Master Pell emerged from the servants’ line, pale and shaking, and caught another before it struck a puddle.

“Master Pell,” Caelan said softly. “Remember your position.”

Pell looked at the page. “I remember it,” he said. “That is why I know this is true.”

A guard seized him by the collar.

The courtyard broke.

It did not happen as one shout, but as a hundred acts of refusal arriving together. The stable hands slammed the gate shut and dropped the iron bar into its brackets. Fenner struck the nearest guard across the wrist with his broom handle. A laundress threw a bucket of scalding water—not boiling, but hot enough—into the face of a soldier rushing toward Elianor. Kitchen workers overturned the table beneath the awning, sending cups and ink across the magistrate’s robes.

The executioner reached for Tomas.

Tomas drove his shoulder into the man’s chest. They fell against the gallows post. The rope swung above them, empty.

“Get him free!” Elianor shouted.

Two stable hands ran forward. One seized the executioner’s arm; the other kicked the stool from beneath the rope and dragged it away. A guard struck him with the butt of a spear. He went down, blood brightening the rain at his temple.

Tomas turned toward him instead of fleeing.

“No!” Elianor cried. “Tomas, go!”

But Tomas bent and hauled the wounded man upright.

Caelan backed toward the awning. For the first time since Elianor had known him, his face showed something unpolished. Not fear exactly. The insult of danger. The discovery that people he had counted could become people who acted.

“Archers,” he shouted. “Call the archers from the west wall.”

The west-wall sentry did not answer.

Mara appeared above the gatehouse.
