She was soaked to the skin, a dark cloak plastered against her shoulders, and one hand gripped the railing. Behind her stood two strangers in the rough clothes of wedding laborers. One held a stolen crossbow pointed at the courtyard guards. The other was cutting the bell rope.

“Mara,” Tomas breathed.

She looked down at him. “You took your time.”

“I was detained.”

The answer, absurdly familiar, passed through the rain like a spark.

Caelan pointed at Elianor. “She has incited treason. Kill anyone who resists.”

The soldiers lifted their weapons.

For one suspended moment, every person in the courtyard seemed to understand the shape of the choice. Obey, and the old order would survive another hour. Resist, and blood would answer blood, with no promise that anything better would follow.

Elianor stepped between the soldiers and the crowd.

“Look at us,” she said to the guards. “Look at the people you are being ordered to kill. They are not rebels in a distant village. They are your cooks, your brothers, your mothers. Some of you have debts written in those pages. Some of you have been paid in promises that Caelan can erase with one stroke.”

A young guard lowered his spear.

The captain struck him across the mouth. “Raise it!”

The young man raised it—not toward Elianor, but against the captain’s knee.

The captain fell with a cry.

Then the workers surged.

They came from the laundry, the kitchens, the stables, the stores. They came with ladles, clubs, knives meant for bread, lengths of chain, and bare hands. The guards tried to form a line, but the rain made the stones treacherous and the courtyard too narrow. A soldier slipped. Three women pulled him down. Another reached Elianor and was stopped by Nessa, who drove a wooden laundry pin into the gap beneath his arm.

Caelan fled beneath the balcony.

Alric watched him go.

The lord of Greyfen looked from the scattered records to the gallows, from his daughter standing in the rain to Tomas helping the wounded stable hand. Something in him seemed to give way—not courage, not yet, but the final brittle support of denial.

“Open the lower armory,” he said.

No one heard him above the shouting.

He stood and shouted again, with what strength remained to him.

“Open the armory! The weapons are for Greyfen, not Arbridge!”

The words carried.

Caelan turned at the foot of the stairs.

Their eyes met across the ruined wedding preparations.

“You will lose everything,” Caelan said.

Alric’s face twisted. “It was lost before you arrived.”

A stone struck the awning. Then another. The magistrate crawled behind the overturned table. Caelan’s remaining men retreated toward the manor doors, while the servants drove them back with cries that had become one voice.

Tomas reached Elianor at last. His bound hands were still tied, but the rope around his wrists had loosened.

“You should have run,” he said.

“I did.”

“You should have kept running.”

“I am tired of leaving you behind.”

His bruised mouth trembled. He pressed his forehead to hers, rain and blood mingling between them.

Behind them, Mara lifted the gate bar just enough for a rush of workers from outside to enter. Beyond the opening, more figures gathered on the road—tenants, laborers, and men carrying tools that could become weapons.

The bell rope snapped.

The cracked bell gave one final, broken note.

No one waited for another command. Greyfen had already chosen.

The revolt began in the rain.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: In Greyfen’s rain-soaked courtyard, Elianor has publicly revealed herself after escaping confinement disguised as a laundry worker. She has denounced Caelan before servants, tenants, guards, and nobles, read copied records proving falsified labor tallies, fraudulent arrears, grain seizures, and planned reprisals, and helped turn the execution crowd into revolt. She is physically exhausted and frightened but standing beside the freed Tomas, determined to protect the household and carry the evidence through the uprising. She possesses the remaining copied records and a quill knife; her relationship with Tomas is openly acknowledged before Greyfen, while Nessa, Pell, Mara, and the workers now act as her allies. She knows Caelan’s authority is collapsing but that his armed followers remain dangerous.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: In Greyfen’s courtyard and manor during the beginning revolt, Alric has witnessed Elianor’s evidence, the attempted execution, and Caelan’s men attacking or threatening household members. He publicly ordered the lower armory opened for Greyfen rather than Arbridge, turning against Caelan after surrendering his authority for fear of debt seizure. He is physically weak, guilty, and emotionally shaken, but has begun using what remains of his lordly authority to aid the servants. He knows the estate’s hierarchy is collapsing and that Caelan’s armed followers may retaliate; his relationship with Elianor remains wounded but no longer purely adversarial.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: At the edge of Greyfen’s courtyard and manor, Caelan has seen Elianor publicly expose his records and watched servants, tenants, and some guards revolt. He ordered the guards to kill anyone resisting, but his line broke and he retreated beneath the balcony and toward the manor with the remaining loyal armed men. He remains physically well, furious, humiliated, and dangerous, still seeking to preserve his control of the records and use Elianor as leverage. His authority over Greyfen has been openly challenged, and he now faces Mara, rebel workers, and the household united against him.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: In Greyfen’s courtyard, Nessa has helped Elianor pass through the laundry route and has openly fought a guard when the revolt began. She remains physically well but frightened and committed to Elianor and the household resistance. She is carrying no major evidence, but knows the laundry routes, guard movements, and servant positions, and intends to help protect Elianor, Tomas, and the other workers as Caelan’s men retreat.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: In Greyfen’s courtyard, Master Pell has publicly confirmed that Elianor’s copied records are genuine after Caelan threatened him. He remains physically shaken and endangered, with his account knowledge and familiarity with the concealed working ledgers intact. He is now aligned openly with Elianor and the servants and must help preserve or interpret the surviving records before Caelan can seize them.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: In Greyfen’s courtyard, Tomas has been pulled from the gallows during the servants’ revolt. He remains bruised, bloodied, and partly bound, but physically capable of moving and fighting. He has reunited openly with Elianor and immediately helped a wounded stable hand instead of fleeing or pursuing Caelan, remaining committed to protecting people and refusing vengeance. He knows the courtyard is in revolt and that Caelan’s remaining men are retreating into the manor; he intends to free others and help Elianor secure a path through Greyfen.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: At Greyfen’s gatehouse and courtyard, Mara has arrived from the north road with two rebel sympathizers who entered among the wedding workers. She helped stop west-wall reinforcements and opened the gate enough for more workers and resistance figures to gather. She is soaked but physically capable, armed through the rebel workers’ improvised weapons and knowledge, and openly allied with Tomas, Elianor, and the household. She intends to organize the revolt, protect the gathered workers, and prevent Caelan from consolidating his armed followers.

On the morning of Tomas’s execution, Elianor entered Greyfen’s courtyard disguised as a laundry worker, publicly revealed herself, and read copied records documenting falsified labor tallies, fraudulent arrears, grain seizures, and Caelan’s planned punishments.

Elianor’s testimony transformed the execution crowd’s fear into open resistance: stable hands barricaded the gates, servants and workers attacked the execution party, and several guards refused or turned against Caelan’s orders.
Mara Quill reached the Greyfen gatehouse with two rebel sympathizers among the wedding workers and helped prevent the west-wall guards from reinforcing Caelan.
Alric publicly ordered the lower armory opened for Greyfen rather than Arbridge, abandoning his passive submission to Caelan as the manor’s servants rose against the execution.
Tomas was pulled from the gallows during the uprising, remained physically bound and bruised, and chose to help a wounded stable hand rather than flee or attack Caelan.

Workers and resistance figures entered or gathered at Greyfen through the opened gate, while Caelan and his remaining men retreated toward the manor buildings as the revolt spread beyond the courtyard.

Elianor and Tomas must reach Greyfen’s armory and records room during the uprising, secure weapons and the surviving estate documents, and prevent Caelan from using the records or Elianor as leverage.
The servants, tenants, and outside resistance workers must escape or be organized before Caelan’s remaining armed followers can retake the courtyard and punish the household.
Caelan must retreat with armed followers toward the chapel or another defensible part of Greyfen, preserving the immediate confrontation that will decide control of the manor.
Tomas must remain committed to freeing and protecting others during the revolt rather than pursuing personal vengeance against Caelan.

chapters.name: The Manor Breaks
chapters.content:
## The Manor Breaks

The first sound Elianor heard after the gates barred was not a shout but a key turning.

Somewhere behind her, in the passage beneath the kitchen, a ring of iron keys changed hands. Then another lock yielded. A door slammed open. The noise passed through Greyfen like a spark through dry straw.

“Stores!” someone cried.

The courtyard had become a churn of rain, mud, and bodies. The execution platform leaned crookedly beside the gallows. One of the horses lay screaming in its traces; the other had broken free and was plunging against the wall. Guards who had remained loyal to Caelan were fighting with stable hands, kitchen boys, and wedding laborers carrying poles, cleavers, and lengths of harness. Others stood frozen, their weapons lowered, watching the old order tear itself apart.

Tomas came toward Elianor with the rope still hanging from one wrist.

She saw blood at his temple, darkening his hair, and bruises rising beneath the torn collar of his shirt. For one terrible instant she thought he would fall. Then he reached for her, and she caught him by both shoulders.

“You’re alive.”

“Not by the gallows’ generosity.” His breath shook. “Are you hurt?”

“No.”

He looked past her. At the far side of the yard, Caelan was retreating beneath the stone balcony. Six men surrounded him, their swords drawn. The lord glanced back once, and the expression on his face was not fear. It was calculation, cold and intact.

Tomas followed Elianor’s gaze. His hand closed around the broken rope.

“He’s going to the inner hall,” she said. “The armory and records room are beyond it.”

“Then we go after him.”

A stable boy stumbled between them. His cheek was split, and one of his hands was clamped over his ribs.

“Tomas,” the boy gasped. “Fenner’s down by the gate. Hobb—”

Tomas turned away from Caelan.

“Where?”

Elianor understood before he explained. “Go,” she said. “I’ll bring the others to the armory.”

His eyes held hers. The rain ran from his lashes, and for a heartbeat the riot fell away: the lodge, the marsh route, the life they had imagined and lost before it began.

“I’ll find you,” he said.

“Find the living first.”

He gave her a brief, fierce nod and went toward the wounded instead of the lord.

Elianor watched him disappear into the crowd. It was the choice she had always loved in him and had sometimes feared: he could look at the man who had condemned him and still see, first, the people bleeding nearby.

“Lady Elianor!” Nessa seized her sleeve. “The stores have been opened, but Caelan’s men are trying to shut the lower doors. Mara says we need the armory.”

“Pell is with us?”

“Here.” Master Pell emerged from the rain, clutching the leather satchel in which he had placed the surviving account pages. His face was gray. “The main stair is watched.”

“I know another way.”

She turned to Alric. He stood beneath the balcony, one hand braced against a pillar. The rain had flattened his silver hair, and the signet ring on his finger was smeared with mud. Around him, the symbols of his house had become meaningless: the Vey banner dragged through a puddle, the carved arms above the gate spattered with blood.

“Father,” she called. “Open the inner passage.”

His head lifted. “Elianor, stop this.”

“Stop what?”

“The servants have lost their senses. Put down the weapons. Order them back to their quarters.”

A crash came from the kitchens. Then a woman screamed.

Alric flinched. “This is not justice. It is a mob.”

“It became a mob when Caelan put a rope around Tomas’s neck.”

“I was trying to prevent the seizure of Greyfen.”

“You gave him Greyfen piece by piece.”

His face folded as if she had struck him. For a moment he seemed less a lord than an old, exhausted man standing in the ruins of a decision he had made a hundred times.

Behind him, the chapel bell began to ring. Not in a measured summons, but in frantic blows. Caelan was calling his men inward.

Alric looked toward the sound. “If the armory is opened, there will be no returning.”

“There is no returning already.”

He stared at her. “You would destroy your own house?”

“No,” Elianor said. “I would stop pretending the house is the stone and not the people inside it.”

Nessa pulled at her arm. “My lady, now.”

They ran.

The hidden passage began behind a panel in the old buttery, where Elianor had played as a child while her nurse searched the manor for her. Nessa struck the catch with the butt of a stolen pistol. The panel sprang inward, revealing a narrow stair smelling of damp mortar and mouse nests.

Pell followed, breathing hard. Two stable hands came after him, each carrying a cudgel. Mara entered last, her wet cloak torn at the shoulder, a short sword in one hand and a ring of keys in the other.

“West gate is held,” Mara said. “The workers have disarmed four guards. More are coming through the yard, but Caelan’s men still have the inner hall.”

“Then we take the hall,” Elianor replied.

“Take the armory first.”

“I know.”

The stair twisted beneath the walls. Elianor led by memory, touching the cold stone as they descended. In the years before Caelan’s arrival, she had learned every concealed route in Greyfen: the priest’s way from the chapel to the cellars, the servants’ stair behind the linen room, the low tunnel that opened beneath the old armory. These had been childish secrets once, places from which she could spy on dinner guests or escape lessons.

Now they were arteries beneath a dying body.

Above them, boots pounded over the floor. A musket discharged. Dust sifted from the ceiling.

One of the stable hands whispered a prayer.

“Do not pray for the house,” Pell muttered. “Pray for the locks.”

The passage ended at a warped oak door. Elianor fitted one of Mara’s keys into the lock. It resisted, then turned.

They emerged behind the armory racks.

The room held little enough: old halberds, hunting bows, three pistols, and a cabinet of powder kept for ceremonial salutes. Yet to the servants gathering behind them, it looked like an arsenal. Hands reached for weapons. Pell began distributing them with trembling efficiency.

“Not the powder,” Elianor warned. “No fire in the records room.”

A young guard stepped from behind the far rack. He wore Greyfen colors, though his sword belt bore Caelan’s blue clasp.

“Lay them down,” he said.

Mara raised her sword. “You first.”

The guard’s jaw worked. His eyes went to the open passage, then to Elianor. “My brother is in the lower yard.”

“Then help us keep him alive,” Elianor said. “Caelan will not spare him if he thinks the revolt can be crushed.”

The guard lowered his sword.

A shout sounded beyond the armory door. The guard moved beside it and lifted the bar.

Three of Caelan’s men burst in.

The room became noise and impact. Mara met the first sword. A stable hand drove his cudgel into the second man’s wrist. Pell, who had never held a weapon in his life, thrust a pike forward with both hands and sent the third stumbling into the wall. Elianor seized a fallen pistol but did not fire. She struck the pommel against a man’s temple, felt bone beneath wet skin, and nearly retched.

When it ended, one attacker lay unconscious, another had fled, and the third was on his knees with Mara’s blade at his throat.

“Where is Caelan?” she demanded.

“Inner hall,” he spat. “He’s gathering men by the chapel stair. He says the records will be burned before he lets the tenants have them.”

Elianor felt the satchel against her side. The copied pages were safe, but the original ledgers remained in the records room.

“To the records,” she said.

They crossed the armory and entered a servants’ corridor. Through a grated opening, Elianor saw the lower courtyard. The stores stood open. Women carried sacks of grain into the rain while tenants formed a line to guard them. No one waited for permission. No one bowed.

Near the well, Tomas knelt beside Fenner, binding the stable master’s shoulder with a strip torn from his own shirt. Hobb was there too, pale and furious, holding a bloodied rake. When Tomas looked up and saw Elianor above him, relief passed across his face before he bent again to his work.

Then a gunshot cracked from the west passage.

The guard who had lowered his sword went rigid. “My brother.”

They ran back toward the courtyard, but Caelan’s men had reached the gallery above it. From the balcony, a captain fired into the crowd below. A kitchen maid fell beside the grain sacks. The people nearest her scattered, and for one instant panic threatened to undo what courage had built.

Alric came through the great doors.

“Stop!” he shouted.

The captain turned. “Stand aside, Lord Vey.”

“That is my household.”

“It belongs to Arbridge now.”

The captain raised his pistol again toward a cluster of unarmed servants. Alric moved without seeming to decide. He seized a fallen sword and thrust it into the man’s side.

The captain stared down at the blade. Alric held him there, both hands wrapped around the hilt, his face contorted with horror. When the body slid away, Alric nearly fell with it.

Caelan appeared behind the gallery rail.

“You weak old fool,” he said. “I offered to save your name.”

Alric looked up at him. Blood ran over his knuckles.

“You consumed it,” he answered.

Caelan’s remaining men surged toward the stairs. The courtyard answered with a roar. Stable hands lifted the barricade from the gate and drove into the gallery. Mara shouted for the workers to hold the doors. Nessa dragged the wounded maid behind the well.

Elianor reached Alric as he leaned against the balustrade.

“Father.”

“Do not call me that as if it absolves me.” His voice was thin. “Take the records. Take everything that can prove what he did.”

“We will.”

“And the stores?”

“Opened.”

He closed his eyes briefly. “Then perhaps Greyfen has a chance, though I do not.”

A fresh clash broke out on the chapel stair. Caelan withdrew through the upper corridor with four armed followers, moving toward the records room and the chapel beyond it.

“Elianor!” Tomas called from below.

She leaned over the rail. “The records room is next. Caelan is going there.”

“I’m coming.”

“No.” She saw the question in his face. “You’re needed here. Keep the gates open. Get everyone out if the fire spreads.”

His mouth tightened. “You know I hate when you’re right.”

“Then live long enough to complain.”

For a second, despite the rain and blood and breaking house, he smiled.

Elianor turned to Pell, Mara, Nessa, and the armed servants. “The records room. We take the ledgers, the deeds, and anyone Caelan has locked inside. No killing unless there is no other choice.”

Mara nodded. “And if there is?”

Elianor looked toward the corridor where Caelan had vanished. “Then we choose the living.”

They moved into the manor.

Behind them, the great bell continued its broken ringing. Doors stood open that had been barred for generations. Keys passed from hand to hand. Grain crossed the threshold without a steward’s mark. Men who had once removed their caps before the Vey crest now tore it from the walls to bind wounds.

Greyfen did not fall all at once. It broke in every lock, every ledger, every hand that stopped asking permission.

And somewhere ahead, beyond the chapel stair, Caelan was running toward the last proof that his power had ever been real.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Inside Greyfen’s manor, Elianor has led Mara, Pell, Nessa, stable hands, and a wavering Greyfen guard through a concealed passage to the armory. She helped seize weapons and disarm Caelan’s attackers, then ordered the group toward the records room while instructing them to choose the living over unnecessary killing. She carries copied records and a quill knife, is exhausted and shaken by having struck a man, and remains openly reunited with Tomas. She knows the stores are open, the lower courtyard is held by the revolt, Alric has turned against Caelan, and Caelan has retreated with armed followers toward the chapel stair and records room. Her immediate goal is to secure the surviving ledgers and free anyone Caelan has confined.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: In Greyfen’s lower courtyard and gallery, Alric first urged the servants to stop the uprising, still fearing that disorder would destroy the Vey house. After witnessing Caelan’s captain shoot at unarmed household members, he killed the captain with a fallen sword and openly rejected Caelan, admitting that Caelan had consumed the authority Alric surrendered. He is physically weak, bloodied at the hands, horrified by his own violence, and emotionally resigned. He has urged Elianor to take the records and prove Caelan’s abuses; he knows the stores are open and the old hierarchy is collapsing.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: Caelan has retreated from Greyfen’s gallery with four armed followers toward the chapel stair and records room after Alric killed his captain and the revolt seized the lower manor. He remains physically well, furious, humiliated, and intent on preserving, destroying, or using the original ledgers as leverage, while still seeking control of Elianor. His authority over Greyfen is effectively broken below, though he retains armed men and a defensible route through the upper manor. He knows Elianor is leading resistance members toward the records and chapel.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: In Greyfen’s manor and courtyard, Nessa has helped Elianor reach the armory through the hidden passage, carried news from the stores and Mara, and helped drag a wounded kitchen maid to safety after Caelan’s captain fired into the crowd. She is frightened but physically capable, armed with the household resistance, and remains fiercely loyal to Elianor and the workers. She knows the lower courtyard and stores are held by the revolt and is moving with Elianor toward the records room.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: Inside Greyfen’s armory and moving toward the records room, Master Pell has protected the copied account pages in his leather satchel and helped distribute weapons despite his fear. He knows the concealed working ledgers and can identify the records that prove Caelan’s abuses. He is pale, shaken, and physically winded but aligned openly with Elianor, Mara, Nessa, and the servants. His immediate goal is to recover and interpret the original ledgers before Caelan can seize or destroy them.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: In Greyfen’s lower courtyard, Tomas has been freed from the gallows and remains bruised, bloodied, and physically capable. He chose to bind Fenner’s wound and help wounded household members rather than pursue Caelan, then kept watch over the opened stores and the gates as the revolt spread. He remains openly reunited with Elianor and committed to protecting people rather than taking revenge. He knows Elianor and Mara are heading for the records room while Caelan retreats toward the chapel, and his immediate goal is to keep the gates open, evacuate people if fire spreads, and defend the living.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: In Greyfen’s manor with Elianor’s resistance group, Mara has helped lead the armed servants through the hidden passage, confronted Caelan’s attackers in the armory, and organized the workers holding the gates and inner doors. She carries a short sword and a ring of keys, is soaked and bruised at the shoulder but combat-capable, and remains committed to protecting the household and securing evidence. She knows Caelan has retreated toward the chapel stair and records room and is accompanying Elianor to confront that danger.
During the revolt, servants opened Greyfen’s stores and began distributing grain without steward permission while tenants and workers formed guards around the supplies.
Elianor led Mara, Master Pell, Nessa, stable hands, and a wavering Greyfen guard through a concealed passage to the armory, where they seized weapons and disarmed or drove off Caelan’s attackers.
Tomas refused to pursue Caelan, instead binding Fenner’s wound and helping protect wounded household members as the fighting spread.
Alric killed a Caelan captain who fired on unarmed household members, openly rejecting Caelan and declaring that Caelan had consumed the Vey name and authority.
Caelan withdrew from the gallery with four armed followers toward the chapel stair and records room, intending to preserve or destroy the estate documents while the revolt held the lower manor.

chapters.name: The Burning Ledgers
chapters.content:
## The Burning Ledgers

The records room lay behind the old steward’s office, where the corridor narrowed and the plaster gave way to bare stone. Elianor remembered it as a place of dust and winter cold. Now smoke drifted beneath the ceiling, and every breath tasted of ash, lamp oil, and the sharp iron smell of blood.

“Here,” Pell said.

He had found the door half-hidden behind a fallen tapestry. Its oak panels were scarred where someone had hacked at the lock. A dead guard lay beneath the window, one hand still curled around a broken pistol. Beyond him, the room remained dark.

Mara lifted her sword. “Caelan?”

“No,” Pell whispered. “He would have taken the chapel stair. The room opens onto it.”

Elianor looked at the narrow staircase beyond the records room in her mind: three steps down into the vault, one turn, then the chapel passage. It was the way Alric’s stewards had carried sealed chests for generations, away from servants’ eyes and visiting creditors. If Caelan had come here, he would know the same paths.

“Then we are not first,” she said.

Nessa pushed the door inward. The hinges groaned.

Shelves rose from floor to ceiling, packed with ledgers bound in cracked leather. Some were swollen with damp. Others bore the Vey crest in fading gilt. A single lamp burned on the central table, its flame wavering in the draft. Two chests stood open, and papers lay scattered around them like pale leaves.

Pell crossed the room with a sound that was almost a sob. “He has been searching.”

“Not thoroughly,” Mara said.

She pointed to the far wall. A section of shelves had been built over a recess, but one board hung loose. Pell knelt, thrust his fingers into the gap, and pulled. The board came away. Behind it lay a row of narrow books wrapped in oilskin.

Elianor felt the room contract around her.

“What are they?”

“The oldest accounts.” Pell wiped his hands on his coat before touching them. “Before my grandfather’s time. Before your father’s.”

He opened the first book. The pages were written in several hands, the ink brown and brittle. Columns recorded rent, seed, labor, penalties. Beside each tenant’s name were marks that multiplied down the years, debts passed from father to son, from widow to child, from a cottage to the body of whoever still lived in it.

Pell read silently at first. Then his mouth tightened.

“What?” Elianor asked.

He turned the book toward her.

At the head of a page was the name of a family she knew: Orrow. The first entry recorded a loan of grain after a flood. The next charged interest on the loan. The next charged for the clerk’s writing, the inspection of the field, the delay in repayment, and the loss of the lord’s expected profit. After ten years, the original debt had become a number no harvest could satisfy.

At the bottom, in a different hand, someone had written: *Labor may be credited in place of coin.*

Elianor’s fingers went numb.

“Their debt was never meant to end,” she said.

“No,” Pell answered. “It was meant to be inherited.”

Mara opened another ledger. Inside were lists of laborers taken from Fenwater, each day entered against a debt that had already been paid. A third contained maps with new boundaries drawn in red. Villages had been divided, strips of pasture transferred, common woodland renamed as Vey property. At the edges, seals showed agreements supposedly witnessed by tenants who could not write their names.

“Fraud,” Nessa said. She had come close despite the blood on her sleeve. “All of it?”

“Not all,” Pell said. “Enough.”

A sound came from the passage beyond the vault: boots on stone, then a low command.

Mara shut the ledger. “We have minutes.”

“Take the books,” Elianor said.

Pell stared at the shelves. “There are hundreds.”

“Then take the truth that can travel.”

She moved to the table and began sorting. The copied pages she had carried from her rooms were spread beneath her hands: Caelan’s staffing rolls, grain seizures, false tallies, orders for reprisals. Pell added the oldest ledgers, choosing those that showed the pattern rather than every instance. Mara tore blank leaves from a register and folded them into packets. Nessa ran to the door and returned with two tenant representatives from the lower hall, a broad-shouldered woman from Fenwater named Sella’s cousin Iven and an old ploughman called Roake.

“They came for instructions,” Nessa said. “The stores are crowded. People are trying to get the wounded out.”

“Good,” Elianor said. “They will carry these.”

She divided the evidence among them. Each packet held a copied account, a map or labor tally, and a page bearing a seal or signature. Pell explained what each proved and where the names could be found in the original books.

“Do not keep them together,” Elianor told Iven. “If one packet is taken, the others must survive. Carry them through the kitchens, the stables, wherever the gates are held. Find Mara’s people beyond the walls. Give copies to every village named here.”

Iven looked down at the pages. “If they see us—”

“They already see you,” Mara said. “That is why they mean to hang us.”

The woman tucked her packet inside her bodice. Roake slid his beneath his shirt. They did not look brave. They looked afraid, and therefore real.

Another command echoed from the chapel passage.

“Go,” Elianor said.

They fled through the office door. Nessa followed them, then paused.

“I’ll get the rest to the gate.”

“Take the west stair,” Pell called. “The gallery is blocked.”

Nessa nodded and vanished.

For a moment, only the lamp flame moved.

Then a familiar voice came from the corridor. “Elianor!”

Tomas.

She ran before Mara could stop her. He appeared through the smoke with Fenner’s blood on his hands and a borrowed sword at his hip. His face was bruised along the cheekbone, and a strip of cloth bound his wrist, but when he saw her he smiled as if the manor were not breaking around them.

“Elianor.”

She reached him and pressed both hands to his coat. “You’re hurt.”

“Not badly. Fenner is alive. Pell?”

“Here.”

Tomas’s gaze went to the shelves. “How long?”

“Long enough to choose what survives,” Mara said. “Caelan’s men are coming.”

“Then we must open the gates.”

Elianor stared at him. “The records room is the safer place.”

“For the records, perhaps. Not for the people.” He turned to her. “The lower gate is jammed with carts and frightened families. The east doors are still barred. If fire reaches the stores, everyone inside will be trapped.”

“We can send someone.”

“Who?” Tomas asked gently. “Everyone who can fight is holding the manor. Everyone who can carry the wounded is already carrying them. I know the gate mechanisms. I can get the east doors open.”

Behind him, a shot cracked. Dust shook from the lintel. Mara swore and drew her sword.

“They have entered the office,” Pell said.

Tomas looked at the ledgers, then at the lamp.

“Burn them.”

Elianor understood at once. “The originals?”

“If Caelan keeps them, he keeps the names. He keeps the chains. He can claim the copies are forged.”

Pell’s hands trembled. “These are generations.”

“Generations of theft,” Mara said. “Let the proof live in a hundred hands instead of dying in one locked room.”

Elianor lifted the lamp.

Oil spilled across the central table. Pell stood frozen until she thrust the lamp toward him. He took it, breathing hard, and tipped the flame onto the nearest ledger.

For a heartbeat nothing happened. Then the oil caught.

Fire ran along the leather binding, bright and hungry. Smoke rolled upward. Pell began carrying books from the shelves, placing them on the table with reverence before the flames consumed them. Mara kicked open the chest and scattered papers across the floor. Elianor fed in the maps, the debt rolls, the signed orders bearing Caelan’s seal.

The room filled with the dry crackle of a past being destroyed.

Names rose in the smoke. Orrow. Fenwater. Vale. Families who had bent beneath numbers written by men who would never know the shape of their fields or the hunger of their children. Elianor watched the ink blacken and curl.

She had once believed the house could be saved by preserving its ledgers. Now she saw that Greyfen had been preserved by them, each page another stone in a wall around the living.

The door burst inward.

A guard entered with a pistol raised. Mara struck his wrist, and the shot shattered a shelf. Tomas seized the man by the collar and drove him against the wall, but did not use the sword.

“Run,” Tomas told him.

The guard stared, astonished, then scrambled through the smoke toward the chapel stair.

“Caelan will be with him,” Mara said.

“Then he knows the fire has started,” Elianor answered.

A beam groaned overhead. Flames climbed the curtains and licked along the rafters.

“Tomas,” she said. “Come with us.”

“To the gates.”

“No. With us.” She caught his hand. “We have the copies. Pell can lead them. Mara can—”

“I can open the doors.”

“You can do more here.”

His expression changed, becoming unbearably tender. “That is what I am doing.”

The firelight moved across his face. For an instant she saw the forester’s lodge, the goshawk’s first flight, rain caught in his hair. She saw the life they had invented and lost before it had begun.

“You promised me,” she said.

“I promised to leave with you.”

“Then leave now.”

He shook his head. “Not while the gates are closed.”

The ceiling gave a sharp, splintering cry.

“Elianor,” he said, “take the evidence. Take Pell. Take Mara, Nessa, everyone you can reach. Get them beyond the walls. If the manor burns, do not let the people burn with it.”

She tightened her grip. “I won’t abandon you.”

“You are not abandoning me. You are carrying what we began.”

“I want to stand beside you.”

“You have stood beside me.” His thumb brushed the blood-darkened knuckles of her hand. “Now stand for them.”

The words struck deeper than any command. He had always refused the easy shape of possession: lord over servant, rescuer over rescued, beloved over beloved. Even now, with fire between them, he would not make her prove love by dying where he died.

“Promise me,” he said.

She looked into his eyes. “I promise to carry the evidence and the people to safety.”

“And you will not come after me until the gates are open.”

Her breath caught.

“Elianor.”

“I promise,” she whispered.

He kissed her once, fiercely and without time. Smoke stung her eyes, but she felt the shape of his mouth, the warmth of him, the impossible fact that he was alive.

Then he released her.

Tomas ran toward the lower stair. Pell gathered the last packet of copied pages. Mara seized Elianor by the shoulder and pulled her toward the servants’ passage as fire spread behind them.

At the threshold, Elianor looked back.

The ledgers burned in a row upon the table. Their pages lifted in the heat, shining briefly before becoming ash. Beyond the chapel passage came Caelan’s voice, shouting orders, promising punishment, demanding that the doors be held.

Tomas’s footsteps answered from below.

Elianor turned away from the records room and ran toward the living. Outside, Greyfen’s gates waited in the rain, and beyond them waited every name the ledgers had tried to bury.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Inside Greyfen’s records room, Elianor helped Pell and Mara select evidence, distributed copied packets proving generations of inherited debt, forced labor, fraudulent land claims, grain seizures, and Caelan’s orders to tenant representatives, and helped burn the surviving original ledgers. She is smoke-stung, exhausted, emotionally torn, and carrying the remaining copies with Pell and Mara through the servants’ passage toward the gates. She remains openly reunited with Tomas and has promised not to follow him until he opens the gates, and to carry the evidence and living people to safety. She knows Caelan is approaching through the chapel passage and Tomas is going toward the lower gates.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: Caelan remains in the upper manor near the chapel passage with armed followers, pursuing the records room after retreating from the lower revolt. He intends to preserve or destroy the original documents and seize Elianor as leverage, but the ledgers are now burning and copies have been distributed to tenant representatives. He is furious and increasingly desperate, armed and physically well, and is moving toward the chapel and the routes leading to the gates.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: Nessa brought tenant representatives to the records room, carried evidence packets toward the held gates, and then departed through the servants’ route to help move the remaining copies and wounded household members out of danger. She is frightened, bloodied at the sleeve but physically capable, armed with the household resistance, and loyal to Elianor and the workers. She knows the records room is burning, Tomas is opening the gates, and Caelan is advancing through the chapel passage.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: In the burning records room, Pell identified the oldest account books proving inherited debts, forced labor, and fraudulent land claims, selected representative originals, explained them to tenant carriers, and helped Elianor distribute copied evidence before setting the originals ablaze. He is pale, winded, smoke-stung, and shaken by destroying generations of records, but carries the remaining copied pages in his leather satchel and is escaping with Elianor and Mara toward the gates.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas reached Elianor in the records room bruised and bloodied but physically capable, with Fenner alive and a borrowed sword at his hip. He helped restrain and spare a guard, then left Elianor, Pell, and Mara to evacuate with the copied evidence while he went toward the lower stair and manor gates. He has made Elianor promise not to follow until the gates are open and to carry the people and records to safety. He remains committed to protecting the living rather than revenge and is heading toward a confrontation with Caelan near the chapel or gates.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: In Greyfen’s records room, Mara helped sort and distribute copied evidence to tenant representatives, fought off a guard without killing him, and helped Elianor and Pell escape as the original ledgers burned. She is smoke-stung, bruised, armed with her short sword and keys, and combat-capable. She is escorting Elianor and the surviving copies through the servants’ passage toward the gates, determined to preserve the evidence and evacuate the household while Caelan approaches through the chapel passage.

Pell selected the oldest ledgers and Elianor’s copied records, and Elianor distributed packets proving inherited debt, forced labor, fraudulent boundaries, grain seizures, and Caelan’s orders to tenant representatives for circulation beyond Greyfen.

Elianor, Pell, and Mara set the surviving original ledgers and supporting records ablaze in Greyfen’s records room so Caelan could not use the names and documents as leverage, while Tomas left to open the manor gates and evacuate the living.
Tomas made Elianor promise not to follow him until the gates were open, and to carry the evidence and the people to safety; they shared a final kiss before separating inside the burning manor.
Tomas must hold or reach the manor gates, opening the east doors so servants, tenants, and wounded household members can escape before the fire and Caelan’s forces overtake Greyfen.
Elianor must carry the copied ledgers and evidence with Pell and Mara through the evacuation, preserving them beyond Greyfen so tenant communities can use them against the fraudulent claims.
Caelan and Tomas must confront one another near the chapel after Caelan attempts to preserve the records and seize Elianor, with the outcome of their refusal or use of violence unresolved.

chapters.name: Dawn at Greyfen
chapters.content:
## Dawn at Greyfen

The chapel bell began to ring without a hand upon it.

A tremor passed through the manor, followed by a roar from somewhere below—the collapse of a ceiling, perhaps, or the great doors of the records room giving way. Smoke rolled along the upper gallery in low gray folds. Through it, Caelan Arbridge climbed toward the chapel with four men at his back, one arm wrapped around a leather case of documents.

He had lost the courtyard, the armory, the gallery, and the obedience of half the household. Yet he still walked as if Greyfen belonged beneath his boots.

At the chapel landing he found Tomas waiting.

The falconer stood between Caelan and the passage to the east stair. His face was swollen where the execution guards had struck him, and blood darkened the collar of his shirt. Someone had given him a sword, but he held it low, its point toward the floor. Behind him, through the chapel’s open doors, rain blew across the flagstones. The altar cloth had caught fire at one corner, and smoke veiled the painted saints.

Caelan stopped.

“So,” he said. “The condemned man has discovered a taste for borrowed steel.”

Tomas glanced at the armed men. “You should have gone while the gates were still shut.”

“The gates are not yours to open.”

“No.” Tomas’s grip tightened. “They belong to everyone you kept behind them.”

Caelan smiled, though his eyes were bright with fury. “You have been whispering that sort of nonsense to Lady Elianor. Ownership is not nonsense, Vale. It is the only language that keeps a house standing. Land, labor, loyalty—each has an owner. Without that order, every hungry hand becomes a claim.”

“Then let Greyfen fall.”

Behind Caelan, one of the men shifted uneasily. The chapel bell swung overhead, striking the same note again and again, though its rope had burned through.

Caelan looked toward the records case. “Your lady has burned the proof. Do you understand what she has done? Those books were law. Names, debts, boundaries. They held the estate together.”

“They held people down.”

“And now you mean to kill me and call that freedom.”

Tomas raised his eyes to him. “No.”

The answer seemed to disarm Caelan more than a threat would have done.

Tomas stepped into the chapel. Rain hissed against the burning cloth. “I was asked to kill you before this day. I refused. I refused because men like you have made a world where every injury demands another injury, where a life is weighed against a ledger and vengeance is mistaken for justice. I will not build the next world with the same hands.”

Caelan’s face hardened. “You will not build anything.”

He drew his pistol.

The shot struck Tomas beneath the ribs.

For an instant he remained upright, staring at the small black mouth of the weapon as if the wound belonged to someone else. Then his sword slipped from his hand. He folded against the chapel door, leaving a red smear across the pale wood.

Caelan’s men surged forward.

A shout rose from below. Mara appeared at the far end of the gallery with Nessa, Pell, and three stable hands behind her. Smoke streamed around them. Mara saw Tomas fall and fired the old armory pistol from her hip. The ball tore through the railing beside Caelan’s shoulder. He staggered back, and the stable hands rushed him.

The fight became a knot of bodies, steel, and splintering wood.

Caelan struck one man across the mouth with the pistol. Another caught his wrist. Mara drove her shoulder into his chest, and all three went down against the chapel threshold. The leather case flew open. Loose pages scattered into the rain.

“Leave him!” Mara shouted. “Take the documents!”

But Elianor was already running.

She had heard the shot from the servants’ passage. Pell had tried to hold her back; she had pushed past him with the copied records clutched beneath her dress. Now she came through the smoke with a shawl over her hair, followed by Nessa and two kitchen workers carrying sacks of grain. Her gaze found Tomas before it found anything else.

He was on his knees.

“Tomas.”

He turned at the sound of her voice. His hand pressed his side, but blood ran between his fingers and down his wrist.

“You promised,” he said.

“I promised not to follow until the gates were open.” She fell beside him. “They are not open.”

“Then you have kept it.”

The words were almost a smile. He tried to rise. Elianor caught him beneath the arm, and together they staggered toward the east stair.

Behind them, Caelan broke free of Mara and fled through the chapel. Two rebels followed him, but the floor shook beneath their feet. A beam dropped from the smoke-dark ceiling, blocking the passage in a burst of sparks. Caelan vanished beyond it.

“Let him run,” Tomas said.

Mara stared at him. “He shot you.”

“Open the gates.”

They descended.

Greyfen had become a living machine breaking itself apart. Servants hurried through the lower hall with bundles, children, buckets, and wounded men. The storehouse doors stood wide, and grain poured across the floor as people filled sacks. Flames licked up the tapestries. Rain blew in through shattered windows, turning ash to black paste beneath their feet.

At the bottom of the stair, Tomas nearly fell. Elianor held him upright while Nessa ran ahead to clear the way.

“The east doors,” Tomas breathed. “The chain is drawn from the gatehouse side. There’s a release lever in the old guardroom.”

“You know this because you have opened them before?”

“Because I have been locked out of them before.”

His knees buckled. Elianor and Mara caught him between them.

“Let me carry you,” Mara said.

“You cannot carry the gates.”

“Idiot.”

“Yes.”

They reached the guardroom. Fenner lay against the wall with his wounded leg bound tight, a stable hand kneeling beside him. He lifted his head when he saw Tomas.

“Vale,” he said. “You look worse than I do.”

“Then stop looking.”

The release lever was jammed. Tomas knelt, swallowed a cry, and thrust both hands beneath the iron bar. Elianor saw the tremor in his shoulders.

“Let me,” she said.

“No. When it gives, it will swing.”

“Tomas—”

“Take the others out.”

He pulled. The bar did not move.

Outside, something exploded in the courtyard. A wave of heat passed through the guardroom. People cried out. Somewhere above, a man was shouting for Lord Arbridge. Somewhere else, the chapel bell continued its ruined ringing.

Tomas braced one boot against the wall and pulled again. This time the mechanism shrieked. The chain loosened by an inch.

“Everyone back!” Mara called.

They crowded against the walls. Tomas hauled the lever down with a raw cry. The iron chain dropped through its housing, and the eastern gates swung outward into the rain.

Beyond them stood the tenants, workers, and wounded who had been trapped in the outer yard. For one suspended moment no one moved. Then the gates became a river of people.

They streamed into the road carrying sacks, children, blankets, weapons, and the names of the dead. Nessa took charge at once, directing them toward the alder bank and the lower fields. Pell shouted that the copied records must remain dry. Mara sent two men back for those still hiding in the kitchens and cellars.

Elianor stayed with Tomas.

“Go,” he said.

“I am going.”

“You are standing.”

“So are you.”

He looked at her, and the effort of it seemed to cost him more than the wound. “You have the pages?”

She pressed a hand against the hidden packets. “Yes.”

“Pell knows which villages receive them. Mara knows who can protect them. Do not let anyone make a monument of this. Not of me. Not of Greyfen.”

The rain struck his face, washing soot into pale trails. Elianor wanted to say that she would make a monument of every moment, that she would carry his name until her own became dust. Instead she said, “You will tell them yourself.”

He looked past her toward the manor. “Is everyone out?”

Mara had returned to the gate, soaked and breathing hard. “The last prisoners from the lower cells are on the road. The laundry women are out. Fenner too.”

“And Alric?” Elianor asked.

No one answered.

A portion of the manor’s southern roof collapsed. Fire flowered through the rain.

Elianor turned back toward the doorway. For a moment she saw her father in the smoke, not as the lord who had signed evictions or the frightened man who had yielded Greyfen piece by piece, but as the boy he must once have been, inheriting a name too heavy to lift. Then a dark shape fell behind the burning windows.

“Father!”

She started forward, but Tomas seized her sleeve.

“No.”

“He may be alive.”

“He may be.” His voice was weakening. “And there are still people behind you.”

The manor groaned. The upper gallery gave way, carrying fire, stone, and the old Vey banners into the hall.

Elianor stopped.

The last hope of rescue left her with the smoke.

They moved farther from the gates, into the muddy road where the refugees gathered beneath the dripping trees. Tomas made it three more steps. Then he sank.

Elianor caught him before his head struck the ground.

“No,” she whispered. “No, not here.”

He lay against her, his weight growing heavier. Mara knelt and pressed cloth to the wound, but Tomas shook his head.

“Save it,” he said.

“For what?”

“For someone who can use it.”

The rain thickened. Behind them Greyfen burned from chapel to stable, its windows glowing like watchful eyes. No guards came from the road. No lord rode to restore the gates. The house had spent itself.

Tomas’s breathing became shallow. Elianor held his face between her hands.

“I love you,” she said. “I should have said it before the gallows, before the fire, before every cowardly bargain.”

“I knew.”

“You cannot know everything.”

“I knew that.”

A cry went up among the refugees. High above the burning roof, a goshawk wheeled through the rain. Its wings beat steadily, one once-broken side as strong as the other. It circled Greyfen, rose on a current of heat, and vanished into the paling clouds.

Tomas followed it with his eyes.

“Good,” he murmured. “It made it out.”

“So will we.”

He looked at her then—not at the lady she had been, nor at the ruined house behind her, but at the woman kneeling in the mud with his blood on her hands.

“Make it mean something,” he said.

“I will.”

The eastern sky turned gray.

Tomas exhaled. His body softened against her, and did not draw breath again.

Elianor remained there while dawn gathered over Greyfen. Around her, the living began to move toward Fenwater, carrying grain, weapons, records, and the wounded. Pell stood silent with his satchel held beneath his coat. Mara watched the road. Nessa counted the children twice.

No one asked Elianor to rise.

At last she lowered her forehead to Tomas’s and listened to the rain fall over the dead manor, the freed road, and the first morning in which Greyfen belonged to no one.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: On the road beyond the opened east gates, Elianor is kneeling in the rain with Tomas’s dead body in her arms. She carries copied records beneath her clothing and is smoke-stained, exhausted, grieving, and newly committed to making his death mean practical freedom rather than a monument. She knows the servants, prisoners, tenants, and wounded escaped; her father died in the burning manor; Caelan fled the chapel confrontation; and Greyfen has collapsed as a ruling house. Her remaining relationships are with Mara, Pell, Nessa, and the displaced Greyfen household, whom she intends to protect.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: Lord Alric is dead inside the collapsed, burning southern manor at Greyfen. Before his death he had turned against Caelan and defended unarmed household members, but he remained physically weak, bloodied, and unable to undo the authority he had surrendered. His death leaves Elianor without her father and leaves the Vey estate ruined and without its former lord.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: Caelan was last seen fleeing through the chapel passage after shooting Tomas; rebels and household fighters overwhelmed his remaining followers, while a falling beam blocked immediate pursuit. He remains physically capable but furious, desperate, armed, and separated from the original records, which burned, though his wider claims and political danger remain unresolved.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: Nessa escaped Greyfen through the east gates with the refugees and helped direct servants, tenants, children, and wounded people toward the alder bank and lower fields. She is frightened, bloodied, capable, armed with the household resistance, and loyal to Elianor. She is now helping count and protect the displaced survivors.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: Master Pell escaped with the surviving copied pages in his leather satchel, keeping them beneath his coat against the rain. He is smoke-stung, pale, winded, and shaken by the destruction of the originals, but knows which tenant communities must receive the evidence and has joined the refugee column beyond Greyfen.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas died at dawn on the road outside Greyfen after being shot beneath the ribs by Caelan. Mortally wounded, he helped release the east gates and refused revenge, ensuring that the last prisoners and household members escaped before collapsing in Elianor’s arms. His borrowed sword lies behind at Greyfen, while his final request was that Elianor turn their loss into freedom.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Mara escaped Greyfen with Elianor and the surviving household, fought Caelan’s followers at the chapel, helped secure the east gates, and confirmed that the last prisoners were free. She is soaked, bruised, smoke-stained, armed with her short sword and keys, combat-capable, and now watching the refugee road while guarding the copied evidence and surviving people.

set.name: Sella
set.description: Sella remains at the Fenwater settlement with resistance networks, tenant records, route information, and laborers prepared to resist. She has not been present at Greyfen’s burning but will receive the refugees and copied evidence through Mara’s network. She remains sturdy, scarred, cautious, authoritative, and resolute, with the goal of protecting the displaced and using the records against noble claims.
Tomas confronted Caelan at the chapel and refused to kill him, declaring that freedom could not be founded on the old world’s ownership and vengeance.
Caelan shot Tomas beneath the ribs during the chapel confrontation; rebels and household fighters then overwhelmed Caelan’s remaining followers, forcing Caelan to flee into the burning manor.
Tomas, mortally wounded, helped Elianor and the household release the jammed east-gate mechanism, allowing the prisoners, servants, tenants, and wounded to escape Greyfen.
Lord Alric died inside the collapsing, burning manor after the final evacuation, unable to restore the hierarchy he had sacrificed his authority to preserve.
Tomas died in Elianor’s arms at dawn on the road beyond Greyfen after confirming that the last prisoners were free; the healed goshawk circled above the burning manor.
The surviving Greyfen household and tenant refugees left through the opened east gates carrying grain, weapons, wounded people, and copied records while Greyfen burned behind them.
Elianor must reject Caelan’s claims over Greyfen, open the manor stores, and protect the surviving servants and tenants from immediate retaliation after the revolt.
Elianor must preserve and use the copied records beyond Greyfen, working with resistance leaders to challenge fraudulent debts and land seizures.
Elianor must decide how to govern or relinquish the ruined estate, transforming Greyfen’s former hereditary service and authority rather than restoring the old order.

chapters.name: What Remains
chapters.content:
The rain did not stop when Greyfen burned.

For three days it fell over the refugees gathered beneath the alder bank, turning the road to black paste and soaking the blankets borrowed from the manor stores. Smoke drifted from the hill in low gray ribbons. Each time the wind shifted, Elianor could smell wet ash, scorched oak, and the bitter iron scent of blood beneath the mud.

She had not left Tomas’s side until they carried him away from her arms. Even then she had followed the men who bore him to the field beyond the road, where the dead were laid beneath canvas. Mara had spoken to her twice before Elianor understood the words.

“He is not alone,” Mara had said. “You are not alone.”

Neither comfort had reached her.

On the fourth morning, Nessa found her standing in the rain with Tomas’s empty cloak folded against her chest. The cloak smelled faintly of smoke. Its torn fastening had been mended long ago with blue thread, a stitch Elianor had made at the forester’s lodge while Tomas pretended not to watch her hands.

“Lady,” Nessa said carefully, “the children are hungry.”

Elianor looked toward the hill. Greyfen’s southern wing had fallen through the night. The tower remained, black against the clouds, but the roof was gone. No banner flew above it.

“Open the stores,” she said.

Nessa’s expression tightened. “The stores are already open.”

“Then keep them open. Count what remains. Grain first. Salt meat, lamp oil, cloth, medicines. No one takes more because they can hold a sword, and no one receives less because they were born in a tenant’s cottage.”

Nessa gave a short, shaken nod. It was the first order Elianor had spoken as Lady of Greyfen, and it did not sound like any order her father had ever given.

By noon, Pell brought her the first account. He had wrapped the surviving copied pages in waxed cloth and carried them in the leather satchel beneath his coat. The original ledgers were ash. The marriage articles, the creditor instruments, and the seals that had made Caelan master of Greyfen had burned with them.

“Burned paper does not burn a debt,” Pell warned.

“No,” Elianor said. “But it prevents men from pretending the paper is sacred.”

He lowered his eyes. “Caelan’s claim is not only paper. Arbridge money paid the advance.”

“Then let Arbridge bring witnesses, receipts, and honest accounts before a court that does not belong to him.”

Pell looked at her as if she had spoken of flying to the moon. “There is no such court.”

“Then we will make one.”

The first letter arrived before the week was over. It bore Caelan’s seal, though the wax was cracked and smeared. A rider from the north had found him alive in a shepherd’s hut beyond the chapel road, fevered from smoke and with two broken fingers. He had been taken under guard to the old priory at Fenwater, where representatives of the resistance were gathering to decide what justice meant now that the fighting had begun to end.

The letter contained no apology. Caelan called Greyfen an Arbridge asset, Elianor his promised wife, and the servants who had fled “stolen property.” He demanded that the refugees be returned and threatened every tenant who sheltered them.

Elianor read it once beside the cookfire, then handed it to Mara.

Mara read more slowly. “He still thinks words can put a collar on a person.”

“He has always believed that.”

“What will you answer?”

Elianor watched sparks rise into the rain-dark air. “Nothing.”

“That may be taken as surrender.”

“Then I will answer in person.”

At Fenwater, the old priory’s refectory became a courtroom because it had four walls, a dry roof, and a table broad enough for papers. Sella sat at its head beside a discharged soldier named Renn and two tenant elders from the marsh. Mara stood behind Elianor. Pell laid the copied records before them one packet at a time.

Caelan was brought in under guard. He wore a torn coat and had lost the polished certainty that once seemed to cling to him like perfume. His face was gray with pain, but his eyes were clear.

“You have no authority to convene judgment,” he said.

Sella gestured toward the windows, beyond which families crowded beneath patched canvas. “Neither did the men who emptied their cottages. Yet they did it.”

Caelan’s gaze settled on Elianor. “You will confirm the marriage articles. You will confirm that Greyfen’s debts are mine to collect.”

“I will confirm that I signed them,” Elianor said. “I will not confirm that signing them made people property.”

“You were promised to me.”

“I was promised away.”

For the first time, something like surprise crossed his face. He had expected shame, perhaps tears, perhaps the old careful courtesy. He had never learned what to do with a refusal that did not ask permission to exist.

The hearing lasted until night. Tenant after tenant named the labor tallies that had been altered, the grain seized, the boundaries moved by a clerk’s knife. Pell produced copies bearing Greyfen’s seals. Mara named the villages raided under Caelan’s orders. A stable hand described the gallows. Elianor spoke last.

“I was raised to believe that an estate was a wall,” she said. “That if the wall stood, those within it were protected. But Greyfen protected its name before it protected its people. My father feared ruin, and I feared helplessness, and Caelan used both fears as his keys. The ledgers show what was done. The living show what it cost.”

No sentence of death was pronounced. Sella ordered Caelan held until the wider councils of Valedorn could hear the charges. His property claims were suspended. The Arbridge advance would be examined beside every seizure and forged account. It was neither vengeance nor absolution. Elianor found the uncertainty harder than a final judgment, but Tomas had refused the easy purity of a killing. She would not ask the new world to be cleaner than the hands building it.

Greyfen’s surviving people returned to the hill in spring.

The manor could not be restored. Half the roof had fallen; the records room was a shell of black stone; the chapel windows gaped over a floor filmed with soot. Alric’s body was found beneath the southern stair and buried in the family plot, though Elianor could not make herself believe the carved Vey names on the graves explained anything about him.

She did not take the lord’s chamber. She slept first in the old schoolroom, then in a repaired room above the kitchens, where rain tapped the shutters and servants came to her without crossing three halls of silence.

The estate was bankrupt. Its mill was pledged, its pastures contested, its harvest stores diminished by war and winter. Creditors arrived with copies of copies, each insisting that some old promise gave him the right to collect. Elianor answered them with Pell at her side and Sella’s court behind her.

She sold the west pasture to the tenants who had worked it, dividing the price across seasons rather than demanding it at once. She sold the mill to a cooperative of millers and grain carriers. She surrendered the ruined hunting grounds to the village, on the condition that no man could fence them against another. The remaining household lands were placed under written agreements: wages in coin or grain, fixed terms, freedom to leave, and no hereditary service.

The old steward protested. “If a servant may simply walk away, who will tend the kitchens?”

“Someone who chooses to work there,” Elianor said.

“And if no one chooses?”

“Then the kitchens will be empty until the work is worth choosing.”

Some servants left. Their departure hurt, though she understood it was not betrayal. Others stayed, not because a Vey seal commanded them, but because Greyfen was still their home. Nessa became keeper of the stores. Pell taught letters in the schoolroom. Mara traveled between the priory courts, carrying witness statements and warnings of armed nobles gathering beyond the river. Sella came twice each year to inspect the agreements and once to accuse Elianor of being too trusting.

“You still think every lord can be persuaded,” Sella told her one autumn.

“No,” Elianor replied. “I think every lord must be prevented from deciding alone.”

That became the work. Not glory. Not a banner. Forms, hearings, grain measures, boundary stones, testimony repeated until men who had once been invisible acquired names in ink. Noble houses called Elianor Vey a traitor. Pamphlets in the southern towns named her the Ash Lady. In the marsh, children called her the woman who opened the stores.

She accepted none of the names.

At the first anniversary of the revolt, Elianor walked to the edge of the hill before dawn. Greyfen no longer smoked. New beams crossed the kitchen roof, and rainwater ran through gutters made from salvaged iron. Beyond the orchard, the east road shone silver beneath the clouds.

The goshawk appeared above the birches.

It circled once, twice, then vanished toward the marsh. Elianor watched until her eyes watered. She still dreamed of Tomas. Sometimes he stood at the lodge door with the repaired glove in one hand, alive and impatient, asking why she had taken so long. Sometimes she heard the shot again and woke with his name broken in her throat.

She had kept his cloak. His knife. A blue thread wound around a scrap of linen. She had not built him a statue. Stone could not carry what he had asked of her.

Freedom had proved smaller and harder than a monument. It was a widow keeping her cottage. A child eating before the adults. A laborer leaving a master’s field at sunset because the agreement permitted it. It was a court listening when the accused owned no horse, no seal, and no land.

Elianor descended the hill as rain began to fall.

Greyfen remained a place of loss. Its walls were broken, its name distrusted, its future uncertain. But no gate barred the road now. No ledger decided the worth of a life. In the kitchens, people worked because they had chosen to stay, and when they chose to leave, the door opened.

She carried her grief with her, not as a chain, but as a promise kept.

And beneath the rain, Greyfen endured without fear.

set.name: Lady Elianor Vey
set.description: Elianor lives in a repaired room above Greyfen’s kitchens and governs the ruined, bankrupt estate without restoring its old hierarchy. She has opened the stores, protected refugees and survivors, sold the west pasture and mill, ended hereditary service on remaining lands, and works with Sella, Mara, and Pell through tenant courts and written agreements. She carries Tomas’s cloak, knife, and a scrap marked by blue thread; she is publicly condemned by many nobles and honored by marsh tenants, while privately grieving Tomas and determined to turn that grief into practical freedom.

set.name: Lord Alric Vey
set.description: Alric is dead and buried in the Vey family plot after dying beneath Greyfen’s southern stair during the fire. His death left Elianor the ruined estate and the burden of confronting the authority he surrendered.

set.name: Lord Caelan Arbridge
set.description: Caelan survived the chapel shooting and the burning of Greyfen but was injured, with smoke damage, fever, and two broken fingers. He is held under guard at the old priory at Fenwater after Elianor and the resistance suspended his claims; he awaits judgment by wider Valedorn councils and remains defiant, insisting that Greyfen and its people are property tied to Arbridge debts.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: Nessa remains at Greyfen as keeper of the stores, where she manages grain, salt meat, medicine, cloth, and oil under Elianor’s rank-blind distribution rules. She is capable, trusted, and helping the surviving household build a voluntary wage-based community rather than hereditary service.

set.name: Master Pell
set.description: Master Pell lives and works at Greyfen, teaching letters in the schoolroom and advising Elianor on the copied records, accounts, and written agreements. He helped preserve evidence after the ledgers burned and supports the tenant courts, though he remains cautious about creditors and legal claims.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas is dead and buried beyond Greyfen after being shot by Caelan while securing the east-gate escape. His sword was left behind in the ruined manor; Elianor keeps his cloak and knife and honors his final request by pursuing freedom without vengeance or a monument to their love.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Mara lives between Greyfen, Fenwater, and the resistance courts, carrying witness statements and warnings about armed nobles. She is combat-capable, trusted by Elianor, Sella, and the displaced Greyfen household, and continues protecting the new agreements from retaliation while challenging Elianor’s remaining faith in persuasion.

set.name: Sella
set.description: Sella remains based at Fenwater and leads the tenant networks and local courts. She inspects Greyfen’s agreements, protects displaced families, and works with Elianor to challenge fraudulent debts, land seizures, and unilateral noble authority; she is cautious, authoritative, and resolute.
Elianor opened Greyfen’s surviving stores without distinction of rank, organizing grain, salt meat, medicine, cloth, and oil for the displaced household and tenants.
At the Fenwater priory, Elianor and the resistance held a public hearing on Caelan’s claims and abuses; his property claims were suspended and he was held for judgment by wider Valedorn councils.

Elianor sold or transferred portions of Greyfen, including the west pasture and mill, to working tenants and cooperatives, and placed the remaining household lands under wage-based agreements abolishing hereditary service.
Elianor, Sella, Mara, and Pell established continuing local courts and written agreements through which tenants could challenge fraudulent debts, seizures, boundaries, and noble authority.
The wider councils of Valedorn must hear the charges against Caelan, examine the Arbridge advance and related seizures, and determine his uncertain legal fate.
